## 2026-08-28 -- two measured detector escapes from `#489`, FILED because neither costs memory safety

### `gdromlatchreuse` -- reusing another site's warn bit scores 19/19 clean

**MEASURED by the pass-2 measuring seat**, which built the mutant in its own scratch tree:
change `#489`'s new `GDROM_W_TOCLEN` to the existing `GDROM_W_LEN` and the 19-row detector
scores **19/19 -- no row reds.**

The two sites then SILENCE EACH OTHER: whichever fires first sets the shared bit, and the
other's diagnostic never appears for the life of the device instance.  Nothing in the detector
observes latch IDENTITY -- every row asks whether a message appeared, never which bit gated it.

> *** AND THE FILE CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT EXACTLY THIS, IN TWO COMMENTS TWENTY LINES
> APART. ***  `dev_dreamcast_gdrom.c` claims near the mask block that *"a new site cannot
> silently reuse another's bit -- the duplicate-key hazard this project already paid for once
> in dev_sh4.c"* -- while the correction added on 2026-08-28, immediately below it, already
> concedes that C permits an explicit duplicate enumerator and that a raw `|= 0x40` at a new
> site still collides.  **The stronger sentence is the older one and it is the false one.**

**FILED, not fixed, and the reason is the severity ordering this project already uses:** the
consequence is a LOST DIAGNOSTIC, not a memory-safety defect.  `#489`'s four other escapes all
re-opened or admitted something; this one only makes the device quieter.  It ranks below every
live defect in the same file.

**COST TO CLOSE: one session.**  Fire `GDROM_W_LEN` first (a `mov.b` store to `GDROM_DATA`),
then a bad TOC, and assert BOTH diagnostics appear.  That is a cross-site latch row, which is
a shape this detector does not currently have at all.

### `gdromonce` -- the `(once)` suppression marker is claimed in prose and pinned by nothing

`#489`'s decline diagnostic ends `... -- declined.  (once) ]`, and the house idiom is N=1 per
device instance **plus an explicit suppression marker** -- `(once)` being the plurality
spelling.  But the detector's regex is

```python
DECLINE = re.compile(r"Read TOC with cnt=-?\d+, not 408 -- declined")
```

which **stops before the marker**.  Deleting `  (once)` from the product string scores 19/19.

*Not a floor breach: the contract claims "loss of the once-latch", which `latch once` does pin,
and the marker TEXT is not among the contract's claims.  So this is coverage debt in the honest
sense -- an unclaimed gap, filed with its escape recorded, exactly as the floor's "above the
floor, measured escapes are COVERAGE DEBT: FILE them" clause directs.*

**COST TO CLOSE: one line** -- extend the regex to `declined\.  \(once\)`.  The measuring seat
checked that this keeps `latch once` = 1, M3 = 2 and M4 = 0, so it does not disturb the three
rows that depend on it.  **Deliberately NOT done in-round**, because changing the regex changes
what two shipped rows measure and would have invalidated a kill table that was running.


## 2026-08-30 -- `#494` pass 1: the two halves the alt-ctrl round deliberately did NOT ship

### `wdcaltdigin` -- a READ of the Drive Address register returns the alt-status byte

`#494` decoded the offset and declined the offset-1 **store**. It left the **read** path
byte-identical, deliberately: the rung-3 witness holds reads constant so the aliased store is
the only variable, and shipping a read fix under that number would have claimed coverage the
witness was designed not to provide.

*** THE DEFECT IS WITNESSED, AND CHEAPLY, WHICH REFUTES THE RULING THAT IT HAS NO ORACLE. ***
Two adjudications held the read half unfixable for want of a bit layout -- bit 7 high
impedance, write-gate representation, active-low drive/head select. The measuring seat refuted
that by measuring, and the reason is that **the test is an INVARIANCE, not a value**:
`status_byte()` never reads `d->head`, and a Drive Address register is by definition a function
of head select. On the committed build a read of `0x3f7` gives `51` at head 0 **and** `51` at
head 15, while the SDH readback of `0xaf` proves the head write landed and `0x3f6` is unchanged
by it -- so the invariance is not "nothing moved". That refutes every candidate model of
`0x3f7` without naming a single expected bit.

**What is missing is the FIX's oracle, not the DEFECT's.** An invariance proves today's value
wrong without saying what is right, and none of the fifteen PDFs under `_scratchpad/` is an ATA
or ISA document (`ls _scratchpad/*.pdf` is the authority, not this sentence). Pinning the bits
from model memory is exactly the `#357`/`#362`/`#365` failure already paid for once.

**Blocked on `wdcaltownership` below:** if the byte belongs to the floppy controller, the right
answer is not a wdc value at all. Note ACCEPT *is* structurally available here, unlike the store
half -- `case wd_sdh` latches `d->sectorsize`, `d->lba`, `d->drive` and `d->head`, so the device
holds the raw material a correct read would need.

### `wdcaltownership` -- `0x3f6`/`0x3f7` are contested, and the tree documents it from both sides

`#494` rejected narrowing the alt region to one byte and owes the reader the reason.

**The tree says twice that these bytes are contested, and the two statements disagree about who
is being displaced.** `src/include/thirdparty/wdcreg.h` compiles the aux-region offset-1 define
out under `#if 0`, annotated *NOT MAPPED; fd uses this register on PCs* -- the wdc does not own
it. `src/devices/dev_fdc.c` carries `#define DEV_FDC_LENGTH 6` with *TODO 8, but collision with
wdc*, registered at `isa_portbase + 0x3f0` -- the floppy is the one truncated.

*** THE ARITHMETIC IS WHY NARROWING WAS REJECTED. *** fdc's stated end-state of 8 ports is
`0x3f0..0x3f7`; the alt region is `0x3f6..0x3f7`; **the overlap is TWO bytes, not one.**
Narrowing wdc to 1 byte frees `0x3f7` and still blocks fdc at `0x3f6`, which wdc must keep. So
the end-state is a two-device **arbitration** design, and narrowing as proposed would have
fixed half a collision and called it done.

A second reason it is not free, measured rather than argued: an unmapped access faults nothing
and the guest parks normally, but it emits one `non-existant paddr` warning **per access** with
no latch and no counter -- the `floodclass` shape, guest-drivable at default verbosity -- a read
then returns `0x00` silently, and under `-T` it sets `running = 0` on **every** CPU.

**Honest bound:** generic ATA *does* define a read-only Drive Address register at that port, so
the `#if 0` annotation is a PC-mapping decision by its own wording and is unsettled on the three
non-PC layouts this device serves (macppc `+0x160`, hpcmips `0x14000386`, iq80321 `+0x402`).
Whatever is decided must claim only what it covers.


## 2026-08-30 -- the no-VPATH rule names four build trees and the gate enforces three

### `novpadfourth` -- the WSL arc tree is invisible to precommit section B

**Found by a measuring seat, not by a check, and that is the whole finding.** On
2026-08-30 `/tmp/gxsec-build` held a **pre-`#494`** `dev_wdc.c` while `build/`,
`build-asan/` and `est/` all carried the fix. The seat caught it by `cmp`-ing its clone's
donor against `GXEMUL-SEC` before measuring — which is a discipline, not a gate.

`precommit_check.sh` section B compares `build/` and `build-asan/` against SEC because
they sit under the Windows project root and it can walk them. **`/tmp/gxsec-build` lives
in the WSL filesystem and the Windows-side checker never sees it.** So the carrier's own
rule — *propagate every edit into them or you measure a stale binary* — names four trees
while the gate enforces three.

*** WHY IT IS WORSE THAN SIMPLY BEING UNCHECKED. *** Scratch clones are made **from**
these trees. A clone of a stale donor `cmp`s CLEAN against its donor and carries no
sentinel, so the two-part clearance **passes on it** — the stale-binary trap reached from
a direction the sentinel discipline cannot cover, which the carrier already records for a
different route. Here it would have measured `#494`-less code in the very file `#494`
edited, in a round reviewing that file.

**REMEDY, and it is not obviously a checker.** Section B would have to reach across the
WSL boundary, which is a different kind of check from every other one it does. The
cheaper form is probably an invocation in the round-boundary step beside the existing
two-part clearance — structure where the decision happens, rather than a checker that
cannot see the thing it checks. A script exists and ran clean
(`regress/artifacts/wdcaltoffset/killtable_20260830/wslpropagate.sh`, sentinel
`WSLPROP_DONE`); what is missing is the **obligation** to run it.

> ### *** CLOSED 2026-08-30. THE ASSUMPTION ABOVE IS FALSE, AND ONE COMMAND SETTLED IT. ***
>
> This entry reasoned that a checker here would be *"a checker that cannot see the thing it
> checks"*, and preferred a round-boundary habit instead. **The WSL tree is visible.**
> `//wsl.localhost/Gentoo/tmp/gxsec-build` reads fine from git-bash, and a `cmp` across
> that boundary completes in **83 ms**. The check was never written; nothing was ever
> preventing it — and the argument for a habit over a checker was resting on a technical
> claim nobody had run.
>
> `precommit_check.sh` now carries a fourth section mirroring the `build-asan` one: a
> `.MUTANT` sentinel row, then a `cmp` per changed `src/` file, keyed on `${GXWSLTREE}` so
> it is testable without touching the real tree.
>
> **Absence skips for two reasons rather than one**, and the second is new: the tree may
> never have been built, *or the distro may simply not be running*, in which case the path
> is unreadable and nothing is wrong. A gate that hard-fails because a VM is asleep is a
> gate that gets switched off.
>
> **Controlled in three states, on the shipped lines rather than a retyped copy** — the
> control extracts the block from `precommit_check.sh` by grep anchor and drives it with a
> synthetic file list, because this round edits no `src/` file and the real list would leave
> the loop empty:
>
> 1. real tree, in sync → **GREEN**
> 2. a copy whose `dev_wdc.c` differs by ONE line → **RED** ← the control that matters;
>    without it the section is a claim, not a check
> 3. absent tree → **SKIP**, not fail
>
> Preserved at `regress/artifacts/wdcatapistswap/killtable_20260830/CONTROL_novpadfourth.out`.
>
> *And the control's own first draft failed in the class this project keeps recording: its
> `awk` range ended on the block's last **message** and stopped one line short of the
> closing `fi`, so `eval` died with "unexpected end of file". Re-anchored on `^fi$`. **A
> range that ends on prose ends wherever the prose happens to sit** — and the extraction now
> prints its own line count, so a range selecting almost nothing is refused rather than run.*


## 2026-08-30 -- `#495` pass 2: two escapes that are coverage debt, not floor breaches

### `wdcatapistswap` -- the guard's flag operand can be swapped, and no row sees it

Replace `d->atapi_cmd_in_progress` in `#495`'s write-arm guard with `d->atapi_st != NULL`
and it **escapes all 22 rows**. The measuring seat measured the damage rather than
reasoning it: a push/pop pair reads `5a,a5` on both legs before a packet command, and
`5a,a5` shipped versus **`ff,ff` under the swap** after one — refused, empty-ring
over-read.

**The mechanism, read from source:** `atapi_st` is allocated at the first dispatch and
**never set back to NULL**. `wdc_new_command_reset()` zeroes the flag, the phase,
`write_in_progress` and the ring pointers, and does not touch it. So after one ATAPI
command the swapped guard refuses **every ordinary data-port write for the life of the
device**.

**Not a clause-(d) breach by the letter of the DEPENDS-ON bound** — `atapi_st` is not
read by the guarded body, so the operand-swap enumeration does not reach it, which is why
this files rather than being repaired in-round. What it shows is that the detector's
ACCEPT side is unpinned: no row asserts that an ordinary data-port write still lands
after a packet command has completed.

**It is not a contrived mutant.** `dev_wdc.c`'s own comment files exactly this refactor,
recording that `atapi_cmd_in_progress` *conflates two roles* — so a future round
separating them could write this swap believing it a simplification.

**Remedy:** one accept row — an ordinary data-port write after a completed packet
command, asserted to land.

> ### *** CORRECTED IN PLACE 2026-08-30 BY THE ROUND THAT CLOSES THIS ROW. TWO SENTENCES
> ### ABOVE DESCRIBE A STATE THAT CANNOT EXIST, AND THE REMEDY LINE INHERITS THE ERROR. ***
>
> **The narrative:** *"a push/pop pair reads `5a,a5` on both legs before a packet command,
> and `5a,a5` shipped versus `ff,ff` under the swap after one"* — with no command in
> between. A packet-fed panel seat challenged that from the inlined facts alone, and the
> tree agrees: `atapi_cmd_in_progress` has exactly **two write sites**, cleared in
> `wdc_new_command_reset()` and set at the packet dispatch. **No completion path clears
> it** — the completion arm sets `PHASE_COMPLETED` and leaves the flag; the only
> `memset(d, 0, ...)` is devinit. So straight after a transfer the flag is still 1, **the
> SHIPPED guard refuses too**, both legs read `ff`, and the differential as described
> shows no difference at all.
>
> **The remedy line above is wrong in the same way**, and it is the more dangerous half
> because it is an instruction: *"an ordinary data-port write after a completed packet
> command"* names a state the shipped probe's row L already measures as **REFUSED on both
> product legs**. A row built to that sentence would have been VACUOUS — green on both
> legs, shipped looking like coverage.
>
> **THE CORRECT REMEDY, and it is what shipped:** the write must follow a **non-packet
> command**, which is the only thing that produces `flag == 0 && atapi_st != NULL`. The
> reset is the sole writer of `flag = 0`; `atapi_st` has one write site and no clear site,
> so once allocated the disagreement is permanent. The clearing command is **load-bearing,
> not scene-setting.**
>
> **The measurement is not disputed — the recorded STATE is.** The seat's run almost
> certainly carried an intervening command this summary dropped. *And the cited artifact
> (`opus495/wave2/run_q3.out`) no longer exists*, while this entry says "all 22 rows" and
> the ledger's witness field says "20/20" — so the escape figure is re-measured on the
> committed probe rather than carried forward. Found by the fable5 seat; the same sentence
> was corrected in the ledger row, and it is corrected here because a claim gets fixed in
> every place it lives, not only the first one found.

### `wdcprobeendian` -- every wdc rung-3 probe has only a little-endian leg

The write arm branches on `cpu->byte_order`, and every rung-3 probe in this family runs
`evbmips -e malta` little-endian only. A mutant applying `#495`'s guard on the LE path and
omitting it on the BE path **escapes all 22 rows** — measured — because no row ever
executes the other branch.

**The same hole exists for every guard in that switch**, not just this round's: the BE arm
mirrors the LE arm and nothing walks it. Closing it needs a big-endian rig for this
device, which is a rig question rather than a row question. Ranked low because the mutant
is a copy-paste asymmetry rather than a shape a plausible edit produces — but recorded,
because *unpinned by construction* is exactly the class this project keeps finding late.

## 2026-08-30 -- `wdcatapistswap` pass 1: two escapes a seat derived, and a miscount of mine

### `wdcwidth4` -- the width family WAS closed on one side only; CLOSED 2026-08-30

*(The heading read "the width family is closed on one side only" -- present tense, on a row whose body re-dispositions it as closed and whose repair shipped in the same diff.  The `es438` state-vs-substance shape: a reader who trusts headings reads it as live.  Corrected after a pass-2 seat found the heading still asserting the old state.)*

The rung-3 probe's K arm claims *"No single width qualifier can refuse both"*, having made
one injection 2-byte and the other 1-byte so that neither `len == 1` nor `len == 2` can
refuse the pair. **That is true of EQUALITY qualifiers and false of the inequality.**

Append `&& len <= 2` -- equivalently `&& len != 4` -- to the `#495` guard and it still
refuses both committed injections, so every defect row stays green; the accept rows stay
green because the flag is 0 after a non-packet command; and **4-byte stores to the data
port land in the ring during DATA-IN**, which is the defect `#495` removed. The write arm
implements `case 4:` explicitly, so this is a width the device supports and no row
exercises.

> ### *** THE PARAGRAPH BELOW WAS THE FIRST DISPOSITION AND IT IS WRONG. A MEASURING SEAT
> ### RE-RAN IT HOURS LATER AND THIS IS A CLAUSE-(d) FLOOR BREACH -- L2, REPAIRED IN-ROUND. ***
>
> **It was filed on a derivation and then MEASURED**, and the measurement is worse than the
> derivation said:
>
> | leg | G | H | I |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | base (pre-`#495`) | a5 | 5a | 00 |
> | shipped `#495` fix | **c2** | **c3** | **c4** |
> | **E4** `&& len != 4` | **a5** | **5a** | **00** |
>

> the pre-fix build, and the detector scores a clean 30/30 sweep. That is not a hypothetical

>
> `if (X)` → `if (X && Y)` on the predicate `#495` **added**, which **dominates** the edited
> lines, is clause (d)'s canonical form -- and `#488`'s adjudication says so in terms.
> `#495` is closed, so the late-dissent rule applies: disposition 2, a measured false pass

>
> **Repaired with ONE instruction and NO new row:** a 4-byte `sw` beside the existing 1-byte

> **And the probe had no 4-byte emitter at all** -- no `sw`, no `lw` -- so the device's

*The original disposition, kept so the correction can be checked against it:*

Above-floor coverage debt: the detector sits above the vacuity floor and this is a
hypothetical edit in an uncovered cell, not a live defect. **Remedy:** a 4-byte injection

*Derived by the fable5 seat from the probe's own closure claim -- it asked what the claim

### `wdcringresetblind` -- the probe cannot see half of `#479`

`wdc_new_command_reset()` does three things: clears the ATAPI flag and phase, clears
`write_in_progress`, and empties the ring. **Delete the ring-emptying line and the probe
scores a clean sweep**, because on the fixed leg the `#495` guard already keeps the ring
empty at every command boundary this probe crosses, so nothing is left for the reset to
discard.

This is a property of the INSTRUMENT, not of the fix: the ring reset is live and
load-bearing on paths the probe does not walk. Low, because it needs a deliberate deletion
to expose and the offline detector covers ring occupancy from the other side -- the two are
complementary, and this is one of the seams between them. Recorded in the probe's BLIND-TO
list in the same round: a contract that does not name its blind spots is the overclaim
clause (e) exists to prevent.

are GRANDFATHERED pre-2026-08-23 and not counted above)`*.

**The two numbers count different things and only one of them is the claim.** The checker
counts CLOSED ROWS carrying PANEL entries, excluding a deliberate grandfather cutoff. I
counted RAW EMPTY FIELDS over every entry of every closed row, grandfathered and non-panel
entries included. My denominator was never the claim's denominator.

> **This is the session's own recurring defect, committed inside a row about counting: a
> TEXTUAL FORM counted where a PROPERTY was meant.** `outcome` being an empty string is a
> textual form; *a closed row whose panel work is ungraded* is the property, and the checker
> already encodes it, cutoff and all. A count that names neither its unit nor its method
> cannot be checked -- and I wrote one while correcting one.

**And the cheapest check was the one I skipped: ask whether a tool already counts this.**
`seat_scorecard.py` had the definition, the cutoff and the population the whole time.
Re-deriving by hand what a checker already derives does not verify the checker; it produces

**The live work is small and was correctly stated from the start:** ten rows --

### `wdcflagswap2` -- a SECOND operand replacement, and the two-vehicle arm does not stop it

Replace `d->atapi_cmd_in_progress` in the `#495` guard with
`d->cur_command == ATAPI_PKT_CMD`. **30/30, clean sweep**, measured on the extended probe.

**This is not the escape the N arm was built for, and the distinction is the whole row.**
`E3` is `&& cur_command != WDCC_RECAL` -- an *exemption* of one opcode, which the second
vehicle (`ATAPI_SOFT_RESET`) defeats, because one conjunct cannot exempt two opcodes.
**E5 is a *replacement* of the flag operand -- E2's own family -- and the two-vehicle
argument does not touch it**: after both RECAL (0x10) and SOFT_RESET (0x08),
`cur_command != 0xa0`, so the guard is false and *both* accept arms stay green.

**Divergence, derived rather than measured:** `wdc_command()`'s no-disk-image early return
sits *after* `wdc_new_command_reset()`, so selecting a nonexistent drive and then writing
`ATAPI_PKT_CMD` leaves `cur_command == 0xa0` with the flag clear -- shipped accepts there,
E5 refuses. Two stores, and probing a nonexistent slave is what a bus scan does.

Ranked below `wdcwidth4` and filed rather than fixed: its harm class is **over-refusal**
and **transient**, where E2's is permanent for the life of the device, and its divergence is
reasoned rather than run.

> **The honest statement of what the accept arm buys, from the seat that measured it:** rows
> B and M differ in exactly one dimension a mutant can read -- whether a packet command has
> ever run. E2 is the arm's only *unique* kill, because at row B `atapi_st` is NULL, so E2's
> guard is false and B stays green. ***"The accept side is pinned" is measurably false***, and
> the probe's contract now says the narrower thing.

## 2026-08-30 -- two harness findings from the `wdcatapistswap` pass-2 panel

### `relrefstale` -- a relative git ref in a round's artifacts goes stale when the round ships

**Twice in one day, in two files of the same artifacts directory**, which is this project's
own trigger for preferring structure over memory.

* **`runswap.sh`** built its base leg from `git show HEAD~1:`. True when written. An
  unrelated commit then landed on top, pushing `#495` down to `HEAD~1` itself — so **both
  legs would have been built from code containing the fix.** Pinned to `67120fd^`.
* **`killswap.sh`** took LEG 0's pre-extension probe from `git show HEAD:`. True *while the
  round was in flight* — HEAD held the 11-row probe, the working tree held 15. **The round
  then shipped**, HEAD became the 15-row probe, and the script refused a run in which there
  was no extension left to measure. Pinned to `e61ccd8^`.

> **The shape is specific and worth naming: a round's artifacts are written while the round
> is UNCOMMITTED, so every relative ref in them is written from a vantage point the round
> itself destroys by shipping.** The artifact is durable; the reference frame is not.

**Both were caught by the scripts' own guards, not by a reader** — each refused to measure
rather than measuring the wrong thing (*"the two legs would be identical"*, *"there is no
extension to measure"*). A reproduction months from now would fail loudly rather than
produce a confident wrong table.

**Proposed structural fix, filed rather than built:** a precommit check warning when a file
under `regress/artifacts/` contains `HEAD~`, `HEAD^` or `git show HEAD:`. Existence-only,
forward-only from a cutoff. Not built in the round that found it — it owes two negative
controls (fire on a relative ref, do NOT fire on a pinned SHA), so it ships as its own
harness round.

*The population is probably larger. Only two files were exercised today; other rounds'
artifacts have never been re-run, so a stale ref there has not yet announced itself. The
count is unknown and is deliberately not guessed.*

### `smhang` -- CLOSED as already fixed

The row says *"selfmutant.py has NO TIMEOUT: a hanging mutant wedges gate 2"*. It has two,
and they are enforced: `BUILD_TIMEOUT` (120 s) and `RUN_TIMEOUT` (60 s), both
environment-overridable, both passed to a `run_bounded()` helper.

**Verified as enforced rather than merely present**, because this project's recurring defect
is a value that exists and is never used — `kill495.sh` computes `WORDS_OK` and references
it nowhere; `panel.sh` printed *"re-firing once"* and re-fired nothing. Here the chain is
complete: `communicate(timeout=)`, then `os.killpg(os.getpgid(p.pid), SIGKILL)`, then a
bounded drain, then a descriptive failure.

> **And the `killpg` is the load-bearing part, not the timeout value.** The file's own
> comment records why: a bare `subprocess.run(timeout=)` kills only the *direct* child, so on
> the `gcc → cc1` shape the grandchild survives and the gate still wedges.

*Found by auditing rows with empty ledger notes. Of 87 such open rows, **85 are documented
here** and only two were undocumented anywhere — the empty field was schema redundancy, and
the stale STATE was the real defect. Only opening the source found it.*

## 2026-08-30 -- a host-kill class #337 fixed in ONE device and nobody swept for the rest

### `widthkillclass` -- a guest choosing an ACCESS WIDTH ends the host

`dev_wdc.c`'s own `#337` comment states the class outright: *"a 3- or 8-byte access to the
data port used to call exit(1) — a GUEST choosing an access width killed the host process."*
It was fixed there. **The same shape survives untouched in two other devices.**

| device | sites | shape |
|---|---:|---|
| `dev_pcc2.c` | 10 | *"TODO: pcc2: non-byte reads and writes of …"* → `exit(1)` |
| `dev_sgi_re.c` | 6 | `if (len != 8) { fatal("TODO: unimplemented len=%i …"); exit(1); }` |

**Reachability is established for `sgi_re` by construction** — `machine_sgi.c:500` calls
`dev_sgi_re_init(machine, mem, 0x15000000)` and it registers at `baseaddr + 0x1000`, so a
guest store of the wrong width to that window ends the host. `pcc2`'s instantiation was not
checked and is not claimed.

> **Method, stated so the count can be checked rather than trusted.** Comments stripped with
> a state machine first — 40% of raw `exit(` hits in `src/devices/` are inside comments, and
> that rate *grows* as the fork de-fatalises, because each fix leaves a comment quoting the
> exit it removed. Then: a terminating call whose nearest six preceding lines mention `len`
> with a comparison, or the phrase `non-byte`. **That is a heuristic** — a starting set, not a
> defect count. Re-derive rather than quoting 16.

**Why one class row and not two device rows:** the fix *shape* is already settled by
precedent. `#337` chose latched decline with an explicit `(once)` marker — the house idiom
(N=1 per device instance; `(once)` is the plurality spelling at 9 of 14 sites). So each round
here is an **application of a decided design**, not a fresh design argument, which is the
cheapest kind of round this queue has.

**Scope discipline — this must not become one round.** More witnesses create more candidate
rounds, never bigger ones. Each takes ONE site; a second joins only if witnessed, in the same
device and semantic class, covered by the same detector with no new oracle. A device's own
sites may satisfy that; two devices will not. **Next step is a rung-3 witness on one site**,
not a fix and not a sweep.

### `sgirekills` -- and my own brief's premise was the thing that broke

`dev_sgi_re.c` carries **21** terminating calls inside `DEVICE_ACCESS` — seven times the
gdrom file, and the top of the census list. Besides the six width guards above, its adjacent
arm kills on a plain **read** (`fatal("TODO: read from CRIME_RE_TLB_A"); exit(1);`), which is
a *different* class: direction/offset rather than width.

> ### The finding that matters is about the queue, not the device
>
> The `gdromcondlies` brief stated as a premise that those were **the last live
> guest-reachable host kills**. That is false, and the first file sampled from the census
> refuted it.
>
> It was written **as a question** (*"have I confused 'the queue knows of no others' with
> 'there are no others'?"*), which is the only reason it was cheap to catch — and it was
> caught before the panel answered.
>
> **A queue-complete claim is not a tree-complete one.** The adjudicating seat had flagged
> exactly this limit about its *own* answer hours earlier — *"my no-other-live-host-kills
> claim rests on the queue and this file's grep, not a fresh tree-wide exit census"* — and
> the brief inherited the gap anyway. The seat named it; I wrote it down as a premise.

**21 is how many live terminating calls sit in that file's `DEVICE_ACCESS` handlers.** It is
*not* a claim that 21 are individually reachable — `dev_dreamcast_gdrom.c:1055` stands as the
proof that such a site can be unreachable and take a hand-derived warrant to establish it.

### `storesidedead` -- a row that tests "the store had NO effect" passes when the store never ran

*** THE SEED SENTINEL PROTECTS LOADS.  STORES HAVE NO EXECUTION WITNESS. ***  Named by the
fable5 seat in `#496`'s adjudication pass, as a REFINE on that round's own finding.

`#496` added `SEED = 0xdead` so an unexecuted LOAD is distinguishable from a load that
genuinely read zero, and `bit()` returns `SEED-NEVER-RAN` so the sentinel cannot itself be
misread as a set bit. Both are right; both are about the READ side.

**A row whose oracle is the CONSEQUENCE OF A STORE has no equivalent.** If the store silently
fails to execute, the device stays in its fresh state — **and for these rows the fresh state
IS the want.** Seven of `gdrom_cond_probe.py`'s twenty-two: `R5b`, `R5c`, `R7`, `R7b`, `R10`,
`R3`, `R4`. Six others (`R1`, `R2`, `R5`, `R6`, `R8`, `R9`) fail safe, because their wants are
values only a live store produces.

> **Why the controls do not cover it, which is what makes this a class rather than a note.**
> The four control rows catch a WHOLE-RUN-DEAD rig, and they are per-run. The contention
> actually measured on `#496` was **per-session intermittent** — the probe forks one gxemul
> per row, so one row's session can die while every other row and all four controls run fine.
> A per-run control cannot see a per-session failure.

**NOT a floor breach.** Every enumerated mutant still reds when the apparatus runs, and no run
has exhibited the false pass. It is a latent apparatus risk, not a measured escape, so it
files under the stopping rule rather than reopening `#496`.

**The sketch, and it costs nothing for five of the seven:** assert the decline announce —
already in the transcript, count == 1 — inside the same row's `got` string. That announce is
the store's own execution proof; it cannot appear unless the guest store reached the device
handler. `R10` needs a trailing canary decline instead, since silence *is* its oracle.

**`R3`/`R4` are the hard pair and no cheap form is known:** a mid-sequence store death leaves
count == 1, which is exactly the want, so the announce trick is circular there.

**Generality, with the sweep deliberately NOT proposed:** any pty-driven probe in this tree
whose oracle is *"the device state did not change"* has the same hole, because not-changing is
what a dead session produces. The population is unmeasured and a sweep would be `#392`'s
shape. What is proposed is the write-time question — ***for each row, what does a dead session
score?*** If the answer is the want, the row needs an execution witness.

|---|---:|---|

>

> `if (len == 4) { … } else if (len != 4) { … } else { fatal; exit(1); }`.
>
> For every integer `len` one of the first two arms is taken, so the third **can never
> execute**. A round that de-fatalised it would be editing unreachable code and its detector
> could carry no row — the vacuous shape in its purest form. The census is what stops that
> being attempted.

**Honest bound:** reachability is derived from address-decode reading, not measured, *except*
for the WIDTH class, which now has the witness above. DIRECTION, BADVAL and BADOFFSET have no
witness, and a round on any of them owes one first.

**The open scope question this does NOT settle:** a WIDTH guard and a DIRECTION guard sit in
the *same arm* at the same offset and are still different semantic classes. Whether they
nonetheless share one fix design is exactly what the next research pass should answer rather

## 2026-08-30 (later still) -- two findings from farming codex while agy was quota-walled

### `widthkillclass` -- the pcc2 half is HALF what I filed, and the mechanism is verified

I filed "dev_pcc2.c 10 sites" with the caveat that its instantiation was not checked and not
claimed. It is now checked: **5 of the 10 width anchors are guest-reachable.**

`cpus/cpu_m88k_instr_loadstore.c`, under `#ifndef LS_1` — i.e. every **non-byte** access:

```c
	/*  Check alignment:  */
	if (addr & (LS_SIZE - 1)) {
		m88k_exception(cpu, M88K_EXCEPTION_MISALIGNED_ACCESS, 0);
```

**and that precedes `cpu->memory_rw()`.** So a misaligned non-byte access raises a *guest*
exception and never reaches the device handler.

MVME187 is the only machine that instantiates it (`PCC2_BASE = 0xfff42000`), and the handler
does `relative_addr %= PCC2_SIZE` with `PCC2_SIZE == 0x40` — **so an odd register offset stays
odd in all 64 aliases.** Odd-offset width guards are unreachable by construction:

| unreachable | reachable |
|---|---|
| VECBASE `0x03`, PSCALEADJ `0x15`, T1CTL `0x17`, T1ICR `0x1b`, SCCICR `0x1d`, SCCRX `0x1f`, SCSIICR `0x2f` | GENCTL `0x02`, T2CTL `0x16`, T2ICR `0x1a`, SCCERR `0x1c`, SCCTX `0x1e` |

**Class total drops 16 → 11** (sgi_re 6 witnessed + pcc2 5 unwitnessed). The 16 *was* a search
space, exactly as the filing said — and the caveat is why the number could be corrected rather
than defended.

Two adjacent non-width kills are **not** this class: a BADVAL reachable by a *byte* write of
`0x04` to GENCTL (which the alignment rule does not touch), and a BADOFFSET. A third is UNKNOWN
and was reported as UNKNOWN rather than guessed.

### `n6` footbridge -- the design is done, and an ACCEPT round would RED THE GATE by succeeding

**The title says nine; there are eight.** Three numbers are in circulation and each is right
about something different: a comment-aware census finds **10** live `exit(`, **2** of which sit
in `DEVINIT` (`unimpl machine type` — construction-time, no guest chooses its machine type),
leaving **8** guest-reachable. The ninth was fixed by `#432` (`35302f2`), confirmed by
`git log -S`. The title is left unedited — titles are identity strings other records grep — but
no future round may quote the nine.

**Two dispositions across three round-groups:**

| group | n | disposition |
|---|---:|---|
| `+0x188` IRQEnable READ | 1 | **ACCEPT** — documented read, and the model *already computes* `d->irq_enable` then dies. Delete the kill, keep the value, no latch, no message. |
| invalid-DIRECTION interrupt accesses (`+0x180`, `+0x184`, `+0x280`, `+0x284`, `+0x18c`) | 5 | decline + bounded announce. **`+0x18c` additionally must not expose `d->irq_enable`.** |
| SDRAM `+0x100`, `+0x104` reads | 2 | decline + an **accurate** announce: these are legal R/W registers the model does not implement, so the message must say *"unimplemented read"*, not *"invalid access"*. |

> ### The trap, and it is the sharpest part
>
> `gate_arm.sh` contains `check "footbridge: the one-instruction kill arm still dies"` keyed on
> row `K1` — and **K1 is the `+0x188` ENABLE-SET read the ACCEPT round would fix.** The round
> turns a green gate red *by succeeding*. K1 must be repointed at `+0x18c` in the same commit,
> or the round reads its own success as a regression.

And once the *last* live kill is repaired, the probe's failability leg — which currently rests
on a real product defect still being there — must become a mutation leg. That is a planned cost
of finishing the cluster, not a surprise to discover at the end.

**Use a per-site latch bitmask, not one shared latch**, or the first access kind to fire
suppresses the first useful report for every other — `#490`'s measured `M3shared` shape.

### `n6` -- two farmed runs of one seat on one brief AGREED on the facts and SPLIT on a design call

Both ran because a `${j}` in my launch command did not expand, so each job read all three
briefs. The accident bought an unplanned replication, which is worth more than the tidy
version would have been.

**Agreed, and these are the checkable facts:** eight guest-access kills not nine (the ninth
removed by `#432`); `+0x188` is ACCEPT; the four writes to read-only status registers are
decline + announce; and WIDTH vs DIRECTION at the `sgi_re` sites are **two rounds, not one** —
they share an address and a probe but not a semantic class.

**Split 1 — how many round-groups.** Run A said three; Run B said four, splitting `+0x18c`
(a READ of the write-only IRQEnableClear) into its own group because it carries an obligation
the others do not: **the code must also stop exposing `d->irq_enable`**, which a plain decline
does not accomplish. Run A recorded the obligation but kept the site grouped. *Run B's split
is better on the round-scope rule's own text — a site needing a state-suppression the others
do not is not covered by the same fix design — but it is a judgement call and is recorded as
one.*

> ### Split 2 proposes a FIFTH option-set member: `IMPLEMENT`
>
> For the two SDRAM Base Address registers (`+0x100` mask, `+0x104` offset), Run A said
> decline + an *accurate* announce. Run B said flatly **"none of the four offered options
> fits"** and proposed implementing them — reset-zero state, masked write/readback.
>
> **The disagreement is real because these registers are legal and R/W.** The four existing
> members all presume the access is either unserviceable (delete / decline / decline+announce)
> or already correctly computed (ACCEPT). A legal R/W register the model never implemented is
> neither: declining announces truthfully and *still returns a wrong answer* to a guest that
> writes then reads back.
>
> **The addition licence puts the burden on `IMPLEMENT`, and that is the right way round.**
> Additions here are licensed by a measured delta or a transferred warrant, never by "it
> cannot hurt" — so implementing two registers owes one of those: a guest that actually reads
> them back, or an in-tree precedent for modelling an SDRAM sizing register. **Until one
> exists, decline+accurate-announce is the licensed choice and IMPLEMENT is the filed
> alternative.**

A round taking these two sites must answer this explicitly rather than inheriting whichever
note it reads first. Recorded now because the four-member option set is carrier doctrine, and
a proposed fifth member is a **rule question** — which goes to the adjudicating seat at a round
boundary rather than being settled in passing.

### `panelargvcap` -- panel.sh warns about the argv cap, then does the thing it warned about

Measured 2026-08-30 on a 38,983-byte brief. `panel.sh` printed:

> 'Argument list too long'. Trim, or point those seats at the file path instead of piping its

…and then launched all seven seats. Two died instantly:

    codex.txt  ->  ".../codex: Argument list too long"   (123 b)
    kimi.txt   ->  ".../kimi: Argument list too long"    (97 b)

**grok survived because it uses `--prompt-file`** — the carrier already names it the one CLI

> **The defect is that the warning is ADVISORY.** It diagnoses the problem correctly, names the

**The remedy is in the warning's own text and costs nothing:** when the brief exceeds the cap,

### `sgitexindex` -- CRIME_RE_TEX indexes with `>> 3` where its three siblings use `>> 1`

Found by the codex seat under the **standing license**, while answering a scope question
about a different defect in the same file.

**The evidence is the sibling comparison, and it is as strong as this kind of finding gets:**
three arms of one handler do it one way and the fourth does it another.

```c
CRIME_RE_TLB_A / _TLB_B / _TLB_C:  int tlbi = ((relative_addr & 0x1ff) >> 1) & 0xff;
CRIME_RE_TEX:                      int tlbi = ((relative_addr & 0xff)  >> 3) & 0xff;
```

Both index arrays of the same kind — `re_tex` is `uint16_t[112]`, and the window
(`>= CRIME_RE_TEX && < CRIME_RE_TEX + 0xe0`) is 224 bytes, which is exactly 112 halfwords. So
window and array correspond one-to-one, and `>> 1` is the byte→halfword conversion.

**The write loop steps `tlbi++` per halfword, so an 8-byte `sd` writes four entries — but
`>> 3` advances the start index by only one per 8-byte step:**

    offset 0x00 -> tlbi 0, writes 0,1,2,3
    offset 0x08 -> tlbi 1, writes 1,2,3,4   <- OVERLAPS THREE
    offset 0x10 -> tlbi 2, writes 2,3,4,5   <- OVERLAPS THREE

So a guest writing the array sequentially **overwrites three quarters of what it just
wrote**, and the top of the window (`0xdf >> 3` = 27, reaching index 30) leaves **entries
31..111 unreachable by any access**.

`>> 1` is right at both ends — `0x00 >> 1` = 0 and `0xdf >> 1` = 111, exactly the last valid
index — which is what makes this a typo rather than a design.

> **This is NOT the width-kill class and must not be folded into it.** `widthkillclass` is a
> guest *ending the host* by choosing an access size; this is **silent data corruption inside
> a legal, correctly-sized access**. Different class, different fix, different detector — the
> round-scope rule's same-class arm fails, so it files rather than joining `#497`.

Ranked **med**: silent (nothing announces it, and the guest gets wrong texture data rather
than a dead emulator), but it corrupts only emulated device state, where a host kill ends the
process.

**A round owes a rung-3 witness first** — the machine and window are already established by
`widthkillclass`'s witness (`-E sgi -e ip32`, TEX at guest `0xb5001600`) — **and an
adjacent-offset oracle, because a naive "the `sd` changed something" accept row stays GREEN
under this defect.** The write does land; it lands in the wrong cells and on top of its
neighbour. The row must write two adjacent 8-byte groups and read back the *first*.

**Source-derived, not measured.** The seat said so and this repeats it: no probe has been run
against TEX. The arithmetic is checkable from the declaration and was re-verified here against
the three sibling arms, but the behaviour has not been observed on a running guest.

> arms, and both were ALREADY `#119` warn-once latches when this was written -- `if (!w) {
> fatal(...); w = 1; } break;` -- not `exit(1)`.  "Verified by walking each guard's block"
> was not true of those two.  The ten kill BLOCKS cover TWELVE register labels (TxCTL and
> TxICR each carry two), which is probably where twelve came from.  The adjudication's
> "5 of the 10" used the right number.  And the two `#119` latches are themselves the
> `staticlatchscope` class and are folded into the fix. ***

**The same class `#337` fixed in `dev_wdc.c` and `#497` fixed in `dev_sgi_re.c`, at twice the
site count.** The message says it plainly: *TODO: non-byte reads and writes*. The author knew
the width was unimplemented and chose to kill rather than decline.

> `sgidewidth`'s exotic widths turned out unreachable because the MIPS core raises ADEL/ADES.
> No such filter helps here: the killing widths are **2, 4 and 8 — all ordinary, all naturally
> alignable.** A plain aligned 4-byte read of `PCCTWO_GENCTL` needs no misalignment, no
> truncation, no unusual instruction.

**No out-of-bounds** — checked specifically, because a false OOB was withdrawn on this exact
shape days ago: `relative_addr %= PCC2_SIZE` caps the index and an explicit end-span guard
(`OB-11`) covers the memcpy path.

**How it was found, because the method transfers.** All four HIGH rows tonight were in

    dev_sgi_re.c   15 exits  11 rows  4 HIGH    heavily examined
    dev_pcc2.c     13 exits   2 rows  0 HIGH    barely examined
    dev_lca.c      11 exits   2 rows  0 HIGH    barely examined

### `sgideprimop` (HIGH) -- a correct driver drawing a point or a triangle ends the host

> ### *** FIXED -- `#500`, this session.  The row text below is kept as the record of what was
> ### found; nothing in it is retracted. ***
>
> `draw_primitive()`'s `default:` arm is now a LATCHED DECLINE with its own bit
> (`SGIRE_W_PRIM_OP = 1 << 9`).  Live `exit(1)` in `dev_sgi_re.c`: **13 -> 12**.
>
> **Witnessed both directions** (`witness_20260831.out` / `..._POSTFIX.out`): TRIANGLE and POINT
> go `exit 1` -> `exit 0` with `-- declined.  (once)`; the RECTANGLE control is unchanged.
>
> **Detector `regress/sgi_de_primop_probe.py`, 21 rows, gate-wired**, every survival row PAIRED
> with a positive post-draw observable because exit status cannot distinguish declined-and-quit
> from died-with-status-0.  Six mutants measured: floor clause (a) 5/21; the `exit(0)`
> reinstatement 14/21 (red on the `live` rows only); the two latch mutants 13/21 and 18/21; a
> bit-alias onto `#498`'s bit 18/21; and a widened op mask 19/21.
>
> **THREE OF THOSE MUTANTS ARE EACH KILLED BY A SINGLE ROW, AND NONE OF THOSE THREE ROWS WAS
> WRITTEN BY THE AUTHOR** -- they exist because glm corrected which latch mutant escapes, kimi
> pointed out every row ran in a fresh session, and opus5 measured a one-hex-digit mask widening
> that swept the detector clean.
>
> **A2's inertness is the correction to carry forward**: the witness's reset-value case used `x`,
> which is not a debugger command, so it never touched memory in EITHER build and its own grep
> filtered the error.  The detector's `reset` rows supersede it by asserting the DRAW message.


`draw_primitive()` reads its op straight from a guest-written register:

```c
uint32_t op = d->de_reg[(CRIME_DE_PRIMITIVE - 0x2000) / sizeof(uint32_t)];
...
switch (op & 0xff000000) {
case DE_PRIM_LINE:       ...
case DE_PRIM_RECTANGLE:  ...
default: fatal("[ sgi_de: UNIMPLEMENTED drawing op = 0x%08x, ... ]"); exit(1);
}
```

The switch discriminates on the **top byte only**, so the domain is 256 values, two are
implemented, and **254 of 256 end the host process.**

**Reached by two ordinary stores:** write the op into `CRIME_DE_PRIMITIVE` — nothing filters it,
the `case` in the register switch only `debug()`s — then write any DE register with bit `0x800`
set, which makes the handler's tail run `if (startFlag) draw_primitive(cpu, d);`.

> **AND IT IS NOT 254 GARBAGE VALUES.** `crmfbreg.h` defines FOUR primitive types —
> `DE_PRIM_POINT` 0x00000000, `DE_PRIM_LINE` 0x01000000, `DE_PRIM_TRIANGLE` 0x02000000,
> `DE_PRIM_RECTANGLE` 0x03000000. The model implements **two**. So a **correct driver drawing a
> POINT or a TRIANGLE — documented hardware, well-formed value — kills the host.** That needs no
> malformed input at all.

**`DE_PRIM_POINT` is `0x00000000`, which is also the reset value** (`memset(d, 0, sizeof ...)` at
construction). The register's power-on state names a documented primitive the model dies on.

**That coincidence settles a detector disagreement between two seats.** fable5 held a survival
oracle cannot see a spurious `draw_primitive` (the host stays alive); kimi held that against a
pristine register file it dies in `default:` and *is* catchable. **Both are right, conditioned on
register state** — at reset the top byte is POINT, so the draw kills and a startFlagged survival
row catches it; with LINE or RECTANGLE programmed it draws silently and survival sees nothing. A
detector must pin the state it relies on, or the row's channel varies with what the guest did
before it.

**It also raises the stakes on `sgidewidth`.** That round must not copy `#497`'s splice because
this tail draws — and the thing it would draw with is lethal on 254 of 256 ops. A naive splice
does not merely cause a spurious primitive; it gives a *declined* access a near-certain host kill.

**Not covered by `sgirekills`**, which scopes itself to terminating calls *inside a
`DEVICE_ACCESS`*; this one is in a plain function and sits in the census's other bucket.

*Found by reading the kimi seat's 133 KB answer, whose verdict line was the literal words
"verdict line first." — a format miss `seat_verdicts.py` files as "answered, no verdict line",
and which I nearly recorded as a non-answer. No other seat engaged with `draw_primitive`'s default
arm. Third instance this session where the body carried what the verdict line did not.*

*No rung-3 witness yet: the reachability above is **read**, not booted. The lifecycle ruling wants
the attempt before this is recorded as unwitnessed.*

### `gxprobepccache` (med) -- a detector row that could not fail, in the shared probe harness

`gxprobe` skips a redundant register assignment when `cache_regs` is on. `_exec_at()` pops
the cached `pc` after stepping — but a driver calling `send("step")` **directly** did not, so
its next `set_reg("pc", a)` was dropped as redundant and the guest executed **nops at the
addresses the row believed it was probing**.

> A clause-(d) latch mutant swept **14/14** against the row written to catch it. The row
> performed one device access and two nops, so it **could not count to two, and therefore
> could not fail.**

**All three explanations were checked rather than one being picked**, as the
mutant-that-will-not-die rule requires: mis-built? no — the diff removes exactly the two
`d->warned |=` lines and all nine variant binaries have distinct md5s. Target dead? no —
measured directly, three unmapped writes give the fix **1** message and the mutant **3**.
Row mis-cut? **yes**, and the cause was in the instrument.

**It bit only rows reusing one instruction word.** A driver alternating two different words
gets a cache miss on `pc` and works by accident — which is why eight of nine variants scored
plausibly and nothing looked wrong. *A vacuous row reads exactly like a passing row.*

**Blast radius, measured — and my first measurement was wrong.** I grepped for probes calling
`send("step")` and found **fourteen**; then checked whether they use gxprobe at all, and
**none does** — every one rolls its own pty plumbing. A grep for the symptom found the wrong
population; the discriminator was whether the file imports the harness.

**Fixed at source rather than documented.** The seat proposed a rule (*any driver stepping
without `_exec_at()` must pop the pc cache*). Removing the footgun is better: the
invalidation now lives in `send()`, so any command that advances the guest invalidates `pc`
wherever it is sent from. Controlled — `step`, `step 3`, `continue`, `c`, `s` fire it;
`print pc`, `reg`, `put w` and the empty string do not.

*And a separate finding fell out: **`gxprobe.py` is not in version control.** `git ls-files`
matches zero; it lives only in `_scratchpad/`. The carrier tells every round to use it rather
than hand-roll pty plumbing — so the tree's recommended instrument is untracked, covered by no
gate, one accident away from being lost, and this defect would have been invisible to
`git log` forever.*

### `holdmarkermulti` (med) -- the hold-marker check cannot fire on its largest cases

`gen_codex_wall.py` exists because section I requires that every `[HELD AWAITING SEAT: ...]`
marker is also named in the queue — its own docstring: *holding a stage and queueing it are ONE
action, not two*. **Its regex accepts a single `[a-z0-9_]+` seat name.** A marker naming two or
more seats contains commas, fails the match, and is neither counted nor required to appear.

> **So the enforcement is strongest on the smallest holds and absent on the biggest.** A stage
> awaiting one seat is policed; one awaiting all seven is not — and a seven-seat hold is, by
> construction, the one carrying the most owed work.

**Measured, not argued:** `sgirekills` is held awaiting `opus5, codex, grok, kimi, glm,
deepseek, minimax` and is reported in no count.

**The fix is a strict token grammar, and the character class this entry first prescribed was
refuted by the panel.** `[a-z0-9_]+(?:[ \t]*,[ \t]*[a-z0-9_]+)*` — not
`[a-z0-9_,\s]+`, which was **measured to span newlines** and, in a ledger holding quoted
markers, manufactures phantom holds. The grammar also kills a `split(", ")` separator mutant
that survived the character class.

> **This entry also called a quotation in `ledgerstatelies` a "built-in negative control". That
> control is VACUOUS** — the row has zero entries and its quotation sits in a row-level field
> `held_rows()` never reads, so the permissive class this entry forbade passes every control and
> renders byte-identically. *A row filed to document a check-that-cannot-fail shipped with a
> check that could not fail.* Caught pre-ship by four seats independently.

**Known limits, stated rather than discovered later:** a marker wrapped across lines stays
invisible (deliberate — admitting newlines re-opens the phantom surface), and a hyphenated
transport id (`kimi-k3`) would be invisible. No ledger seat id needs one today — checked.

**And the real detector is `--check`, not the controls.** Of nine mutants a seat built, only
reverting the comma is killed by the controls; section I2 kills three more.

*Found while defanging stale markers: the count did not move for the multi-seat ones, and a count
that does not move is not thereby correct — the same tell the carrier records from the stuck 27.*

### `otherkilldeath` (med) -- a DEATH-ONLY oracle, and the round fixed its mirror image
### while shipping this one

`sgi_re_width_probe.py`'s catch-all row captures the transcript and **throws it away** --
`row("other kill", how, "exit1", ...)` uses only how-it-died -- while its six `ld kill`
siblings twelve lines above compute a text membership test and report `exit1+txt`.

> **So the row's note claims IDENTITY — *the catch-all is untouched* — on an oracle that
> observes only DEATH.** Any edit keeping the arm fatal while changing what it *is* passes.

**Measured**, with the prediction filed before building: altering the catch-all's message text
while leaving `exit(1)` untouched scores **35/35 — zero red rows.** The matched control
(altering one *read* arm's text) scores **34/35**, reddening `tlb_a ld kill`. The pair is the
point: it proves the six siblings are failable and this one is not.

**It is the `d_returnzero` lesson mirrored onto the death side.** That was a survival-only
oracle where survival is the shared answer; this is a death-only oracle where death is. Same
shape, opposite polarity — and the round repaired the first while shipping the second.

**Finding it discharged an obligation the two tables never did.** Across all 41 preserved probe
outputs, **seven rows were red under no mutant in either table**. `PRETABLE.out` names their
channel, but no mutant exercising it was ever built — so for those seven the CHANNEL line was
satisfied **on paper**. Six are now measured failable; **one remains blind, and it is this row.**

**Coverage debt, not a floor breach**, and the reasoning is recorded so nobody re-argues it:
(a), (b), (c) pass and the row does red on a null medium; the catch-all is not a predicate the
fix *depends on*, so the bounded (d) closure does not reach it; and clause (e)'s contract says
*silent **removal***, which this mutant is not — **the contract is precise even though the
row's inline note overclaimed.**

*Fix is one line — the text membership test its siblings already carry. Deliberately not done
in-round: editing a shipped detector row means re-measuring, and the stopping rule fixes only
measured false passes and wrong records. This is a row weaker than its note claimed, and the
note has been corrected to say so.*

### `gatedevicesplit` (low) -- filed because a comment already claimed it was

The `#497` gate comment ended *"the right answer is a `gate_devices.sh` split ... **Filed,
not done**"* -- **and it was not filed.** No ledger row, no queue entry, under any
phrasing. Caught by the pass-2 seat while that comment was still **staged**.

> *That is the gap-closes-itself shape: a claim that a process step is complete, shipping
> in the same commit as the thing it excuses. A future reader greps for the row, finds
> nothing, and cannot tell whether the split was considered and rejected or forgotten.*

**And the precedent claim was one step short**, which the same seat measured. I wrote that
`gate_arm.sh` already runs footbridge and PIT probes, *"neither an ARM instruction test"*
-- true, **but both run `-E cats`, this gate's own ARM machine**, and the PIT wiring
comment says outright that it was placed there *because* "this is the only gate whose
machine it shares." So `#497`'s probe is **not** the third instance of an existing
accretion -- it is the **first probe in this gate on a foreign machine AND CPU family.**
My words were true; my implication was generous to my own decision.

**Forcing criterion, so this cannot sit forever:** *the next device probe wired into
`gate_arm.sh` converts this from FILED to OWED.* The accretion story guarantees each
addition makes the next cheaper, which is how a least-bad accommodation becomes permanent.

**Operational cost, named rather than left to be discovered:** a red row in `gate_arm` can
now mean an SGI/MIPS device regression -- an attribution trap for whoever reads the

### `agyreservation` (med) -- the owner's ruling lives in the carrier as PROSE, and
### `panel.sh` fired the seat anyway within two hours

The owner ruled on 2026-08-30 that **agy is RESERVED FOR MEASUREMENT and held out of routine
panels** — it is the only compile-and-measure seat *not* behind the Agent-tool transport, and
therefore the roster's insurance against the outage that once cost a round all its measuring
capacity at once.

**The ruling was written into the carrier. `panel.sh` was not touched.**
`grep -ci 'reserved for measurement' panel.sh` returns **0**, its AGY block is unconditional,
and `panel_20260830_214531/agy.txt` is an 11 KB answer from a routine panel fired *after* the
ruling.

> *This is the carrier's own structure-first finding, measured against itself: knowing a rule
> and having it fire on the right object are different problems, and only the second is solved
> by writing more. A rule that earns its second instance while sitting in that file has proven
> it was mis-filed as prose. **This one earned its first in under two hours.***

**The fix follows the `OLLAMA4` precedent, and that precedent's warning is the load-bearing
part:** a variable, plus a conditional **banner, launch, seat check and verdict roster**. The
carrier records why all four — blanking the variable alone once left a *phantom seat that
answered the seat check*. The agy hazard inverts: a missing seat would read as a **failure**
where the truth is a deliberate omission.

**And that distinction is the ruling's whole cost clause:** a seat *deliberately not fired* is
a different thing from a seat *failure*, and a different thing again from *agreement*.
Conflating them is what the seat ledger exists to refuse — so the check must print
**DELIBERATELY NOT FIRED** by name, every panel.

*Deferred, not forgotten: a panel was running when this was found, and bash reads scripts
incrementally by byte offset, so editing `panel.sh` mid-run corrupts that run. The urge to
edit arrives exactly when you are watching it run, which is why the rule exists.*

### `witnesssilent` (low) -- 13 witnesses are ungated by design, so a rotted one looks
### exactly like a working one

`check_probe_wiring.py` reports **13 witnesses correctly ungated** -- and *correctly* is
the right word. Gating a witness would **manufacture** a regression, because a witness is
built to INVERT after its fix: `#496`'s reads 15/15 pre-fix and 11/15 post-fix, and its
record says so.

> **But ungated means unrun, and unrun means a witness whose arms rot is indistinguishable
> from one that works.**

`n6` supplies the concrete instance: `fbpending_witness.py` scores a row on a death at the
very site `n6`'s ACCEPT round removes, and **no gate runs it** -- so when that round ships,
the witness breaks on disk and nothing anywhere says so.

**The remedy is not an invention.** `fbpending_drain_probe.py` already carries `EXPECT_CAP`
defaulting to `-1 = report only`, its scoring gated on `EXPECT_CAP >= 0`. Run-but-do-not-
score exists, is understood, and supplies the transferred warrant the addition licence
requires -- that plus a measured instance, never *it cannot hurt*.

**And it is harder than it looks, which is why this is filed rather than built.** A witness
is *supposed* to change score after its fix lands, so report-only output is **noisy by
construction**: a flipped row is the expected inversion, or a real break, and the raw
output cannot tell them apart. Making it useful means each witness recording its
**expected post-fix score** -- a change to what every witness in the tree must carry, which
is an owner decision rather than a round's.

*Ranked LOW deliberately: apparatus about apparatus, competing with four open HIGH rows
that are live host kills. Filed so `n6` can name it rather than discover it.*

### `fbfiqsilent` (med) -- the FIQ column lies quietly where the IRQ column kills

`n6` is about to ACCEPT the `+0x188` IRQEnable read on the warrant that the DC21285 prose
makes it a documented read-only register. **That same prose covers `188h` and `288h`
jointly** — and `case FIQ_ENABLE_SET:` has a write arm and then `break;`, with **no read arm
at all**. Verified by opening the file. A guest that sets FIQ bits and reads them back gets
**zero: wrong value, no kill, no announce.**

> **It is not in the eight-kill census, and that is the point.** Same semantic class, same
> one-line fix shape, same row shape — differing only in that the IRQ column *kills* where
> the FIQ column *lies quietly*. Shipping the IRQ accept while leaving its FIQ twin silently
> wrong and unnamed is exactly the asymmetry the sibling-parity line exists to catch.

**And it is a COLUMN, not a site:** `FIQ_ENABLE_CLEAR`'s read side is also a silent constant
zero while its IRQ twin kills. Worth **one sentence** in the decline round's `PRETABLE.out`
rather than five separate discoveries later.

*Found by the sibling-parity check firing at DESIGN time, which is where it is supposed to
fire — while adjudicating a different question about round ordering.*

### `sgideoob` -- ~~WITHDRAWN~~: a FALSE out-of-bounds, filed and refuted the same evening
### found it

> *** WITHDRAWN. The arithmetic below skips one line and that line refutes it. ***
> `relative_addr &= ~CRIME_DE_START` (`0x0800`) runs **immediately before** the index
> computation, so `relative_addr` is capped at `0x7ff`, `regnr` at **511**, and
> `regnr+1` at **512** -- in a `[DEV_SGI_DE_LENGTH / sizeof(uint32_t)]` = `[1024]`
> array. **512 slots of headroom.** The `mte_reg` twin is identical.
>
> **The real class is narrower and better stated:** *is the array sized to the INDEX
> RANGE or to the FULL WINDOW?* Sized to the index range and the `+1` overflows
> (`re_linear_a[32]`, `re_tlb_x[256]`); sized to the full window and the over-sizing is
> what prevents it. Kept rather than deleted so the next reader finds the refutation
> instead of re-filing the row.

The original text follows.

`DEVICE_ACCESS(sgi_de)`'s `len==8` arm writes **both** `de_reg[regnr]` and `de_reg[regnr+1]`
into `uint32_t de_reg[DEV_SGI_DE_LENGTH / sizeof(uint32_t)]`. At the top of the window,
`regnr+1` indexes one past the end.

**Same shield and same trap as `sgilinearoob`.** Guest paths cannot reach it — an 8-byte
access must be 8-aligned and the top offset is only 4-aligned — but the debugger's `put d`
prints a warning and **proceeds**. That does **not** give this row a witness; **it takes one
away.** A `put d` reproduction bypasses the guest instruction path entirely and would be
laundering rather than witnessing.

> **The shape is now a class, not a coincidence.** `sgilinearoob` (`re_linear_[ab][tlbi+1]`
> into a `[32]`), the TLB arms' unmasked loop increment, and now `de_reg[regnr+1]`: three
> sites, one form — **a store whose arity is fixed by the ACCESS WIDTH while its index is
> bounded only by the OFFSET MASK.** A future round should ask whether the bound belongs at
> the index computation rather than at each store.

*Surfaced by the adjudicating seat while designing `sgidewidth`, and explicitly kept out of
it: that round's decline does not touch the `len==8` arm, so folding it in would be scope
creep rather than adjacency.*

### `exitcensus` (med) -- the reachability bucket over-counted by 14.4%, and I had just
### declared this tool free of exactly this defect

`exit_census.py`'s **per-file totals are correct**. Its **BY-ENCLOSING-CONSTRUCT split was
not**, and that is the half that ranks.

`MARK` is `^(DEVICE_ACCESS|DEVINIT|DEVICE_TICK|static\s)`. A plain **non-static** function
definition -- `void draw_primitive(...)`, `void do_mte_transfer(...)` -- is therefore not a
boundary, so every terminating call inside one was attributed to the preceding
`DEVICE_ACCESS`.

> **That bucket is a REACHABILITY CLAIM used to rank defects** -- the tool tags it, in its own
> words, *"on a guest access path BY CONSTRUCTION"*. Over-counting it over-states how many
> host kills a guest can actually reach.

Measured tree-wide over `src/devices` (118 files, 172 live calls):

```
DEVICE_ACCESS    97 -> 83     a 14-call, 14.4% over-count
static           51 -> 13     the same defect from the other side: a plain function
                              FOLLOWING a static one was inheriting `static`
```

**Controlled against a hand-derived fixture.** `dev_sgi_re.c`'s true split was derived by hand
and independently reproduced by two seats: `DEVICE_ACCESS` **15** (sgi_re 13 + sgi_de 1 +
sgi_mte 1), plain functions **6** (draw_primitive 1 + do_mte_transfer 5). Before the fix the
tool put all 21 in `DEVICE_ACCESS`; after it, exactly 15/6.

**The first draft of the fix had a defect of its own, caught before shipping**: the new
pattern also matched `DEVICE_ACCESS(foo)` lines, giving two marks at one offset. Harmless
*today* -- at equal offset the `DEVICE_ACCESS` label sorts last and wins -- but that is a
silent dependence on sort order inside a tool whose output ranks defects. Excluded; duplicates
measured 0 across five files.

**Consequence already in the tree:** `sgirekills`' title read *"21 terminating calls inside
DEVICE_ACCESS"*, taken faithfully from the wrong figure. Corrected.

*The honest shape: I diagnosed this defect correctly by hand this evening, then wrongly
concluded the shipped tool did not have it -- because I checked the number people quote
(per-file) rather than the number that ranks (per-construct).*

> left empty, repaired at exactly the address the mutant had used, leaving the symmetric cell
> open for the next pass.  Pass 1 found *width* unpinned, pass 2 *component*, pass 3 *direction*
> AND *position*.  The measuring seat's warning is the reason pass 4 is shaped differently:
> *"adding two more rows at the corner I just named will produce a fourth."*
>
> So pass 4 does not patch cells.  It enumerates the catch-all's FIVE INPUTS -- `relative_addr`
> (component AND position within it), `writeflag`, `len`, `idata`, `d->warned` -- closes every
> cell in one diff, and writes into the probe's CONTRACT which cells are covered and which are
> **deliberately not**, so a later escape is *"outside the contract, as stated"* rather than a
> fourth breach.
>
> **GATE, at 50 rows, run ALONE and IN FULL: PASS -- 506 checks, 0 FAIL, rc=0, with
> `sgi_re unmapped rows emitted/green/red` at 50/50/0 and both L2 repair rows green.**  Log at
> `regress/artifacts/sgireunmapped/killtable_20260831/pass4/gate_arm_pass4_50rows.log`.  That was
> the round's one KNOWN GAP -- the gate had passed at 48 rows and had not been re-run after the L2
> repair -- and it is now closed.  Pass 4 owes only its pass 5.
>
> **`M2` is this project's own newest rule un-transferred by one hop**, and that is the part
> worth carrying: the carrier says an accept row at a window's BASE tests the near bound twice
> and the far bound never.  That was applied to the six named windows IN THIS VERY FILE and not
> to the catch-all's first component, whose four rows all sat at the base.  One hex digit --
> `>= CRIME_RE_LINEAR_A` to `- 0x10` -- swept 36 rows clean.
>
> **And the gate defect is the one a green probe could never show.**  Both rows added by pass 2
> were named exactly 16 characters; the probe prints names through `%-16s` and the gate's
> per-row pattern needs two spaces.  `got=0` against `want=1` **on a fully green build** --
> found by two seats independently, and shipped because the gate SCRIPT was never run after the
> rows were added, only the probe.  Repaired structurally: `row()` now asserts
> `len(name) <= 15`.


`DEVICE_ACCESS(sgi_re)`'s final `else` -- the unmatched-address arm -- prints a `fatal()`
per direction and then `exit(1)`, **with no width predicate at all.** Every other kill in
that handler needs the guest to choose an unusual access WIDTH (the six `len != 8` arms) or
a DIRECTION (the six read arms). This one needs neither: **any width, either direction, any
unmatched address.**

**The door, derived rather than asserted.** `memory_device_register` covers
`baseaddr + 0x1000` for `DEV_SGI_RE_LENGTH` = `0x1000`, and the handler restores the full
offset with `relative_addr += 0x1000`, so the dispatched range is `0x1000-0x1fff`. The six
windows occupy `0x1000-0x17ff` with one internal gap:

```
  TLB_A     0x1000-0x11ff        TEX       0x1600-0x16df
  TLB_B     0x1200-0x13ff        LINEAR_A  0x1700-0x177f
  TLB_C     0x1400-0x15ff        LINEAR_B  0x1780-0x17ff

  UNCOVERED 0x16e0-0x16ff   (32 bytes)
            0x1800-0x1fff   (2048 bytes)   = 2080 bytes -> exit(1)
```

Guest KSEG1: a single `lb` at **`0xb5001800`** ends the host process.

> *** IT SURVIVES BOTH ROUNDS THAT LOOK LIKE THEY WOULD FIX IT, WHICH IS WHY IT IS FILED
> BEFORE THE NEXT COMPLETENESS SENTENCE SHIPS. *** `#497` repairs the six WIDTH guards and
> never reaches this arm. `sgirekills` as scoped repairs the six READ arms *inside* the
> windows and never reaches it either. A reader of either round record could reasonably
> conclude the device no longer kills on a stray access. **It does.**

**Its fix cannot be ACCEPT**, and that is what keeps it out of `sgirekills`' round rather
than a scheduling preference: nothing backs an unmapped address, so there is no stored value
to return. DECLINE plus a latched `(once)` announce -- a different fix design, so the
round-scope rule's same-fix-design arm fails.

**Witness: none yet, and it is ONE ROW on an existing script.** The machine, window and
harness all exist from `widthkillclass`'s witness (`-E sgi -e ip32`); add one `lb` at
`0xb5001800` and expect `exit1` with `[ sgi_re: unimplemented read from address 0x1800 ]`.

*Found by the adjudicating seat while RANKING the other four `sgi_re` rows -- not by looking
for it. An earlier audit had listed this arm as "1 unhandled offset fallback" and never
asked whether it was reachable. **A census that enumerates a site without ranking it is how
the widest door stays open.***

### `sgidewidth` (high) -- a SEVENTH live width kill, one guest `sb` away

The scope question on `#497` was hiding it. `grep -n 'len = %i not implemented'
src/devices/dev_sgi_re.c`:

```c
	} else {
		fatal("sgi_de: len = %i not implemented\n", len);
		exit(1);
	}
```

The `else` of an accept set of `{4, 8}` — so **len ∈ {1,2,3,5,6,7} ends the host process**,
and a single guest `sb` to the DE window does it.

**It does not join `#497`, and the reason is the joining clause working rather than being
dodged:** different registered device (`sgi_de`, its own `memory_device_register`), accept set
`{4,8}` not `{8}`, and — the part that settles it — **its registers are READABLE**, so its
accept rows read back through `odata` while `sgi_re`'s read back through debug lines. Second
fix shape, second row species.

> **But it MUST be named in `#497`'s PRETABLE and round record.** A round called
> `widthkillclass` that fixes six of seven live width kills *in the same file* and does not say
> so writes the false-unanimity record the late-dissent rule forbids.

The four handlers share one `struct sgi_re_data` from a single malloc, so whatever latch
infrastructure `#497` lands is already reachable here — the fix is cheap once the witness
exists, and the witness is one row away using `#497`'s own script.

### `sgimtewidth` (med) -- a one-byte store silently ZEROES the adjacent register

`if (len == 4) {…} else if (len != 4) {…} else {…}`. The second arm is reached by **every**
width that is not 4, including 1 and 2:

```c
	d->mte_reg[regnr+1] = idata >> 32;
	d->mte_reg[regnr]   = idata;
```

For a one-byte store `idata` is a byte, so `idata >> 32` is **0** — the store clobbers
`mte_reg[regnr+1]` with zero. No diagnostic, no decline: the device quietly loses a register
the guest never addressed. A mis-service, not a kill, which is why it is med.

> ### The trap, and it is why this is filed now rather than when someone touches it
>
> The dead third arm is `fatal("[ sgi_mte: UNIMPLEMENTED read/write len %i ]"); exit(1);` —
> unreachable for every integer `len`, as `sgirekills` records. **It documents an intent to
> reject unusual widths.** A naive future repair of the unreachable-arm defect — reordering to
> `len==4 / len==8 / else` — would **resurrect that `exit(1)` as a live width kill.**
>
> So when the unreachable arm is worked it must land as a DECLINE, never a revived exit.

*Two defects in one arm structure pointing opposite ways: today it serves widths it should
refuse, and the obvious tidy-up would make it kill on widths it currently serves.*

### `sgilinearoob` (med) -- the width guard `#497` removes is holding an OOB WRITE shut

Found by the opus5 seat while auditing whether `len != 8` should be declined or *implemented*.
Every element re-verified by opening the file.

Both LINEAR arms compute `int tlbi = ((relative_addr & 0x7f) >> 2) & 0x1f;` — so `tlbi` ranges
**0..31** — then write **both** `[tlbi]` and `[tlbi+1]` into `uint32_t re_linear_a[32]` /
`re_linear_b[32]`. **At `tlbi == 31` the second store writes index 32, one past the end.**

> **It is unreachable today for exactly one reason: `len == 8` forces 8-byte alignment.**
> `(0x78 & 0x7f) >> 2` = 30, so the largest reachable `tlbi` is 30 and `tlbi+1` is 31 — the
> last valid index. Permit `len == 4` and offset `0x7c` gives `(0x7c & 0x7f) >> 2` = **31**,
> and index 32 is written.

From the declaration order (`re_tlb_a`, `re_tlb_b`, `re_tlb_c`, `re_tex`, `re_linear_a[32]`,
`re_linear_b[32]`, `de_reg[]`): `re_linear_a[32]` overlays `re_linear_b[0]`, and
`re_linear_b[32]` overlays the start of `de_reg[]` — **a different engine's registers**. That
is a layout fact, not a guarantee: a struct reorder changes *which* field is hit, not whether
the write is out of bounds.

**This is why `#497` must DECLINE rather than IMPLEMENT**, and it converts a stylistic
preference into a measured-from-source argument. The brief asked whether `len != 8` is
"secretly an IMPLEMENT case." It is not — implementing narrower widths at the LINEAR arms
would **make this OOB live**.

**And it is the second such fact in the same audit.** The TLB/TEX store loop reads
`data[hwi]*256 + data[hwi+1]`, so a `len == 1` access reads `data[1]` — one byte past the
*caller's* buffer. Two different over-reads, both held shut by the same guard, neither noticed
until a seat was asked whether the guard could be relaxed.

**The round owes a sentence, not a row.** `#497` does not touch these lines and cannot make
the OOB live — a latched decline keeps `len == 8` mandatory. What it owes is a comment at the
site saying *why* the guard is mandatory, so a future round reading "unimplemented width" as
an invitation to implement one is warned where the decision happens.

*Source-derived, not measured: no probe has driven a 4-byte LINEAR access, because the shipped
code kills the host before reaching the store. It cannot be witnessed without first
introducing the defect.*
