### `lcaconfwidth` (low) -- filed 2026-08-31: the kill diagnostic can name a value that would not have killed

`dev_lca.c`'s `LCA_IOC_CONF` guard is:

```c
if (idata & ~1) {
        fatal("TODO: Write to unimplemented bit of IOC_CONF: 0x%x\n", (int)idata);
        exit(1);
}
```

`idata` is 64-bit. A write of `0x100000000` has `idata & ~1` TRUE, so the host dies — while
`(int)idata` truncates to zero and the diagnostic prints `0x0`. **The message names a value that
would not have triggered it**, so a future reader debugging the death is told the wrong cause.

That is a WRONG RECORD emitted by product code at the exact moment of the kill, which is the one
place a wrong record is hardest to recover from: the process is gone and the log is all that is
left. The fix is the printf specifier, not the guard.

> #### *** THIS LINE NAMED THE WRONG SPECIFIER **AND** CLAIMED IT WAS THE FILE'S OWN IDIOM.
> #### Both halves are false.  Corrected 2026-09-07, caught by the grok seat answering the
> #### witness-design brief and verified here by reading the file. ***
>
> It said the fix is `` `0x%llx` with a `(long long)` cast, the file's own idiom elsewhere ``.
> **`dev_lca.c` uses `PRIx64` five times and `%llx` never.**  The five sibling arms twelve to
> ninety lines away -- TB_ENA, W_BASE0, W_MASK0, W_BASE1, W_MASK1 -- all read:
>
> ```c
> 				fatal("TODO: LCA_IOC_TB_ENA value "
> 				    " (0x%" PRIx64") has unimplemented "
> 				    "bits.\n", (uint64_t)idata);
> ```
>
> **Note they KEEP the cast** -- `(uint64_t)idata`, widening rather than narrowing.  An earlier
> draft of the design brief said to *drop* the cast, which would have been a third wrong form.
> **The correct repair is the sibling line, copied:** `0x%" PRIx64` with `(uint64_t)idata`.
>
> *A record that names a fix AND asserts it matches the surrounding code is the most costly
> kind to get wrong: it discourages the one check -- reading a sibling -- that would catch it.
> Verified safe to change: no gate, hygiene grep or probe in `regress/` matches on this
> message's text.*

**Deliberately NOT folded into `lcabadval`**, which is about the guards themselves. They interact
and the ordering matters: `lcabadval`'s rows must match the `fatal()` TEXT rather than the exit
status (see that row's confound), so any row written against this arm inherits this bug's output.

*Found by the `lcabadval` rung-3 seat as an aside while answering a different question, and
re-verified by reading the arm.*

> ### *** CENSUSED THE SAME DAY: THIS IS A CLASS, NOT A SITE.  Widened low -> med. ***
>
> **The derivers, because the two numbers answer different questions and only one of them is a
> defect count:**
>
>     grep -rc '(int)idata\|(int) idata' src/devices/*.c | grep -v ':0$'
>
> plus a window scan for those casts that sit in a diagnostic at a site which then `exit(1)`s.
> On 2026-08-31 the first gave **309 casts across 70 device files** and the second **45 host-kill
> sites**, about twenty carrying an explicit full-width guard.
>
> **MOST OF THE 309 ARE NOT DEFECTS AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT** — an 8- or 16-bit register loses
> nothing through `(int)`. The defect needs BOTH halves: a guard testing the FULL 64-bit value
> (`idata & ~MASK`, `idata != CONST`) AND a diagnostic printing the truncated one. Then a write
> whose only distinguishing bits are above bit 31 dies while the message reports a value that
> would have been accepted.
>
> *** THE SHARPEST INSTANCE, verified by computation and by reading the arm: `dev_pvr.c`'s
> `if (writeflag == MEM_WRITE && idata != 0x0cff0000)` paired with `(int) idata`. *** A guest
> writing `0x1_0cff0000` fails the 64-bit compare and the host dies — and the message prints
> `0x0cff0000`, **exactly the value the code says is acceptable**. The diagnostic tells a
> maintainer the guest wrote the correct value and died for it.
>
> **Severity, reasoned rather than assumed:** none of this changes *whether* the host dies — the
> guards are unchanged. It changes what the log says about *why*, at the one moment the log is all
> that survives. A records-correctness defect in product code, not a control-flow one.
>
> **NOT a one-line sweep.** Which sites are genuinely reachable with a >32-bit datum depends on
> register width and the guest paths that reach them, and a blanket edit to 45 diagnostics is the
> unlicensed addition this project refuses. The honest first round is the ~20 full-width-guard
> sites, ordered by whether a guest can deliver a >32-bit write at all.

### `mtetlbflood` (low) -- filed 2026-08-31: an unlatched guest-drivable `fatal()` in the MTE

`dev_sgi_re.c`'s MTE `switch (dst_tlb)` implements TLB A/B/C and LINEAR_A/LINEAR_B. `dst_tlb` is
a **3-bit guest-controlled field** — `(mode & 0x1c) >> 2` — so values 3 (`MTE_TLB_TEX`), 6
(`MTE_TLB_CLIP`) and 7 reach `default:`.

That arm is a bare `fatal()` with **no `exit(1)`**, so it is *not* a host kill — but it carries
**no latch either**, so a guest looping over MTE operations floods host stdout without bound.
`floodclass` family. The house idiom is `N = 1` per device instance with the suppression marker
in the message text; **derive the marker's spelling and count rather than quoting one** — that
figure has been wrong in this file twice.

**Distinct from `sgideprimop`**, which is the drawing-op switch in the same file and *does*
`exit(1)`. Both are guest-driven `switch` defaults in `dev_sgi_re.c` and a round touching one
should say explicitly that it is not touching the other.

*Found by the `sgitexindex` seat as a residual while checking an unrelated question, and
re-verified by reading.*

### OPEN -- filed 2026-09-01 from `#500`'s pass-4 panel: three residuals the panel raised and
### DECLINED to reopen in-round, plus one cell disclosed as uncoverable

Filed under the stopping rule: none is a MEASURED FALSE PASS against the shipped detector's
floor, and none is a WRONG RECORD.  The grok seat named the first three and said plainly it
was not asking for them to be reopened; recording them so a future round does not rediscover
them as findings.

**`sgideprimopdraw`** -- *** THE DETECTOR HAS NO DRAWING ORACLE, AND ONE MASK CELL IS
THEREFORE UNCOVERABLE RATHER THAN UNCOVERED. ***  Narrowing the `draw_primitive()` selector
mask at bit 24 or 25 -- `op & 0xff000000` -> `& 0xfd000000` -- collapses the two IMPLEMENTED
cases onto each other (LINE `0x01000000`, RECTANGLE `0x03000000`) instead of restoring a host
kill.  Every row stays green, **correctly**: both values are still accepted and the guest still
runs.

Seeing it needs an oracle for what was DRAWN, and there is none to build at reset.  Verified
by reading rather than taken from the seat that raised it: `horrible_getputpixel` returns
early at `if (!(tileptr & 0x80000000))` in `dev_sgi_re.c`, and for `tlb_mode` 0-2 the pointer
is `d->re_tlb_a[tile_nr] << 16`, which is zero on a reset machine.  **So even a *successful*
draw writes nothing any row could watch.**

> *This is a MISSING CHANNEL, not a missing row, and the distinction decides the disposition:
> adding rows cannot close it, so it is DISCLOSED in the probe contract and in the pass-5 kill
> table -- which builds the mutant anyway and PREDICTS ITS ESCAPE IN WRITING, before the run.
> A predicted escape is a measurement; an unpredicted one is a breach.*

A round that gives this device a drawing oracle -- a guest that programs a TLB entry with the
valid bit set, then reads back the tile memory -- closes this cell and the two below at once.
That is the round to file, not more rows.

**`sgideprimrdpair`** -- `rd surv` is the file's one survival row with no positive companion.
The `print v0` in that session IS the START-aliased read, and no row consumes it, so
`draw_primitive(); if (writeflag == MEM_READ) exit(0);` keeps both `rd` rows green.  That is
the `exit0oracle` class -- exit status cannot distinguish *declined and quit* from *died with
status 0* -- applied to the one arm this detector left unpaired.  Settled design rather than
this diff, but it is true of the shipped composite and should be said out loud.

**`sgideprimemptybody`** -- `case DE_PRIM_RECTANGLE: break;` with an emptied body scores
`count(DRAW) == 0` and the guest runs on, so every accept row passes.  The `* liv` companions
catch DEATH, not a silent NO-OP.  Same drawing-oracle gap as `sgideprimopdraw`; it is the
accept side of the same missing channel.

*Provenance: `_scratchpad/panel_20260901_192203_500p4` (grok, codex, kimi).  All three were
raised by seats that explicitly declined to reopen them in-round, which is the disposition the
stopping rule asks for and is recorded here as such.*

**`pcc2defaultkill` FIXED -- #501, 2026-09-05.**  READ side keeps the byte the memcpy served and announces it as

**`pcc2iackmodel` -- SCCTXIACK (0x25) and SCCMOIACK (0x23) have no acknowledge semantics (LOW; AFTER `pcc2c040kill`).**
#501 declines writes there and serves 0 on reads like every other uncased offset; on the real part an IACK read
returns the interrupt vector and acknowledges.  The in-tree model for the shape is the cased `SCCRXIACK` arm
(clears the INT bit, calls `reassert_interrupts()`), which is exactly why this waits: that path enters the
C040 kill, so `pcc2c040kill` ships first.  Also note the SCCRXIACK arm has NO writeflag test (a guest WRITE
acknowledges too) -- do not copy that.  The board manual says a mapped IACK with no interrupt pending can time
out with a transfer error (`vmesbcp2.txt`, 6-33..6-34) -- `return 0` would be a defensible model of THAT.

**`pcc2anngrid` -- the default arm's announce grid (channel x arm x width) has four disclosed open cells (LOW, harness;
clause-(e) coverage debt, every one measured or derived at #501 pass 4 and DISCLOSED in the detector's contract).**
(1) the len-2 WRITE announce is never emitted -- the probe's one `st.h' is latch-silenced -- so a write-value or
width-label mutant scoped to len 2 passes 46 rows (Opus MO2/MO4 MEASURED 46/46): closure is ONE instruction and one
row, `ST_H(7, 0x2c)' in the `dir wr text' session counting `0x2c (len 2): 0xaabb -- declined'; (2) the len-4 READ
value: every aligned uncased word reads zeros (Opus MO1 `data[len>>2]' MEASURED 46/46) -- an `st.d' at T2COUNT would
put 0x99 at 0x14 through the counter arm's raw memcpy, but that route IS the filed `pcc2counter8' defect, so rowing
it couples the detector to a bug: decide with `pcc2counter8'; (3) the announce's OFFSET label is pinned at five
offsets (Opus MO3 `ra < 0x14 ? ra : 0' MEASURED 46/46) -- one `alias msg'-style count per class closes it; (4) every
exact value anchor is EVEN, so `& ~1' on an announce operand passes (codex) -- use odd test values; (5) `alias msg' (the
fold-naming row) has no non-lethal kill in any table -- one fold mutant (`%= 0x80', or the fold removed) would give it one
(the #501 regress review, Fable, 2026-09-05).  All five ride
the NEXT change of this instrument (each owes a table re-run and a gate), which is why they are filed, not rowed.

blocks) and `warned_unimpl` (#501) are per-instance fields, but every probe session is a fresh process, so no
row can distinguish a per-instance field from a function-static (codex, pass 1).  A fixture that constructs two
pcc2 instances in one process and announces from each once would.  Shared with the width chain; filed, not owed.

**`pcc2defaultkill` PROMOTED TO HIGH (2026-09-04 fix review; Fable 5.1 adjudicating, GPT-6 Astra concurring).**
The unimplemented offsets are REAL PCC2 registers the one in-tree guest driver writes: OpenBSD 2.2
`if_ie.c:609` stores `pcc2_lancirq` (IEICR, 0x2a), `:612` `pcc2_lancerrirq` (0x2b), `:655`
`pcc2_lancerrstat` (IEERR, 0x28) -- verified by grep in `_guest-src-openbsd22` -- plus GPIO_ICR 0x18,
SCSIERR 0x2c, the printer block 0x30-0x37, SPEED 0x38 and SCCTXIACK 0x25; none has a `case`, so any
access, READ included, reaches `default:` and its `exit(1)`.  Ranked FIRST, above `pcc2c040kill`, because
that one needs a GENCTL write the in-tree guest never makes.  **RE-BASED 2026-09-05 (Fable design seat,
verified from the tree): `if_ie` NEVER ATTACHES on the emulated mvme187** -- `machine_mvme88k.c:106` installs
`unreadable` at 0xfff46000, the ie0 address, and `if_ie.c:407-409` fails its match on `badpaddr()` there, so
the driver's PCC2 writes never run on this model.  The ranking rests on the RUNG-3 WITNESS and severity (one
guest byte load or store to any of 43 offsets ends the host), not on the driver.  Witness (measured
2026-09-05, `regress/artifacts/pcc2defaultkill/witness_20260905/`): a GUEST `st.b` or `ld.bu` to IEICR ->
exit 1 with the arm's own 'unimplemented' line first; the debugger's `put b` does NOT reach the arm.  Option set for pass 1: DECLINE + latched announce / BACKED ACCEPT (the register array
already backs every offset and the memcpy read path already serves it) / FAULT.

Found by the adjudicating seat while ranking `pcc2widthkills`, and it is filed rather than
folded into that round because the predicate class differs: **offset decode, not access
width.**  The round-scope rule takes one site and admits a second only in the same semantic
class under one fix design; these are two classes in one file.

> **The reason it matters that it has NO ROW, rather than merely being unfixed:** without one,
> `pcc2widthkills`'s contract has nothing to point at when it declines to claim that wide pcc2
> reads are safe.  A round that fixes the width kills and says nothing about the decode kill

Not yet witnessed and NOT claimed to be: no reachability analysis has been done on which

### `clausedbound` -- RULE QUESTION: does clause (d)'s DEPENDS-ON bound admit enclosing-function values?

**2026-09-03, filed by `#500` pass 14 at the measuring seat's request.**  Not a code defect; a
question about the carrier's own rule, and one the seat declined to rule on alone.

The bound, as written: *"predicates DOMINATING the diff's edited lines, walked up only to the
ENCLOSING FUNCTION BOUNDARY; and operand swaps drawn ONLY from fields the guarded BODY reads."*

The case: `|| (drawmode & DE_DRAWMODE_XFER_EN)` on `draw_primitive()`'s latch guard swept the
shipped 47-row detector clean (MEASURED, with a control both ways).  `drawmode` is read by the
enclosing FUNCTION, three times above the switch, and not by the guarded body.  **By the
letter of the bound it is outside clause (d).**

**But the carrier's own exemplar of a qualified condition is `if (X) -> if (X && writeflag ==
MEM_WRITE)` -- and `writeflag` is likewise an enclosing-function value, neither a dominating
predicate nor a body-read field.**  So the rule's own illustration falls outside the bound as
written.  That is the documented exemplar-vs-rule tension, and it decides whether a measured
clean sweep of this shape is an L2 floor breach (repair in-round) or coverage debt (file).

**The detector was repaired REGARDLESS** (`dec regs`, pass 14): the fix is one session and the
flood is guest-reachable on an ordinary path.  What is filed is the RULE, not the fix.

**Proposed reading, for adjudication, not adopted:** DEPENDS-ON includes every value the
enclosing function has computed or read BEFORE the guard executes -- which is what the
`writeflag` exemplar already assumes -- bounded still by the enclosing function.  The cost is a
wider (d) enumeration per fix; the benefit is that the bound stops excluding its own example.

### `tablebasenotfull` -- a kill-table driver that proceeds past a BASE below full score

**2026-09-03, second measured instance.**  Severity LOW (harness practice).

Pass 13 found the table-11 driver's negative control was a comment with no refusal behind it.

and proceeded through all nine remaining cells.  In this instance proceeding was RIGHT (one
known row, nine valid cells, and the canary had done its job), so the disposition is not
simply "die on BASE < full".

**What a driver should do, for adjudication:** say LOUDLY that BASE is not full and name the
rows; continue; and mark every subsequent cell's score as *read with N rows subtracted*.  A
`die` throws away valid cells; a `say` alone is the check-that-cannot-fail shape.  The middle
form -- announce, continue, annotate -- is what pass 14 did by hand and should be the driver's.

*** THE FROZEN-INSTRUMENT RULE IS WHY THIS WAS RECOVERABLE: the live probe was corrected while
the table ran, the table kept scoring its frozen copy, and the two never mixed. ***

### `pcc2c040kill` (HIGH) -- a LEGAL byte write to GENCTL ends the host

**2026-09-03, surfaced by the `pcc2widthkills` pass-1 panel (fable5 and kimi, independently);
the panel found it while auditing the width fix and noted that "ten kills removed" would read as
"file clean" unless this one is cited.**

`dev_pcc2.c`, `reassert_interrupts()` (around `:189-195`): if GENCTL has bit `0x04` set
(C040), the function does `fatal("pcc2: C040 interrupt assertions... TODO"); exit(1);`.  GENCTL
is written by the guest through its own arm at the LEGAL width (`ld.b`/`st.b`), and that arm
calls `reassert_interrupts()` on every write.  So **a single byte store of `0x04` to
`0xfff42002` ends the host** -- no width trick, no misalignment, an ordinary register write.

It was mentioned once in prose under `widthkillclass` as "a BADVAL reachable by a byte write"
with no row id, which is the same gap `pcc2defaultkill` closed for the offset kill.  Filed now
with an id so the width round's contract can point at it.

**ROW-DESIGN TRAP for the width round, recorded here because it is where a reader looks:**
every GENCTL lane value in a width-round row must keep bit `0x04` CLEAR, or a DELETE /
fall-through mutant trips THIS kill and the row dies for a reason not under test.

Witness owed (rung 3, one session): `st.b 0x04` to `0xfff42002` on the committed build ->
`exit1`.  Not yet run; the width round's witness is the template.

### `pcc2counter8` (MED) -- the counter/compare arm accepts an 8-byte write and raw-copies through neighbours

**2026-09-03, found by the codex seat on the `pcc2widthkills` pass-1 panel.**

The `T1CMP / T2CMP / T1COUNT / T2COUNT` arm does `memcpy(d->pcctwo_reg + relative_addr, data,
len)` for any `len` within `PCC2_SIZE`.  The hardware guide lists 8/16/32-bit cycles only.  An
8-byte write at `T2COUNT (0x10)` raw-copies through `PSCALE (0x14)`, `PSCALEADJ (0x15)`,
`T2CTL (0x16)` and `T1CTL (0x17)` -- bypassing the per-register write semantics those arms
implement (masks, read-modify-write, COVF clear, `reassert_interrupts`).  A guest can set timer
control bits through a path that skips their arm.

Not a host kill; a semantic bypass.  Deliberately NOT folded into the width round -- it is a
different defect (accepts too much, rather than kills) in a different arm.  Reachability: `st.d`
to `0x10` is 8-aligned, so it is guest-reachable by construction.


*2026-09-04 (Opus seat, pcc2widthkills pass 8): the labels above were swapped (the header says 0x16 = T2CTL,
0x17 = T1CTL); corrected in place.  And the path is GUEST-reachable: 0xfff42010 is 8-aligned, so a
guest `st.d` lands raw bytes on both timer-control registers -- the width detector's `rb t*ctl b27'
rows now use exactly this path to hold TxCTL bits 2-7 set, and say so.*
### `checkcunwired` -- check C (commit message vs diff) can never run from the hook that exists

**2026-09-03, found while retrying a blocked commit.**  Severity LOW (harness), but it is the
enforcer of mechanical rule 1 -- *write commit messages from the diff, never from intent* --
and it has been reporting `no commit-message file passed -- check C skipped, NOT passed` on
EVERY commit this session, as a soft WARN that nobody reads.

**The mechanism, verified by reading:** `precommit_check.sh` takes the message file as `$1`
(`MSGFILE=${1:-}` at :32) and only runs check C when it is present (:1137).  The installed
`.git/hooks/pre-commit` calls `bash "$ROOT/tools/precommit_check.sh"` with NO argument.  A
pre-commit hook has no message to pass -- git has not collected it yet -- so from that hook
the check is unreachable BY CONSTRUCTION, not by omission.

**This is the check-that-cannot-fail shape with a twist: the check CAN fail, but the road to
it is never taken, and its "skipped" line is soft, so the commit proceeds.**  Passing a
message via `git commit -F <file>` does not help; the hook still does not forward it.

**What works today:** run `bash tools/precommit_check.sh <msgfile>` BY HAND before committing.
**The fix is a `commit-msg` hook** (which does receive the file as `$1`) invoking the same
script -- a harness change owing two negative controls (a message citing an untouched path
must FAIL; a message citing only touched paths must PASS).  Its own round.

### `pcc2widecompose` (LOW) -- per-lane composition of a wide PCC2 write, the faithful upgrade to DECLINE

**Filed 2026-09-03 -- and the round's own record had said "FILED" for hours before it was.**
The codex seat on `pcc2widthkills` pass 2 found the claim in the code comment and the
CHANGELOG with no entry anywhere.  A "filed" that names no row is a wrong record.

`pcc2widthkills` shipped writes as DECLINE + latch because every write arm uses `idata`,
which is the addressed byte only at `len == 1`, and eight arms have per-register semantics
(masks, read-modify-write, clears; seven of the twelve blocks call `reassert_interrupts()`).  The faithful
alternative the pass-1 panel named is COMPOSE: decompose a wide write into `len` byte
accesses, each dispatched through its own arm with its own semantics and side effects.

**Warrant in the tree:** `mvme_pcctworeg.h` says the registers accept 8/16/32-bit cycles;
the read side already composes lanes in address order; the counter arms already accept wide
writes by memcpy.  **Warrant against, measured by a seat:** `_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/
mvme88k/dev/pcctworeg.h:8` declares these registers `volatile u_char`, and the driver code
uses byte accesses -- one real OS shows NO demand for wide writes to the byte registers.

**Hazard, named by the seat that proposed it:** COMPOSE must live INSIDE the byte-register
arms.  Applied before the switch it would route bytes +1..+3 of a legal word write to a
counter register through `default:`, a NEW kill on a working path.

**Reopen condition:** a measured guest (a driver trace, a PROM disassembly) that wide-writes
one of the twelve byte registers.  Until then DECLINE is the honest model and this is the
recorded upgrade path, not a defect.

### `pcc2assertflood` (LOW, floodclass) -- the interrupt (de)assert trace prints on every tick while a pcc2 interrupt is pending

**Filed 2026-09-03 while hand-verifying the `pend2 *' row shape for `pcc2widthkills` pass 6.**
`reassert_interrupts()` in `dev_pcc2.c` prints `[ pcc2: IPL = 1, MASK = 0 => ASSERT ]` each time
it runs with an unmasked interrupt pending -- and it runs from `DEVICE_TICK(pcc2)` every 2^14
instructions plus on every qualifying register access.  A guest that arms timer 2 (compare 1,
count 0, IEN, CEN) and spins saw six of these lines in a two-second free-run at quit; a guest
that leaves an interrupt pending indefinitely floods the log for as long as it runs.  The line
is printed by `debug()` (`dev_pcc2.c`, the `=> %s` line in `reassert_interrupts()`): verbosity-gated at
default settings, so it floods under `-v` and while single-stepping, where `debug()` prints -- a
narrower exposure than a `fatal()` flood, which is why this is LOW.  `floodclass` family; the house idiom is a per-instance latch with an
explicit `(once)` marker, or printing only on a CHANGE of the asserted state (the ASSERT/DEASSERT
edge), which is what the message's own wording suggests it was meant to be.  Not the width
round's business; filed.  Witness available: the `pend2 *' session in `regress/pcc2_width_probe.py`
reaches the state on unmodified `mvme88k -e mvme187`.

### `pcc2iclrdec` (LOW, coverage debt) -- the TxICR interrupt-clear decrement is exercised by no row in the tree

**Filed 2026-09-04 by the kimi-k3:cloud substitute seat on `pcc2widthkills` pass 7 (packet-fed,
reasoning from the inlined TxICR arm).**  The arm's clear branch, `if (ICLR && (reg & INT) &&

a BYTE write carrying ICLR while an interrupt is pending -- and the width detector's `pend* *`

count goes to -1 (or 2) while INT is cleared, and nothing reads it afterwards.  Outside the width
round's clause-(d) closure (the branch does not dominate the diff's edited lines; it is

observe that a second poll never sees INT again (pending consumed) -- and its twin with a
SECOND fired interrupt to distinguish `--` from `= 0`.  Belongs to a timer-semantics round, not
to this one.

Rows `trapfrozenuser` (MODE) and `trapfrozensfd1` (SFD1) added.

*and SFD1*** -- the constant's comment listed only MODE, an L4 corrected in v20: a comment that lists SOME of

## 2026-09-06 — `83df95c` pass 2: the review that commit never got, and what it found

**`wdcconsumedattempts` (MEDIUM).**  In `dev_wdc.c`'s ATAPI accounting arm,
`int consumed = len == 4 ? 4 : (len >= 2 ? 2 : 1);` is computed **from `len` alone** — it counts the helper
CALLS the arm makes, not the pops that succeeded.  `wdc_get_inbuf()` returns `(uint64_t) -1` on an empty ring
and returns **before advancing the tail** (verified by reading: the early return sits three lines above the
advance), so with `q` bytes queued a width-`w` access pops `min(q, calls)`.  When the ring under-runs
mid-access, `consumed` over-counts and `atapi_len` is decremented by more than the guest received.

*** That is the exact defect `#341` exists to fix, quoted three lines above the expression: *"the count
reported has to be the count that happened."* ***  `#341` replaced `len` with this expression, which is right
whenever the ring holds enough bytes and wrong in precisely the residual case the same round was reasoning
about.  **DERIVED, NOT MEASURED** — no witness shows a guest reaching an under-run mid-access on the ATAPI
path, and the over-read is already announced by the `warned_inbuf_overread` latch, so the silent-corruption
claim is unproven.  A round owes the rung-3 attempt.  *Worse observable, unanalysed: the arm accumulates with
`odata += (wdc_get_inbuf(d) << 8)`, so a failed pop folds the sentinel's bits into the value the guest reads,
not only into the count.*

**Corrected in place (L4), product comment.**  The census shipped by `83df95c` stated the eight pop counts
unconditionally; they are **call counts** and hold only while bytes remain.  Now qualified, with the mechanism
and the `consumed` caveat named.  *Two seats derived the same expression and neither noticed it counts
attempts — the seat that went to the helper found it.*

**And a nuance that makes the original round's claim weaker, from the kimi seat:** the wording `83df95c`
replaced — *"a 3- or 8-byte access consumes 1 or 2"* — was **vague, not false**.  The true value is 2, and 2 is
a member of the set `{1, 2}`.  So the shipped trailing note reads as a correction of a falsehood when it is
really the sharpening of an imprecise sentence.

**Claim settled that nobody else could reach:** the ring predicate after `#484` **holds** — `N = 512*513`, the
`(head+1)%N == tail` guard refuses the store, both producers respect it, occupancy stays in `0..N-1`, so full
and empty are distinguishable and `head == tail` means empty.  **No detector row depends on the old wording**,
checked across all four files the commit touched.

## 2026-09-06 — filed from the Codex passes (five briefs, five substantive answers)

**`irqassertedunread` (LOW — filed HIGH off one grep, de-escalated the same hour by the pass it was filed
pending).**  Six CPU families set `cpu->cd.<arch>.irq_asserted`; exactly three are consumed (arm, m88k, ppc).
**alpha, i960 and riscv have no reader anywhere**, and there is no alternate delivery mechanism.  But the three
are not alike: **i960 and riscv are DEAD SCAFFOLDING** — neither executes a second instruction (i960's switch is
only `default: goto bad;`; riscv implements compressed NOP/ADDI and sends the 32-bit branch to `bad`) — so there
is no guest to miss an interrupt and the disposition is scaffold cleanup.  **alpha is a genuine hole at the
CPU/PAL level**: `kentry` is stored with no reader and `PAL_OSF1_rti` is named but unimplemented, so removing
`lcabadval`'s two interrupt exits leaves *both* forwarding and delivery unfinished.  *Corrected my census:
`cpu_dyntrans.c` also delivers MIPS and SH interrupts through differently-named state, invisible to a
single-identifier grep — the correlate-not-the-class shape.*  Source-derived, no guest boot run.

**`lunancpus3` (LOW).**  `luna_absentcpu_probe.py` boots only `-n 1`, `-n 2` and `-n 4` — all powers of two — so
any `ncpus`-dependent fold that is the identity there is invisible to every row.  **kimi NAMED this family on
pass 5 before a member existed**; a member is now MEASURED: `cpu < (d->ncpus & -d->ncpus)` scores **37/37, a
total escape** (`killtable6_codexpred/`).  Disposition unchanged and disclosed: clause-(e) debt, not a clause-(d)
breach — the bit-trick does not *read* like the same check, and every single-token weakening of that bound is
rowed and dies.  **Closure is one `-n 3` session and closes the whole family**; check first that `-n 3` boots the
committed rig.

**`m88ksfd1row` (LOW — a RULE QUESTION for the 2026-09-09 adjudication, not a defect).**  Does the ADDITION
LICENCE authorise a detector row with **zero measured delta** whose benefit is telling you *which* axis fired?
`#502`'s `trapfrozensfd1` is redundant against its own mutant (58/58 without it), and codex ruled the attribution
warrant does not transfer — the anchor rule repairs *self-comparing* oracles, and row demand is bounded "per
enumerated mutant, never per attribution need".  **Kept pending adjudication on the same seat's own next

## 2026-09-07 — three rows filed from the `#504` triage pass

**`sgirebufuninit` (HIGH — `dev_sgi_re.c`: `uint8_t buf[8]` is never initialised, and the guest picks how
many of its bytes are used).**  `horrible_getputpixel()` declares the buffer with no initialiser and no
`memset`.  Two independent fields of ONE guest-written mode word decide how much of it is used —
`color_mode = mode & DE_MODE_TYPE_MASK` (bits 4-7) says how many bytes an arm FILLS, and
`bufdepth = 1 << ((mode >> 8) & 3)` (bits 8-9) says how many are TRANSFERRED — and **nothing anywhere makes
them agree**; `grep -rn '>> *8) *& *3' src/devices/` finds the decode, its own `#100` comment and the two
XFER siblings, and no guard.  Two reachable paths in opposite directions: a **PUT** writes bytes no colour
arm assigns into guest-visible memory, and a **GET** builds a 32-bit colour out of bytes the read never
filled, which `draw_primitive()` then stores.

*** THE PROVENANCE IS THE SHARPEST PART: `#95` WAS THIS FORK'S "central uninit-leak fix" CLAIMING TO CLOSE
*THE WHOLE CLASS*, AND `#100` IN THE SAME BATCH EDITED THIS EXACT ARRAY. ***  `#100` grew it `buf[4]`→`buf[8]`
because the guest can demand 8 bytes — fixing a stack OVERFLOW — and never asked what fills the bytes it had
just added.  `#95` zeroes device **READ** buffers for `len` bytes, so it cannot reach a `MEM_WRITE` and cannot
reach bytes past `len`.

**PASS 1 CORRECTED MY OWN FRAMING, AND THE CORRECTION MADE IT WORSE.**  The brief drove the PUT path with mode
`0x1320` (depth field 3).  The grok seat objected that the header documents only `DE_MODE_BUFDEPTH_8/16/32`
and **field 3 is undocumented** — verified against `crmfbreg.h` before being accepted — so my vehicle was the
weak one, while `DE_MODE_TYPE_CI` (colour type **zero**, the reset value) assigns only `buf[0]` and
`BUFDEPTH_32` transfers four, making **`0x1200` a fully documented leak of `buf[1..3]`**.  The same seat
settled the question the brief had left open: **the destination is RAM, not a device**, so `#95`'s pre-zero
does not run *at all* on either path.  Severity is under active adjudication — grok argues MEDIUM, and that
call is held until the full roster lands rather than taken from one seat.

**`sgiwidthwiredobl` (LOW — `sgi_re_width_probe.py`'s contract states an obligation that was discharged in the
commit that wrote it).**  Its `other decl` contract closes *"…which MUST BE GATE-WIRED — unwired, that coverage
exists nowhere."*  Measured: it **is** wired, by `9f666a8`, **the same commit**; `gate_arm.sh` runs the probe,
its row list checks all three named rows by name, and the block reports 50 rows emitted, 50 green, 0 red.  So a
reader concludes coverage exists nowhere when it is wired and passing.  That is the carrier's
present-tense-description class, and it is worse than an ordinary stale line because it reads as an
**outstanding obligation** — a future round could redo finished work.  Repair is to DEMOTE it in place, since
the reasoning (unwired coverage exists nowhere) is exactly why the wiring was done.  **Deliberately not fixed
on the spot: the gate was running and about to execute that probe, and Python reads a script whole at startup,
so an edit between runs hands two runs different instruments** — a records-only change would have been
invisible in the diff and visible in the measurement, which is the worst combination.

**`codexsubjectrefusal` (LOW — a codex content-filter refusal survived neutralisation, and the trigger is not
what it first appeared).**  Filed earlier in this session and recorded here so the queue and the ledger agree.
The first diagnosis — that the refusal keyed on the SUBJECT — was wrong; re-testing showed **design briefs are
answered while witness briefs are refused**, so the trigger is the reach-the-defect FRAMING rather than the

## 2026-09-07 — two new defects from the `sgirebufuninit` pass-1 panel, both found by the codex seat on a brief about something else

Both arrived under the standing *"if, while verifying a claim, you found something ELSE — say so"* licence, and
both were **verified at HEAD before filing**.  The seat's verdict was **GO-WITH-CHANGES**, and it sits at the
END of a 317 KB answer, which is why the extractor scored it a format miss — *a seat with no verdict line gets
its body read, and this is the third time that has paid.*

**`sgirergbroundtrip` (MED — the RGB colour arms are off by one byte position).**  The two arms disagree about
which byte holds which channel:

    PUT  case DE_MODE_TYPE_RGB:   buf[0] = *color >> 24;  buf[1] = *color >> 16;
                                  buf[2] = *color >> 8;   buf[3] = 0;
    GET  case DE_MODE_TYPE_RGB:   *color = (buf[1] << 24) + (buf[2] << 16) + (buf[3] << 8);

PUT stores the top three bytes at indices **0,1,2**; GET recombines from **1,2,3**.  Storing `0x11223300` gives
bytes `11 22 33 00`, which GET reads back as **`0x22330000`** — a round trip through the model's own RGB mode
does not return what was written.

*** WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE BUG: EVERY ANALYSIS THIS WEEK, MINE INCLUDED, CALLED THE FOUR IMPLEMENTED COLOUR
ARMS "CORRECT" AND SUSPECTED ONLY THE `default:` ARMS. ***  The `sgirebufuninit` brief says it outright —
*"NO colour arm writes `buf[4..7]` — not one of the five, including the four CORRECT ones"*.  codex:
*"Calling all implemented color arms 'correct' is unwarranted."*  The phrase had been repeated unchecked across
three documents.  **Which side is wrong is deliberately NOT decided here**: RGBA is symmetric 0–3 on both
sides and ABGR is reversed on both, so RGB is the lone asymmetric pair — but whether the hardware packs RGB at
the low or high three bytes is a datasheet question, and a round taking this owes that reference or a real
framebuffer comparison.

**`sgimtedepth4dead` (LOW — `do_mte_transfer()`'s `if (depth == 4)` can never be true).**
`depth = 8 << ((mode & MTE_MODE_DEPTH_MASK) >> MTE_DEPTH_SHIFT)`, with mask `0x00000300` and shift 8 — a
two-bit field, so `depth` is only ever **8, 16, 32 or 64**.  The guarded block is dead code.  codex reads the
dead block as the intended RGBA construction, leaving *"its helper calls retain CI"*; **that half is not
verified here** and is what a round would have to establish.  *** IT ALSO REFUTES A PREMISE OF
`sgirebufuninit`: that brief asks whether callers constrain the (colour type, depth) pair, and this is a caller
that TRIES to and FAILS SILENTLY. ***  LOW because a dead branch corrupts nothing by itself; the severity lives
in the missing construction, which is unestablished.

**And a correction to `sgirebufuninit`'s own scope claim, from the same seat.**  Its class scan reported six
unpinned-length and five stack-buffer-write sites and concluded `dev_sgi_re.c` is the class's only member.
Codex found **four write sites both scanners missed** — `dev_dec21143.c` descriptor writebacks (nested argument
commas defeat the comma-splitting, which the brief *had* disclosed as a limit) and `dev_dreamcast_maple.c`
response writes (casts prevent recognition of the buffer argument, which it had **not**).  All four are safe,
**so the conclusion survives and the denominator does not** — different claims, which the brief conflated.
The sharp part is methodological: *"Agreement between scanners sharing parsing limitations is not exhaustive
corroboration."*  Both scanners split arguments with the same regex, so **they are one deriver run twice** —
the identical lesson this project already paid for on the `sgirekills` count, where two agreeing greps both
counted comment lines.

**`sgigbeconvover` (LOW — `dev_sgi_gbe.c`'s tile-line conversion loop runs past what was read).**  Raised by
the codex seat as a narrowing of one of my own SAFE verdicts in the `sgirebufuninit` class scan, and verified:

    cpu->memory_rw(..., buf, len, MEM_READ, ...);      /* fills len bytes   */
    for (int i = 0; i < 512; i += bytes_per_pixel)     /* reads 512 -- not len */

`len < 512` is reachable on the last tile column (`partial_pixels * bytes_per_pixel`), so up to 511
uninitialised bytes are fed through `get_rgb()`.  **Scope kept to what is demonstrable, matching the seat's own

*The neighbouring OB-14 clamp shows someone already reasoned about this loop's bounds once — and bounded the

## 2026-09-07 — four rows from ONE scoped codex invocation on `dev_lca.c`, plus the warrant `lcabadval` was missing

All four came from a single read-only codex run (`regress/artifacts/lcabadval/codex_scoping_20260907.txt`),
the second run under the new §C5 discipline — neutral language, reading scoped to `src/` and `regress/*.py`.
It completed at 297,783 bytes with **zero** content-filter flags, on a device unrelated to the one that
produced the rule. **Every claim below was verified against the source before filing; one of the four I found
by reading the function while checking codex's table, not from the answer itself.**

**`lcabadval` (HIGH, existing) — the severity warrant it was missing.**  Each window guard STORES the value
and *then* ends the process:

    d->window_mask_0 = idata;                          <- the store LANDS
    if (idata != 0x700000ULL) { fatal(...); exit(1); } <- then the process ends

And **zero is a documented encoding** — `alpha_lcareg.h` defines `IOC_W_MASK_1M` as `0x0`, the 1 MB window.
So a guest selecting the smallest documented window size kills the emulator; likewise `W_BASE1`, whose one
accepted constant carries the `WEN` *window enable* bit, so a driver **disabling** a window is killed too.
That is `#504`'s warrant at a second device: documented values the model dies on, not junk ones.

**Its RANGE site is also far more reachable than the row said.**  It was recorded as `ofs > len`; in fact
`relative_addr >>= 5; ofs = relative_addr & 3;` — **`ofs` is guest address bits 5-6**, so an ordinary 1-byte
access at an address with those bits set to 2 or 3 ends the process.  That is address decoding, not a value
whitelist, and it belongs to a different disposition class from the six value guards.

**`lcaisalane` (MED) — three defects in eleven lines.**  The guard is `>` where `>=` was meant, so
`(len,ofs) = (1,1)` and `(2,2)` pass, perform a real downstream read, and **return all zeros** because no `i`
ever equals `ofs` — the guest is told the device answered zero when that lane was never asked.  The read path
**discards** the failure result the write path returns.  And `uint8_t byte;` is **uninitialised** and consumed
if that discarded read failed — **the fourth instance of the uninitialised-consumption family today**,
alongside `sgirebufuninit`, `sgigbeconvover` and `#95`'s incomplete class closure.

**`alphapfnoffset` (HIGH, provisional) — the page-table walk drops the within-page offset.**
`(*return_paddr) = ALPHA_PTE_TO_PFN(pte3) << pageSizeShift` returns a page base, and `memory_rw` then computes
`offset = paddr & offset_mask`, which is zero — so every walked access FILLS FROM its page's first
bytes. (*Not* "lands at": the fast path recomputes the offset, so a cache HIT is correct and the
corruption is the slow-path fill. Corrected 2026-09-07 from the retrospective pass 2.)
**Codex's hedge is correct and I verified it:** both direct-mapped paths mask the vaddr and *keep* the offset,
so only the real walk is affected.  **HIGH is provisional on reachability** — `memory_alpha.c` carries seven
TODOs and an explicit "not yet implemented" exit, so a bootable config may never reach the walk, in which case
this is latent.  A round settles reachability *first*; the fix is adding the offset back.

**`alphavmkill` (MED) — a guest virtual address ends the host.**  `vaddr == 0xfffffffd80000000` hits
`fatal(...); exit(1);` inside the `ptbr == 0` bootstrap arm, so it is reached early in a boot on an address the
kernel chooses.  **The disposition is genuinely not obvious**, which is why it is filed rather than fixed:
declining leaves the guest with a wrong translation to fault on somewhere less legible, so this may be one of
the rare sites where a loud stop beats continuing — and if so the round's product is a record saying so plus a
latch, not a removal.

**`lcashiftub` (LOW) — `0x800 << dev` reaches `2^31` in a signed 32-bit `int`**, undefined behaviour.  The
irony is worth the line: **that loop is the file's own precedent for graceful degradation** — its `dev >= 21`
fallback has a commented-out `exit(1)` and substitutes a safe default, which `lcabadval` cites as a
transferable in-tree warrant.  The safe path contains UB.  `0x800U` fixes it; the first question is whether a
UBSan sweep already flags it, and if not, why not.

## 2026-09-07 — CORRECTION to this morning's `alphapfnoffset` entry, plus two more Alpha rows

**MY OWN OVERCLAIM, CORRECTED.**  The entry above says of the Alpha page-table walk:

> `offset = paddr & offset_mask`, which is zero — so **every walked access FILLS FROM its page's
> first bytes** (not "lands at" — the fast path recomputes the offset; the corruption is the
> slow-path fill).

**"Every" is too broad.**  A codex reachability pass (`regress/artifacts/alphapfnoffset/codex_reachability_20260907.txt`)
enumerated **all 8,192 offsets** — confirming the walk yields offset zero throughout and differs from the
offset-preserving address for **8,191** of them, and confirming the masking paths preserve offsets across
**three** bootstrap alias regions, not the two I had read.  But: *"Slow-path accesses consume the incorrect
physical offset, but cached Alpha loads/stores calculate `addr & 8191` themselves.  Subsequent cache hits can
therefore access the correct within-page bytes."*  **So the corruption is confined to the slow path**; once a
page is cached the load/store instructions recompute the offset and read the right bytes.  HIGH stands, but on
the narrower warrant.

**Reachability is neither "live" nor "latent".**  There is *no source barrier* to a guest-instruction witness
on the existing `eb164` description, and the smallest decisive observation is **one completed guest data
access** that reaches the walk with a nonzero page offset and whose caller completes on the returned page-base
address — a PTBR watchpoint or a walker-entry breakpoint is explicitly **not** enough, since reaching the walk
is not the same as an access completing wrongly.  What the seat could not supply: *"I cannot name a
demonstrated working Alpha OS boot from the allowed files."*  So the honest status is **witnessable in
principle, unwitnessed in fact.**

**`alphafaultclaim` (MED).**  *"The fork's claim that a failed Alpha walk causes the caller to raise a fault is
unsupported by this path.  The translator returns zero, the memory worker returns failure, and the Alpha data
instruction abandons the access without delivering an Alpha exception."*  That is an **L4 wrong-record
candidate in a comment the fork added itself** — `memory_alpha.c`'s `not_found` label carries a `#194
(Codex/Fable)` note reasoning about exactly this.  It also **corroborates a standing carrier claim from a new
direction**: the option-set rule already records that member 5 (FAULT) has no Alpha equivalent, derived from
`memory_rw.c`; this reaches the same conclusion from the instruction side.  Any round reaching for FAULT on an
Alpha device now has two independent reasons not to.  **Not verified by me** — recorded as stated, with its
citations.

**`alphaswpctxreg` (LOW).**  `swpctx` writes the old context into `a0` while the ABI wrapper in `alpha_cpu.h`
reads it from `v0` — a silent wrong value rather than a crash, which is the harder kind to notice.  **Not
verified by me**, and filed rather than confirmed because the Alpha queue is now four rows deep and none has a
witness.  It is the cheapest of the four to check, so a round taking any Alpha item should settle it first.

**THE BOOT QUESTION IS ANSWERED AND IT REVERSES MY CONCERN.**  I had flagged the risk that the Alpha queue was
accumulating well-analysed rows on a machine nothing can exercise.  A scoped codex pass
(`regress/artifacts/alphapfnoffset/codex_boot_20260907.txt`) settled it: *"EB164 or AlphaServer 4100 provides
the required unmodified machine description.  There is no architectural requirement to boot an OS first."*
Debugger word writes go through the memory helpers, Alpha fetches and decodes through its actual memory path,
and the shared breakpoint machinery applies — **which is exactly the rung-3 cold-debugger shape the ladder
admits.**  All four previously filed Alpha defects classify as **cold-debugger reachable**.

The qualification that matters for `alphapfnoffset` specifically: the walk needs page-table state, and *the
ordinary bootstrap identity mapping bypasses the walk* — so its probe must first establish a non-zero
`apcb_ptbr` and a valid three-level table.  That is real work, and it keeps that row the hardest of the five
despite being the most severe if reached.

**`alphaswpctxptbr` (HIGH) — `swpctx` clobbers the page-table base register.**  Raised by the same pass under
the found-something-else licence, on a brief that asked only whether Alpha can run anything, and verified by
reading before filing:

    // Update all variables in the pcb simultaneously:
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ptbr   = new_ptbr;      <- correct
    ...
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ptbr   = new_flags;     <- *** should be apcb_flags ***

**`apcb_ptbr` is assigned twice and `apcb_flags` is never assigned at all.**  `alpha_translate_v2p()` opens
with `base = cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ptbr << ALPHA_PAGESHIFT`, so **after any `swpctx` the page-table walk reads
its tables from an address derived from the flags word** — every translation after a context switch walks
garbage.  And `apcb_flags` retains the outgoing context's value, a second and quieter defect from the same
line.  The comment directly above asserts what the code does not do; that is the **second** comment-versus-code
contradiction in this one function, the other being `alphaswpctxreg`.

**Fix: one token.**  The intent is not in doubt — `new_flags` is loaded from the context block and would
otherwise be dead, and `apcb_flags` exists in the struct and would otherwise never be written.

*** IT IS A CONFOUND FOR `alphapfnoffset`'s WITNESS AND MUST BE FIXED FIRST. ***  This defect corrupts the
walk's BASE; that one corrupts the walk's RESULT.  A probe that sets up a context via `swpctx` and then
observes a bad translation cannot attribute it without pinning which of the two produced it.  Fixing this one
first is certain, one token, and removes a confound from the harder row.

## 2026-09-07 — CORRECTION to `alphaswpctxptbr`, plus two more Alpha rows and a refuted prediction

**TWO OF MY SUPPORTING PREMISES WERE WRONG AND THE ENTRY ABOVE STATES ONE OF THEM AS FACT.**  It says:

> **`apcb_ptbr` is assigned twice and **`apcb_flags` is never assigned at all**.**

**False.**  `grep -rn apcb_flags src/` returns `cpu_alpha_palcode.c:221` — **`wrfen` assigns it** from
`r[ALPHA_A0]` and writes it back to PCB memory, and `swpctx` itself *reads* the field when saving the outgoing
context.  The honest statement is narrower and still a defect: **`swpctx` never assigns `apcb_flags` when
LOADING a new context**, so the incoming context's flags are dropped and the outgoing context's value persists
across the switch.  *Never written anywhere* was not true.

Second, I wrote that `new_flags` *"would otherwise be dead"*.  It has exactly one use — the erroneous PTBR
assignment — so it is unused but **not dead in the current program**: it changes PTBR.  My phrasing implied a
compiler would flag it; it would not, because the bad line consumes it.

**A QUALIFICATION THAT BOUNDS `alphaswpctxreg`:** the handler captures its input into a *local* `a0` before
dispatch, so overwriting `r[ALPHA_A0]` does **not** change which context is loaded.  That defect is purely a
wrong return value — a reporting bug, not state corruption.  I had not established that.

**SCOPE: TWO CHANGES, NOT ONE.**  I intended to fix both in one diff (same function, same class).  The design
pass ruled them two under the reopening rule, and I accept it: the observables differ — a guest register versus
internal PCB state reachable only through a translation — so one test cannot cover both without a new
observation, which is what that rule forbids.

*** AND MY OWN PREDICTION WAS REFUTED, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING AS MUCH AS A FINDING. ***  I argued that with
two wrong-destination assignments in one function a **third was "more likely than not"**, and asked for the
whole handler and the surrounding PALcode cases to be read.  They were.  **There is no third.**  A predicted
class that does not materialise is a result, and it stops the next round hunting for one.

**`alphatbinegsel` (MED) -- *** FIXED AND CLOSED 2026-09-10 AS `#520`; see the CHANGELOG round block. The reading below stands and was CONFIRMED at rung 3 before the edit (5/7 committed, 7/7 fixed); it is kept because it is what the round was reproduced from. *** ** `tbi`'s selector is compared as **unsigned**, so enumerating gives
`-2 → VADDR, -1 → VADDR, 0 → ALL, 1..3 → VADDR`, while the header requires all-entry and all-per-process
invalidation for the negative selectors.  So `tbi(-1)` — the OS saying *invalidate everything* — invalidates
one address.  **A TLB flush that silently flushes almost nothing is the dangerous direction**: the guest
believes stale translations are gone.  Not independently verified by me.

**`alphactxfail` (MED).**  The context save and load ignore every memory-access failure, and `ctx` changes
before loading finishes with no check before committing the PCB.  *** THE INTERACTION WITH `#95` IS THE SHARP
PART — the third time tonight that fix has surfaced with an unconsidered edge. ***  `#95` zeroes the caller's
buffer on a device read so a partial fill cannot leak host memory, which is unambiguously right; here that
same zeroing means **a failed load returns a well-formed zero instead of an error**, and the caller, which
checks nothing, commits it to the PCB.  A safety fix that converts a detectable failure into a plausible value
is worth knowing about generally.  Not independently verified by me.

## 2026-09-07 — `sgimtedepth4dead` raised LOW → HIGH: the dead branch is the MECHANISM, not a curiosity

**I FILED THIS SAYING "a dead branch cannot itself corrupt anything".  THAT IS WRONG.**  The finding was in the
kimi seat's pass-1 answer — a file I had already opened and under-read — and is verified here:

    src_mode = (src_tlb << 10) + (((mode & MTE_MODE_DEPTH_MASK) >> MTE_DEPTH_SHIFT) << 8);
    dst_mode = (dst_tlb << 10) + (((mode & MTE_MODE_DEPTH_MASK) >> MTE_DEPTH_SHIFT) << 8);
    if (depth == 4) {                     <- DEAD: depth = 8 << field, so 8/16/32/64, never 4
            src_mode |= DE_MODE_TYPE_RGBA;
            dst_mode |= DE_MODE_TYPE_RGBA;
    }

The constructed modes carry **no colour bits**, so the colour type is `0x00` = **CI**, and the only thing that
would make them RGBA is the dead branch.  **So the MTE path always runs CI** — and CI's PUT arm fills only
`buf[0]` while the transfer is `bufdepth` bytes:

    MTE_DEPTH_8  = 0 -> bufdepth 1   matched, no leak
    MTE_DEPTH_16 = 1 -> bufdepth 2   fills buf[0], writes 2 -> 1 uninitialised byte per pixel
    MTE_DEPTH_32 = 2 -> bufdepth 4   fills buf[0], writes 4 -> 3 uninitialised bytes per pixel

**All three are documented constants.**  kimi: *"every MTE_TLB_A/B/C fill with MTE_DEPTH_16/32 leaks
buf[1..3] per pixel (documented MTE_DEPTH values!).  This is the strongest reachability evidence: PROM/NetBSD
`crmfb_fill_rect` uses this path."*  That gives `sgirebufuninit` an **all-documented** reachability vehicle on
a path a real driver uses — where every argument I had recorded relied on the DE path and conceded that PATH
A's maximal form needs the undocumented depth field 3.

*** AND IT CHANGES THE FIX ORDER IN A WAY THAT WOULD HAVE BITTEN. ***  Repairing `depth == 4` **alone** would
switch the MTE path to RGBA, which fills `buf[0..3]` — **accidentally masking the leak at depth 32** while
leaving depth 16 (2 bytes, RGBA fills 4) and every DE-path case untouched.  A round fixing only this would
*look* like it had fixed `sgirebufuninit` and would not have.  That is the shape the vacuity floor exists to
catch, surfacing before either round starts.

**It also settles a correction I had recorded without noticing what it implied.**  The codex seat told me *"not
all seven call sites receive those register words — the two MTE sites construct their own modes."*  I filed
that as a narrowing of my reachability claim.  **Constructing them is exactly what makes them leak** — the two
corrections are one fact seen from opposite sides.

**Both file-reading seats independently reached the same detector requirement:** the oracle must assert
**values, not determinism**.  kimi's proof is the sharper: post-fix PATH B yields a deterministic value *and*
the `bufdepth`-sized mutant yields the previous pixel's bytes, which are **also** deterministic under stack
reuse — so *"a determinism oracle CANNOT catch the mutant."*

## 2026-09-07 — `sgilinearnegidx`: *** WITHDRAWN THE SAME DAY — THE FINDING IS FALSE. ***

*** `tile_nr` IS **UNSIGNED**, SO THE `>= 32` GUARD REJECTS EVERY NEGATIVE `x`.  THE ENTRY BELOW IS
KEPT VERBATIM — THIS PROJECT CORRECTS IN PLACE AND QUOTES WHAT IT REFUTES — BUT NOTHING IN IT IS A
DEFECT.  READ THE CORRECTION AT THE FOOT OF THE ENTRY BEFORE ACTING ON ANY OF IT. ***

### (superseded) a guest-chosen physical write address, found by a packet-fed seat

**FOUND BY THE `glm` SEAT** — a transport that cannot read the repo and had only the function inlined.  It
noticed that one guard's precondition excludes the very mode the other guard assumes:

    if (!linear && (x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= 2048 || y >= 2048))   <- SKIPPED when linear
            return;
    ...
    case 4: tile_nr = x >> 12;
            if (tile_nr >= 32)                                   <- bounds ABOVE only
                    return;
            tileptr = 0x80000000 | (d->re_linear_a[tile_nr] << 12);

`x = -1` gives `tile_nr = -1`, which passes `>= 32`, and indexes `re_linear_a[-1]`.

*** THE READ VALUE BECOMES A PHYSICAL ADDRESS, AND THE MEMORY IT READS IS GUEST-WRITABLE. ***  `offsetof`
**measured** (not derived — `regress/artifacts/sgilinearnegidx/offcheck.c`): `re_tex` ends at 1760 and
`re_linear_a` begins at 1760, **zero padding**, so `re_linear_a[-1]` is `re_tex[110]` and `re_tex[111]` — both
written by the guest through the `CRIME_RE_TEX` store arm.

**The chain, each step read from the source:** guest fills `re_tex[110..111]` → sets `CRIME_DE_XFER_STEP_X`
negative (an `int32_t`, and the check at `:734` only **announces and continues**) → `src_x += step_x` drives
`src_x` negative → linear-mode GET skips the sign guard → `tile_nr = -1` passes → `tileptr` is the two
guest-written halfwords shifted left 12 → `memory_rw(…, tileptr + ofs, buf, bufdepth, MEM_WRITE, PHYSICAL)`.
**The guest selects the physical destination of a device write, bypassing translation.**

**NOT ESTABLISHED, and a round owes each:** no witness — every step is reachable by reading, none observed;
`sgitexindex`'s overlapping TEX writes complicate *which* values land in `[110..111]`, affecting
controllability rather than reachability; and whether any real driver drives a negative step is unknown.

**Not a duplicate of `sgilinearoob`** (the same array's *above* bound, in a different function), and **must
not be folded into `sgirebufuninit`** — that is about buffer *contents*, this about the write *destination*,
and a memset fixes nothing here.

**A note on the seat, because it cuts against expectation:** the doctrine says packet-fed transports supply
attack *reasoning* rather than repo fact, and are never equivalent votes on the tree.  That held exactly — glm
could not confirm the struct layout or the caller, and said so.  What it could do was notice a contradiction
between two guards in code it had been handed, and **that was the strongest single finding on the brief.**

### *** THE CORRECTION.  Measured 2026-09-07, hours after the entry above was written and committed. ***

**The declaration is three lines above the code the entry quotes**, in the same function, inside a range I had
already printed to my own screen earlier in the session:

    :204   int tile_nr_x = x / tilewidth_in_pixels;
    :205   int tile_nr_y = y >> 7;
    :207   unsigned int tile_nr = tile_nr_y * 16 + tile_nr_x;      <- UNSIGNED
    ...
    case 4: tile_nr = x >> 12;             <- converted to unsigned ON ASSIGNMENT
            if (tile_nr >= 32)             <- 4294967295 >= 32 is TRUE
                    return;                <- IT RETURNS

    x = -1      ->  x >> 12 = -1  ->  as unsigned = 4294967295  ->  >= 32  ->  REJECTED
    x = -8192   ->  x >> 12 = -2  ->  as unsigned = 4294967294  ->  >= 32  ->  REJECTED

**The guard I called "bounds ABOVE only" is a COMPLETE bound**, because the conversion folds every negative
value into the rejected range.  No out-of-bounds read, no guest-chosen tile pointer, no write primitive.  The
chain is broken at its FIRST link and every later link is therefore moot.

**WHAT SURVIVES:** the `offsetof` measurement is TRUE and is preserved at
`regress/artifacts/sgilinearnegidx/offcheck.c` — `re_tex` does end at 1760 and `re_linear_a` does begin at
1760 with zero padding.  It is a correct measurement of a path nothing can reach, so it supports no finding.

*** HOW THIS HAPPENED, recorded because the process failure is the only thing of value left here. ***

* I wrote *"the chain, each step read from the source"* and *"every link is now verified by reading"*.  I did
  verify the link I DOUBTED — whether `src_x` is masked in the linear path — and never checked the **type of
  the index variable**, which is the most basic property of an index and the one that decides the question.
* I reached for `offsetof` precisely to avoid trusting hand arithmetic about the struct.  **That rigour was
  real and it was aimed at the wrong link.**  Care taken on one step does not transfer to a step you never
  thought to question.
* The seat that found it was asked the same subject **without the chain** — *"which array indexes are bounded
  on one side only?"* — and answered in its verdict line.  The chain-shaped version of that same question had
  been REFUSED by the same seat hours earlier (see §C5).  **The refusal did not stop a bad question; it
  delayed a correct answer**, and in the interval I escalated the finding, wrote it into a commit message, and
  reported it as the session's most severe result.
* **Commit `15633bb`'s MESSAGE carries this claim as its headline and cannot be edited.**  This entry and the
  ledger row are the correction a reader must reach — the same treatment `de96f11`'s over-broad RMW claim
  already has.

**And a note on the note.**  The paragraph above about the packet-fed seat is still true about what glm did:
it noticed a real asymmetry between two guards in code it had been handed.  What it could not do — exactly as
the doctrine says — is check the declaration, because the type is a repo fact and it is packet-fed.  **The
doctrine's warning was about crediting such a seat with repo fact, and that is precisely the error I then
made on its behalf.**

## 2026-09-07 — `sgirespanchk` (LOW, filed): the index is bounded, the write SPAN is not

Split out of the withdrawn row above rather than folded into it, **because a withdrawn entry is the worst
possible place to hide a live finding.**  From the same audit's verdict line, which refuted the negative-index
claim and then continued:

> *"There are missing checks on complete write SPANS in TLB_A/B/C and LINEAR_A/B, whose safety depends on
> caller alignment."*

**A span check is a different question from an index bound.**  An index can be in range while the multi-byte
access starting at it runs past the end of the array — the bound answers *where does it start*, the span
answers *where does it finish*.  Nothing in the withdrawn chain bears on this, and the refutation of that
chain does not touch it.

**OWED before this is worth a round:** the arrays and their declared sizes; which accesses are multi-byte and
how the width is chosen; and — the load-bearing one — **whether any caller can present an unaligned or
oversized span, since the verdict explicitly conditions the safety on caller alignment rather than asserting
a defect.**  That is a reading task, and it is exactly the shape the codex seat answers cleanly.

### *** AND IT WAS ALREADY ANSWERED, IN THE BODY OF THE SAME ANSWER, BEFORE I FIRED A SECOND RUN TO ASK IT.
### MED → LOW. ***

I filed the paragraph above from the seat's VERDICT LINE without reading its body.  The body enumerates the
overruns — a TLB loop starting at 255 touches 255, **256, 257, 258**; a LINEAR pair starting at 31 touches
31, **32** — and then discharges the very question I had just written down as owed:

> *"These are **handler robustness gaps**, not established guest out-of-bounds writes.  For the normal SGI CPU
> access paths checked, eight-byte accesses have eight-byte alignment.  Enumerating aligned addresses gives
> TLB starting indexes `0,4,…,252`, and LINEAR starting indexes `0,2,…,30`; their complete spans fit.  **I
> verified the alignment handling in the ordinary access code and unaligned-access helper, rather than
> accepting the device comments.**"*

— naming `src/cpus/cpu_mips_instr_loadstore.c` and `src/cpus/cpu_mips_instr_unaligned.c`.  **That is exactly
the checked-versus-assumed distinction this entry was filed to demand**, and the seat drew it in those words.

**What remains open is one word — "checked".**  The MIPS load/store paths were verified; a DMA engine, a
device-to-device access or the debugger's `put` reach a device handler without going through a CPU load, and
those were not enumerated.  A second read-only audit is running whose Q4 asks precisely that; it was written
and fired *before* this body was read, so its answer will be independent rather than a re-confirmation.

*** FIFTH UNDER-HARVEST OF THE SESSION, AND THE FIRST TO COST A WHOLE INVOCATION. ***  The previous four took
a seat's finding and dropped its refutation.  This one dropped the seat's own **discharge** of an obligation,
which I then wrote into a row and spent a codex run re-asking.  **A verdict line is a summary written against
the brief's framing, and is the least likely part of an answer to carry a qualification** — this project
already says that about corrections; it is equally true of discharges.

**Five side-checks harvested from the same body, none of them asked for:** `de_reg[1024]` at `[regnr]` and
`[regnr+1]` reaches at most 512; both static `rop_used[256]` arrays are masked `& 255`, which supplies *both*
bounds; `zerobuf[4096]` is length-capped then page-shortened, never enlarged; `buf[8]` takes enumerated
lengths 1/2/4/8, all of which fit — with the seat volunteering that its *initialisation* is a separate
defect, which is `sgirebufuninit`, already filed.

**And one finding that is not a span question at all:** *"the coordinate rectangle check does not by itself
establish the TLB capacity bound."*  At depth field 3 (`bufdepth` 8, tile width 64) the pre-guard `tile_nr`
reaches **271**, not 255 — the `x, y < 2048` rectangle admits indexes past the end of a `[256]` array, and it
is the *later* `tile_nr >= 256` guard that rejects them.  Both guards are present, so nothing is broken.
What is worth recording is that **they are not redundant**, and an edit deleting the second as "already
covered by the rectangle check" would open a sixteen-element overrun.  A clause-(d)-shaped hazard in code
nobody is currently editing — noted, not filed.

## 2026-09-07 — `#505` pass 1: three rows filed from one panel, none of them the round's subject

*Every one came from a seat answering a question about byte order and volunteering something else. The
found-something-else licence produced three of this session's filed rows.*

### `sgirgbscanoutrow` (LOW) — the round's strongest evidence is observed by no row

`#505` chose the RGB **GET** as the defective arm on a warrant from a *different device*:
`dev_sgi_gbe.c`'s scanout composes a 32-bit tile pixel as
`(buf[0]<<24)+(buf[1]<<16)+(buf[2]<<8)+buf[3]`, and `CRMFB_MODE_TYP_RGB8` then takes R, G and B from
bits 31..24 / 23..16 / 15..8 — **byte 0 is R and byte 3 is unused.** That is the whole reason the pad
is known to live at `buf[3]`, and it is non-circular precisely because it comes from the consumer
rather than from either arm under test.

**No row observes it.** The detector drives the drawing engine and reads the destination word back
through a guest load; it never reaches scanout. So it cannot distinguish a tree where DE and GBE agree
on the container from one where both were changed consistently and wrongly.

**A row would need a different probe SHAPE** — drive a DE draw, make GBE scan the tile out, and put the
oracle on `dev_fb_access` output. That is not another row in this probe, which is why it is filed
rather than added; the detector is above the floor without it.

*Filed by `#505`'s own PRE-TABLE CLAIM→ROW check, as an explicit no-row sentence rather than an
omission — an unrun check and an inapplicable one must not render the same.*

### `sgirebufshiftub` (LOW) — `buf[i] << 24` on a `uint8_t` is signed-shift UB, on all four arms

Raised by the **grok** seat. `buf[i]` is `uint8_t`, which the usual arithmetic conversions promote to
**signed `int`** — not unsigned, because `int` represents every `uint8_t` value. So for any byte ≥ 128:

    0xaa = 170;   170 << 24 = 2,852,126,720   >   INT_MAX (2,147,483,647)

which is undefined behaviour under C99 6.5.7p4. Compilers produce the wrapped value everyone expects,
which is why it has survived — but this tree runs a UBSan sweep.

**Pre-existing and on all four GET arms**, not on the one `#505` edited: the shipped RGB arm used
`buf[1] << 24` identically. `#505` replaced one instance of the idiom with another, which is the right
minimal-surgical choice — casting one line would leave the file internally inconsistent for no measured
gain. **Filed, not fixed, and the seat that raised it agrees**: *"not unique to RGB, not a reason to
block."*

**Owed before a fix round:** whether the UBSan sweep already reaches this function. If it does, the
absence of a report is a finding about the sweep, not about the code.

### `sgilinearnegidxpostmortem` (LOW) — a rule question raised by my own false HIGH finding

See the `sgilinearnegidx` withdrawal above. The question is **not** "be more careful": I applied the
discipline — identified the link I doubted, verified it by grep, ran an `offsetof` rather than trust
hand arithmetic — and **every one of those was aimed at a link I had already decided to question.** The
defeating fact sat in a declaration I never thought to read.

Queued in full for the 2026-09-09 adjudication, asking (1) whether the premise-audit instruction needs a
**self-directed twin**, since it currently tells *seats* not to ratify my premises and nothing tells me
to enumerate the premises I never questioned; (2) whether *"a chain resting on an index or a bound
quotes the DECLARATION of every variable in it"* earns a template line or is one instance wearing the
clothes of a class; and (3) what it means for §C5 that the chain-shaped brief asking for this exact
chain to be attacked was **refused**, while the same seat asked without the chain put the refutation in
its verdict line.

## 2026-09-07 — `artifactcaseclobber` (LOW, fixed in place): a rename that differs only in CASE is a CLOBBER on this filesystem

**A committed 145 KB artifact was silently replaced by a 14 KB one, and nothing reported it.**

Preserving a codex refusal log, I copied it to `codex_REFUSED_20260907.err` — believing that to be a
new name beside the existing `codex_refused_20260907.err`. **On Windows the filesystem is
case-insensitive: they are the same file.** The `cp` overwrote a tracked artifact from an earlier
session (`tokens used 41,373`, 145,011 bytes) with today's (`tokens used 17,631`, 14,221 bytes).

**Nothing caught it at the time.** `git status` showed ` M` on a tracked file, which is what every
edited file shows. The `cp` succeeded. The only visible symptom was a diffstat line —
**`2876 ++------` on a file I had not knowingly edited** — and that surfaced only because the owner
asked how much work was outstanding and I went to count it.

> **A RENAME THAT DIFFERS ONLY IN CASE IS NOT A RENAME HERE.** Preserving one artifact beside another
> needs a name that differs by a WORD, not by capitalisation.

**FIXED IN PLACE:** the tracked log restored from HEAD; today's preserved as
`codex_witnessdesign_refusal_20260907.err`.

**SWEPT, because one instance is not a population:** 4,793 tracked paths and 3,930 files under
`regress/artifacts/` checked for case-insensitive duplicates — **zero collisions**. The incident was
isolated.

*This is the immutable-artifact rule's own failure mode arriving by a new route. That rule says a
measurement cited in a durable record must live at a durable path, because a reused filename makes the
citation point at something else. Here the filename was not reused — it was **aliased**, and the alias
was invisible in every tool I use to check.*


### `sgireput8tail` (low) -- filed 2026-09-07: `#505`'s detector has no row establishing that an 8-byte PUT's tail is initialised

Raised by the codex seat answering the Q4 *"name the row you expect to stay green"*.

`rgb depth64` and `rgb tiled64` widen the SOURCE READ to eight bytes; their DESTINATION is still a
four-byte RGBA write. So the ten-row detector drives an eight-byte read and never an eight-byte
write, and **nothing in it would redden if the PUT arms left `buf[4..7]` untouched at bufdepth 8.**

Coverage debt, not a floor breach: the shipped detector satisfies (a)-(f) and this is a cell no
enumerated mutant of `#505` distinguishes. Row demand is per enumerated mutant, never per uncovered
state. It becomes live the moment [[sgirebufuninit]] ships, because a zero-fill fix's own accept side
is exactly this cell.
