tests is true:

1. the refusal check grepped **stdout**; a content-filter refusal writes nothing there and puts
   `ERROR: This content was flagged...` on **stderr**, so it printed `refusal hits: 0` on a refusal
   that had already destroyed 108,432 tokens of completed work;
2. the script exited 0 while holding `rc=1`, so the harness reported the task COMPLETED;
3. **the fix introduced a third defect**: grepping stderr freely for wall text reported `wall: 3` on
   a HEALTHY seat, because codex streams the source it reads into stderr -- and all three hits were
   this project's own ledger prose about seat walls.

`tools/cxlaunch.sh` anchors stderr tests on codex's own `^ERROR:` lines and greps stdout freely;
exit 7 refusal, 8 wall, 6 empty-with-neither, else `rc`. Controlled in four states.

*`panel.sh` already had a better, POSITION-based discriminator (head/tail 400 bytes) with the
incident that taught it recorded in its own comment. A claim here that it did not was false and is
corrected: the consolidation should take position as the base test and add format where a seat's own
error prefix is known.*

### `alphaclrfen` (low) -- filed 2026-09-07: `PAL_clrfen` is named and user-mode-whitelisted but has no `case`

Volunteered by the grok seat while enumerating every `apcb_flags` reader for `#507`'s fix review.

`PAL_clrfen` (`0xae`) is named in the palcode file and appears in the user-mode whitelist, but the
dispatch switch has **no `case` for it** -- so a guest that calls it falls to the default arm, which
sets `cpu->running = 0` and stops the machine.

**NOT verified by me**, recorded as the seat reported it; a round on this owes the reading first. It
is the same shape as `#507` (a PAL entry that does not do what its name says), and an unimplemented
PAL call is member 7 (IMPLEMENT) territory rather than a decline -- declining a context-flag
operation leaves the machine in a state the guest cannot reason about.


### `negrowclass` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: an inequality row scores every NON-OBSERVATION green

*** THE FIVE UNGATED INSTANCES ARE ALREADY REPAIRED AND MEASURED (see the CHANGELOG round block).
THIS ROW CARRIES THE **GATED** ONES, WHICH OWE A GATE RUN AND SO ARE NOT A RIDER. ***

A row written `row(name, got, FORBIDDEN, negate=True)` asserts only `got != FORBIDDEN`. Every state
in which **nothing was measured at all** satisfies that: `"absent"` (the print regex missed),
`"died"` (the guest never started), and `0x0` (the memory was never backed). So the row goes green
on failures strictly worse than the one its own note claims to guard against.

**MEASURED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, 2026-09-07**, by running each probe against `/bin/true` -- which
execs and exits instantly, so every readback is a non-observation:

    pre-repair   swpctx notflags / swpctx mapped / walk stored / walk mapped / kill notzero   ALL ok
    repaired     the same five                                                                ALL FAIL
    HEAD         alpha_harness 10/10   alpha_pfnoffset 7/7   lca_confwidth 6/6   (unchanged)

**The detectors never escaped** -- an equality sibling (`swpctx ptbr`, `walk off`, `kill fired`)
reds on a non-observation in every one of the five. What was wrong was each row's NOTE, which
claimed a control the row did not have. That is **L4, a wrong record**, and it is why these were
corrected in place rather than filed.

**STILL OPEN -- the same class in GATED probes, each owing a targeted gate run:**

    sgi_re_rgb_probe.py          `rgb not corrupt`     gate_arm.sh
    sgi_re_randompixel_probe.py  `lin_b not src`       gate_arm.sh

The repair is mechanical and identical: compute `obs = v.startswith("0x") and v != "0x0"`, then
assert the positive `obs and v != FORBIDDEN`. **Row NAMES must not change** -- the gates match on
`^<name> .* ok$`, so a renamed row silently stops being tested (the padded-column trap).

*And a defect the repair itself introduced and the control caught: two notes were written with an
escaped newline, so `row()` printed them across two lines and the `FAIL` marker landed on the
second -- invisible to exactly that gate pattern. Flattened, re-measured. **A repair is not safer
than the thing it repairs.***

### `probeneedleterm` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: unterminated needles accept longer numbers

From the same codex audit. Distinct from `negrowclass`: these rows DO observe a value, and then
accept a wrong one because the pattern has no right-hand boundary.

* **`pcc2_default_probe.py` `srvd val text`, `srvd half text`** (gated, `gate_arm.sh`). The needles
  end at `0x34` and `0x56` without terminating the value. Codex's counterexample: change the
  diagnostic's `data[0]` argument to `data[0] << 8` in `dev_pcc2.c`; the reports become `0x3400`
  and `0x5600` and **both rows still pass**. It states that by inspection this preserves all 46 row
  predicates on an otherwise passing build. `wide rd srvd` has the zero mirror -- appending a
  literal `abc` after the `%02x` gives `0x00abc`, which still satisfies its `0x00` needle.
* **`sh4_val_probe.py` `V22 TCR timer_hz`** (gated, `gate_sh_rounding.sh`). It tests
  `clocks[0].startswith("520833")`. Changing the P64 calculation from `pclock/64.0` to
  `pclock/6.4` gives `5208333.281250` -- **ten times wrong**, retains the prefix, and does not
  contain the forbidden P4 string. The row prints the observed clock; the defect is its comparison.
* **`m88k_exc_probe.py` `Sess.cr()`, `gpr()`, `pc()`** (gated, `gate_m88k_rounding.sh`). They
  capture `[0-9a-f]{8}` with no right boundary, so appending a literal `0` to the control-register
  format turns `0x00010006` into `0x000100060` and the capture still reads the expected value.
  Codex is explicit that this establishes acceptance of a **wrong diagnostic value**, not an
  independently demonstrated CPU-state escape.

**NOT MEASURED.** Codex says so plainly: *"These are source-derived counterexamples, not executed
mutant results."* Each needs its mutant built before any claim is made about it.

### `gdrommappedvacuous` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: four `gdrom map` controls prove nothing

`gdrom_data_probe.py`, `gdrom_decline_probe.py`, `gdrom_toclen_probe.py` and the nested
`gdrompionull` PIO detector each call `printed()` and convert **any** `0x...` result to `"mapped"`.

Codex's counterexample: remove the main GD-ROM window's device registration. The access then falls
to `memory_rw.c`'s zero-filled successful read, `printed()` returns `0x0`, and the control still
reports `"mapped"`. **These rows do not establish that the GD-ROM handler served the access** --
which is precisely what the witness ladder's DEVICE-SIGNATURE control exists to establish, and what
`sgi_mte_fill_probe.py`'s `devsig` row does correctly by reading a value RAM cannot produce.

Other device-behaviour rows in those probes can reject the edit, so this is a misleading control
rather than a whole-detector escape.

### `sessionechosat` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: the debugger's own ECHO satisfies the liveness check

Volunteered by codex while tracing `sessionrefused` below -- the standing "if you found something
else, say so" channel.

`sh_intprio_probe.py` and `sh_iprbcd_probe.py` verify a live session by sending `print 0x1234` and
accepting `"0x1234"` **anywhere** in the transcript, ignoring the final read's return value. The
debugger **echoes command characters**, so the string is present because it was TYPED. Codex's
counterexample: remove the numeric response entirely and the verification still passes on the echo.

That is the check-that-cannot-fail family in its purest form -- a liveness control that answers the
same whether or not the thing it tests is true. The repair is to anchor the match to the RESPONSE
position rather than searching the whole buffer, which is the discriminator `panel.sh` and
`seat_verdicts.py` already use for seat answers.

### `sessionrefused` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: host death is scored as a successful refusal

`sh_intprio_probe.py` `irq14 imask`, and `sh_iprbcd_probe.py`'s `iprc_lo`, `raise_lo` and `lower`
through `run_deliver()`/`run_deliver2()`, convert a `session()` FAILURE into the string
`"refused"` -- which is the value those negative rows want. So a build that ends the host process
whenever an interrupt is pending, BL is clear and IMASK masks its priority scores those rows GREEN.

This is `negrowclass` one step further along: not merely green on a non-observation, but green on
the specific catastrophic outcome the probe exists to rule out. **A failed session must never map
onto a legitimate expected value.**

### `printedvariants` (low) -- filed 2026-09-07: 20 copies of `printed()`, four different contracts

Codex censused all 20 definitions: **7** first-match in the original hexadecimal spelling, **10**
first-match integer-normalised at full width, **2** first-match normalised AND masked to 32 bits,
**1** LAST match. All 20 return `"absent"` on a miss.

**And a wrong record it found while counting:** both masked helpers (`sgi_re_rgb`,
`sgi_re_randompixel`) describe their normalisation as matching `sgi_re_width`, **whose `printed()`
does not mask**. `sgi_de_width` separately exposes a `printed32()` and keeps full-width reads
elsewhere.

Codex explicitly declined to recommend a class-wide gating checker, and gave its reason rather than
a preference: its screen selected 79/79 files, so **13-of-25 is a selected sample, not a precision
figure**, and recall across ~95 helpers is unmeasured. Several candidate signals have legitimate
uses -- `got if alive else "died"` can fail correctly, first-match selection is sometimes
deliberate, and a greedy `+` behaves differently from `{8}`. A shared helper would need explicit
sample selection, missing-result handling and a width policy; globally replacing "first" with
"last" would break legitimate callers.

*Audit denominator, stated because a search without one is not checkable: 79 top-level probe files
screened, 25 reviewed in depth, 20/20 `printed()` definitions read, plus one nested detector. The
remaining 54 received screening only. No probe, gate or binary was executed and no file was
changed.*


### `armbfxwidth32` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: UBFX/SBFX build their mask with `1 << 32`

Found by a codex class hunt for bits-vs-bytes confusion; it is not that class, and the seat said
so plainly rather than forcing the finding into the question it was asked.

**VERIFIED HERE BY READING, not taken on report.** Both decoders compute the width the same way:

    cpu_arm_instr.c:4486   ubfx:   int width = 1 + ((iword >> 16) & 31);
    cpu_arm_instr.c:4493   sbfx:   int width = 1 + ((iword >> 16) & 31);

so `width` reaches **32**. Both handlers then recover it with `ic->arg[2] >> 16` and build

    cpu_arm_instr.c:1316   ubfx:   uint32_t mask = (1 << width) - 1;
    cpu_arm_instr.c:1340   sbfx:   uint32_t mask = (1 << width) - 1;

`1` is a plain `int`, so at width 32 this is a shift by the full width of the type -- **undefined
behaviour**, and the value the mask takes decides the result the guest sees at
`x &= mask`. On the common host lowering (shift count taken mod 32) the mask becomes **0** and
the instruction returns zero instead of the whole register.

**`UBFX rd, rn, #0, #32` is a legal encoding** -- the architectural constraint is
`lsb + width <= 32`, which `lsb = 0, width = 32` satisfies -- so this is guest-reachable, not a
decoder-only curiosity.

**`sbfx` has a SECOND site at the same width:** `uint32_t topBitMask = 1 << (width-1);` at
`:1344` evaluates `1 << 31` on a signed `int`, which overflows. The `width < 32` test that would
have saved it is at `:1345`, **after** the shift.

*The BFI decoder two blocks up (`:4474-4480`) is correct and is worth keeping as the contrast: it
packs `msb`, not a width, and its handler never shifts by a value that can reach 32.*

**Cheap to fix:** the repair is `width == 32 ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1)`, plus hoisting
the `width < 32` test above `topBitMask`. **The `U` is NOT cosmetic -- see the pass-1 correction
below.**

> ### *** THE PASS-1 PANEL (2026-09-07) MADE THIS ENTRY WRONG IN THREE WAYS, EACH IN THE DIRECTION
> ### OF UNDERSTATING IT.  Corrected here; every element re-verified by reading before the edit. ***
>
> **1. THE DEFECT IS TWO WIDTHS WIDE, NOT ONE.  `width == 31` IS ALSO UB** -- and it is reachable
> through utterly ordinary encodings, unlike the exotic `#0, #32`.  Found independently by the
> kimi substitute, minimax and deepseek:
>
>     width == 32   ->  1 << 32   shift COUNT >= type width          C99 6.5.7p3
>     width == 31   ->  1 << 31   2^31 not representable in `int`    C99 6.5.7p4  <-- MISSED
>
> `UBFX rd, rn, #0, #31` needs only `widthm1 == 30`, so this is the common case rather than the
> corner one.  **This also kills the "if the encoding is UNPREDICTABLE the disposition changes"
> escape hatch**, because width 31 is legal beyond argument.
>
> #### *** BUT UB AND WRONG-ANSWER ARE DIFFERENT CLAIMS, AND ONLY ONE WIDTH IS OBSERVABLY BROKEN.
> #### Derived by walking the values rather than by accepting the seats' framing. ***
>
> Three seats said the defect is "two widths wide".  That is right about the LANGUAGE and needs a
> qualifier about the SYMPTOM.  With `r1 = 0x89abcdef`:
>
>     width  correct       likely today  observable?
>     32     0x89abcdef    0x00000000    YES -- the whole register becomes zero
>     31     0x09abcdef    0x09abcdef    no  -- same answer
>      8     0x000000de    0x000000de    no
>      1     0x00000001    0x00000001    no
>
> **At width 31 the expression is undefined TWICE and wraps back to the right answer:** `1 << 31`
> yields `INT_MIN` on the common lowering, and `INT_MIN - 1` wraps to `INT_MAX` = `0x7fffffff` --
> which is exactly the correct mask for a 31-bit field.  At width 32 the count-UB gives `1`, the
> mask becomes `0`, and the instruction returns zero instead of the register.
>
> **THIS IS A PREDICTION ABOUT A LOWERING, NOT A MEASUREMENT**, and it is labelled so for the same
> reason grok labelled its own: grok set out to measure the host lowering and reported plainly
> that it did not finish.  *Nothing here rests on it -- the fix is required by the language
> regardless, and a future compiler is free to exploit either UB.*  What it changes is the
> ROUND'S SEVERITY SENTENCE, which must not say "broken at 31 and 32", and the WITNESS, whose
> single red row is width 32.
>
> *** AND IT MAKES THE SMALL-NONZERO ROW LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN PRUDENT. ***  The width-32
> symptom is **exactly zero** -- indistinguishable from an instruction word that never executed.
> `UBFX r0, r1, #4, #8` on that value gives **0xde**: a small nonzero answer that only a correctly
> encoded, correctly executed instruction can produce.
>
> **The encodings derive from the decoder rather than from memory**, and self-check against its
> own mask `(iword & 0x0fe00070) == 0x07e00050`:
>
>     UBFX r0,r1,#0,#32  -> 0xe7ff0051      UBFX r0,r1,#4,#8  -> 0xe7e70251
>     UBFX r0,r1,#0,#31  -> 0xe7fe0051      UBFX r0,r1,#0,#1  -> 0xe7e00051
>
> Field positions read out of `X(to_be_translated)`: `rd = (iword>>12)&15`, **the source is `rm` =
> `iword & 15`, NOT `rn`** -- `rn`'s bits 19:16 are occupied by `widthm1`, which is why the ubfx
> block takes `rm`.  *Getting that backwards is precisely the hand-assembled-encoding trap.*
>
> **2. THE `(uint32_t)` CAST IN THE m88k TEMPLATE IS LOAD-BEARING, and this entry's source brief
> said the opposite.**  It stated *"the guard is what avoids the undefined shift, not the cast"*.
> Half wrong: the GUARD defends `w == 0` (which m88k spells as 32); **the CAST is the only thing
> defending `w == 31`.**  Three seats corrected it.  So `1U` in the repair above is required, not
> style.
>
> **3. *** THERE IS A FOURTH SITE, AND THIS ENTRY CITED IT AS THE CONTRAST CASE -- THE ONE THAT IS
> CORRECT. ***  Raised by minimax, which asked the question the brief did not: *"BFI's 'correct'
> claim is decoder-only -- the handler could plausibly hit the same class."*  Verified by opening
> the file:
>
>     cpu_arm_instr.c:1370   X(bfi)   uint32_t mask = (1 << width) - 1;
>                                     int width = msb - lsb + 1;   msb,lsb in {0..31}
>
> **`msb = 31, lsb = 0` gives width 32; `msb = 30, lsb = 0` gives 31.**  BFI has the identical
> defect at both widths.  The DECODER is genuinely different (it packs `msb`, not a width) and
> that is all the brief actually checked -- *a contrast drawn at the decoder and asserted about
> the handler.*
>
> **AND TWO MORE OF THE SAME CLASS IN THE SAME FILE**, found by grepping `1 <<` rather than by
> reasoning:
>
>     cpu_arm_instr.c:2685   is_userpage[index >> 5] & (1 << (index & 31))
>     cpu_arm_instr.c:2823   is_userpage[index >> 5] & (1 << (index & 31))
>
> `index & 31` reaches 31, so both evaluate `1 << 31` on a signed `int`.  *The file's author knew
> the idiom somewhere -- `:2216` writes `(uint32_t)1 << 27`.*
>
> #### *** AND BFI HAS A **THIRD** UB REGION THAT NO SEAT NAMED AND I DID NOT EXPECT: A NEGATIVE
> #### SHIFT COUNT.  Found by WRITING THE ENUMERATION the brief's own opener demands, in order to
> #### check the width-31 claim -- it returned a domain I had not considered. ***
>
> `msb` and `lsb` are INDEPENDENT five-bit fields, so `width = msb - lsb + 1` is not confined to
> the positives at all.  Walked rather than reasoned:
>
>     ubfx/sbfx  width = 1 + ((iword>>16)&31)        domain   1 .. 32
>     bfi        width = msb - lsb + 1               domain -30 .. 32
>
> **Every `msb < lsb` encoding gives a negative width, and `1 << negative` is undefined by the
> same clause as the count-too-large case (C99 6.5.7p3).**
>
> *** THE COUNT WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED, 2026-09-07, BY THE PASS-2 glm SEAT, WHICH ENUMERATED IT FROM THE BRIEF'S OWN WIDTH FORMULA. ***  This said "496 of the 1024 (msb, lsb) pairs".  Walked:
>
>     width  < 0   465      width == 0   31      width <= 0   496      msb < lsb   496
>
> **496 is the `msb < lsb` population, not the negative-shift one.**  465 pairs give a strictly NEGATIVE count; the other 31 give width exactly 0, where `1 << 0` is DEFINED and the mask becomes 0 -- semantically wrong, not undefined.  *Still nearly half the encoding space, and still against the two single values that are UB in ubfx/sbfx -- the conclusion is unchanged and the number was wrong.*
>
> ARM specifies `msb >= lsb` for BFI and calls the rest UNPREDICTABLE, **and that is the point
> rather than an excuse: an UNPREDICTABLE GUEST ENCODING MUST NOT PRODUCE UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR IN
> THE HOST.**  The emulator has to do something defined -- decline, take the Undefined Instruction
> exception (this file already routes unknown encodings there, `#312`), or compute a defined
> result.  It currently shifts by a negative amount.
>
> *This is the enumerate-do-not-reason instruction firing on its author.  I wrote the walk to
> confirm a claim three seats had already made; it returned a region none of us had named.*
>
> **SO THE SITE COUNT IS SIX, NOT TWO**: `ubfx:1316`, `sbfx:1340`, `sbfx:1344` (`topBitMask`),
> `bfi:1370`, and the two `is_userpage` tests.  Whether they belong in one round or two is a scope
> question for the design pass; the bit-field three are one semantic class, the `is_userpage` pair
> is another.

**AND A LIMIT ON WHAT CAN BE CITED: THE ARCHITECTURAL LEGALITY OF `widthm1 == 31` IS NOT SETTLED
BY ANY LOCAL SOURCE.**  Derived, not assumed: `grep -ci 'ubfx|sbfx' _scratchpad/ddi0100i.txt`
returns **0** -- DDI 0100I is ARMv5 and these are ARMv6T2 instructions.  deepseek flagged exactly
this as not-checkable-from-the-packet and it is right.  **Per the standing rule (cite only what
you have READ in these files), no page number may be cited for this**, and a round resting on the
`lsb + width <= 32` constraint must either obtain a v7 manual or state the premise as unverified.
*The `width == 31` case above makes this much less load-bearing than it was, which is the main
practical consequence of finding it.*

**Witness vehicle: NOT the existing gate, but the capability is ESTABLISHED and the exemplar is
in-tree.**  Measured: `grep -rn -i 'ubfx|sbfx' regress/` matches in exactly two files and **both
are a codex log's own quotation of the source**, not a probe row.  `gate_arm.sh`'s 358 real-decode
checks do not reach these handlers, so this round owes a NEW witness. *An absence like that is
worth as much as the defect: it says how the defect survived.*

> #### *** BUT "no ARM example exists" WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG, AND I CHECKED BEFORE ASSUMING IT.
> #### Every ARM probe in `regress/` plants and executes instruction words. ***
>
>     arm_flags_probe.py        put_w=68  pc==11  step=5     <- the exemplar
>     arm_writeback_probe.py    put_w=21  pc==2
>     arm_endian_probe.py       put_w=11  pc==1   step=1
>     arm_memcpy / strlen / idle / fold_marker / footbridge_sites   put_w=3..5 each
>
> `arm_flags_probe.py`'s `run_flags(iw, rn, rm, cin)` takes **an arbitrary instruction word**: it
> execs `-V -A -E testarm -M 64`, plants a preamble, then `iw`, then `MRS`/`STR` to capture the
> result, sets `pc` and `step 5`, and reads the answer back from a known address.  **A ubfx/sbfx
> witness is that function with a different `iw` and a register-value capture instead of a flags
> capture.**  grok's "rung-3 is achievable" is therefore confirmed by construction, not by opinion.
>
> *** AND THE ONE HAZARD THAT COMES WITH IT, from this project's own scar: THE CONSTANTS ARE
> HAND-ASSEMBLED HEX. ***  `SUBS_R6_R6_R7 = 0xe0566007`, `MRS_R3_CPSR`, `STR_R3_R4` -- every one a
> literal.  The hand-assembled-encoding trap has bitten four times here, once in a COMMITTED gate
> row that measured the wrong register for months, and its signature is always the same: **a wrong
> register field yields 0, and a row that accepts 0 as a legitimate answer passes by accident.**
>
> **So the witness owes a row expecting a SMALL NONZERO value**, e.g. `UBFX` of a middle field
> whose correct answer is neither 0 nor 0xffffffff.  Without it, the `width == 32` case -- whose
> predicted broken answer is **exactly 0** -- would be indistinguishable from a mis-encoded
> instruction word that never executed.  *That is the single most likely way this round produces a
> confident wrong result, and it is designed out before the first line is written.*

### `dec21143deadclamp` (low) -- filed 2026-09-07: three unreachable size guards and one always-true test

Same hunt. Static, source-derived, **not measured** -- and the seat was explicit that this was
static analysis with nothing executed.

In `dev_dec21143.c`, `dec21143_tx()` computes

    buf1_size = tdes1 & TDCTL_SIZE1;                       /* mask 0x000007ff */
    buf2_size = (tdes1 & TDCTL_SIZE2) >> TDCTL_SIZE2_SHIFT; /* mask 0x003ff800, shift 11 */
    bufsize   = buf1_size ? buf1_size : buf2_size;

Both masks (from `tulipreg.h`) bound their fields to **0..2047**, so `bufsize` cannot leave that
range. That makes three guards dead: `bufsize < 0` at **:752** and **:784**, and
`bufsize > 65536` at **:754**. Their clamp assignments have no current effect.

**The neighbouring comparison at :786 is NOT dead** -- `bufsize > 65536 - d->cur_tx_buf_len`
involves the accumulated length -- and the seat drew that line itself rather than sweeping the
whole neighbourhood into the finding.

Separately, `dec21143_rx()` initialises `writeback_len = 4` at **:353** with no later assignment,
so `writeback_len > 1` at **:468** is always true. The transfer length is
`sizeof(uint32_t) * writeback_len`, which is unit-consistent -- **this is redundancy, not a
format-selection error**, and is recorded as such rather than as a defect.

*Disposition: documented-only unless someone shows a path that widens `bufsize`. A dead clamp is
not a live defect; it is a place where a future widening of the field would silently lose its
guard, which is why it is written down rather than deleted.*

**The hunt's own denominator, because a search without one is not checkable:** 224 C/header files
screened (122 `devices/`, 102 `cpus/`, including 50 generated), 60 shortlisted expression sites
traced across 18 files. **No additional bits-vs-bytes sibling was confirmed** -- and two close
candidates were positively CLEARED by derivation rather than left ambiguous:
`dev_sgi_gbe.c:171` (`bitdepth / 8` gives {1,2,4,8}, both `== 1` and `== 2` reachable) and
`dev_px.c:145` (`bitdepth >> 3` gives {1,3}, both branches reachable). So `#509`'s comparison
appears to be an isolated slip, which is a more useful result than a padded list.


### `armbfxwidth32` PASS-1 PANEL, 2026-09-07 -- SIX SEATS, CONVERGED, AND THE ROUND IS READY

Panel `_scratchpad/panel_20260907_174941`. **Seven transports fired, six answered.** kimi CLI
WALLED (403 weekly) and its seat COVERED by the `kimi-k3:cloud` substitute; agy deliberately not
fired (measurement reserve); Opus 5 and Fable 5 deliberately not fired (held for 2026-09-09).

**WHAT ALL SIX AGREE ON:**

* `1 << width` is UB at **BOTH** 32 (C99 6.5.7p3, count >= type width) **and 31** (6.5.7p4,
  `2^31` unrepresentable in `int`). **The 31 case is the common one** and it removes the
  "maybe the encoding is UNPREDICTABLE" escape entirely.
* **`1U` is MANDATORY, not style.** The brief said the m88k guard rather than its cast is what
  avoids the UB; three seats corrected that -- the guard defends `w == 0`, the CAST defends
  `w == 31`.
* **SITE 3 (`topBitMask = 1 << (width-1)`) is a second live UB**, and the `width < 32` test that
  would moot it sits on the NEXT line.
* **F3 (reject at decode) and F4 (document only) are OUT** -- the encoding is defined.
* **F1 with `1U`, or F2 (`(uint32_t)((1ULL << width) - 1)`), are both correct.** glm checked F2
  explicitly: `1ULL << 32` is representable in `unsigned long long`, and `- 1` then truncates to
  `0xffffffff` on the cast.

**AND grok INDEPENDENTLY REACHED THE BFI FINDING FROM THE SOURCE**, having read the handlers, the

> #### *** AND THE REFUSAL SHAPE IS A `§C5` FINDING: ASKING FOR A RANKING BY EXPLOITABILITY IS
> #### CONSTRUCTION FRAMING, EVEN WHEN THE TASK IS A CENSUS. ***
>
> `BRIEF_TEMPLATE.md` §C5 records three codex triggers: vocabulary, unscoped archive reading, and

### `armbfxwidth32` — THE WITNESS MACHINERY, ANSWERED FROM SOURCE 2026-09-07

A codex capability pass (framed as *what exists*, not *build me one* — the §C5 discriminator) read
**all eight** ARM probe files and the debugger/CPU machinery. Verdict: **YES, the capability
exists**; seven of the eight plant executable words with `put w`, and the eighth
(`arm_idle_probe.py`) loads a raw file and uses `put w` only for seed DATA.

*My own grep had counted `put w` in all eight and would have called all eight code-planters. The
count was right and the reading would have been wrong — the seat distinguished code from data.*

**FIVE FACTS THAT CHANGE HOW THE PROBE MUST BE WRITTEN, each with its source:**

1. *** `r10`–`r15` ARE NOT REGISTERED DEBUGGER NAMES. *** `arm_cpu_new()` exposes `r0`–`r9`, then
   **`sl`, `fp`, `ip`, `sp`, `lr`**, plus `pc` and `cpsr` (`ARM_REG_NAMES`, `cpu_arm.h`). A row
   doing `print r10` does not read a register — it fails a lookup. **This is the padded-column
   trap's cousin: the probe would report `absent` and a negate-style row would score it green.**
2. *** A DIRECT `cpsr` PRINT CAN SHOW STALE NZCV. *** The settings access does not synchronise the
   separate execution-flags field; only `arm_cpu_register_dump()` and the architectural status-read
   handler do. **Any flags-based row must read flags the way the architecture does, not with
   `print cpsr`.** Not needed for `ubfx` (it writes a GPR), but it would have bitten a sibling round.
3. **No guest cache maintenance is required.** `put w` → `store_32bit_word()` → the CPU memory
   function calls `invalidate_code_translation()`, and ARM's invalidator resets the **entire 4 KiB
   instruction page** (translated PC-relative loads can hold cached literals). Interactive debugger
   entry also resets code and address-translation caches.
4. **Byte order differs between the two candidate machines.** `testarm` keeps the constructor's
   **little-endian**; `barearm` sets **big-endian** and adds a 128 MiB mirror at `0xa0000000`.
   Both default to SA1110, supervisor mode, **MMU disabled**, so `arm_translate_v2p()` treats
   virtual as physical. Base RAM is `[0, R)`; both harnesses request `-M 64`, i.e.
   `0x00000000–0x03ffffff`. **`put w` writes through `cpu->byte_order`, so one literal word works
   on either** — but a probe that also plants DATA must know which machine it is on.
5. **The top of RAM is occupied and it is not only the halt stub.** `testarm` writes a 12-byte halt
   stub at `LR = SP+32` with `SP = R−4096`, and — the part I would not have guessed —
   **`arm_cpu_new()` writes a PROM hook at `R−8`** when PROM emulation is on, *before* `barearm`
   changes byte order. Plant low.

**AND THE FAILURE SIGNATURE OF A MIS-ENCODED WORD IS BENIGN AND DETECTABLE**, which matters
because this round's real symptom is *exactly zero*: a word the decoder cannot translate reaches
the shared `bad` label, which reports, sets `cpu->running = 0` and redirects to `nothing_call`.
**It stops the virtual CPU; it does not exit the host.** So a bad encoding shows as *the machine
stopped*, distinguishable from *the instruction ran and returned 0*.

> **BUT NOT EVERY STRAY ENCODING IS SAFE:** `arm_coproc_15()`, `arm_coproc_i80321_6()` and
> `arm_coproc_xscale_14()` still call `exit(1)` on unsupported operations. **A probe must not emit
> coprocessor encodings by accident** — which is a live risk when hand-assembling, since a wrong
> bit can turn a data-processing word into a CP one.

*** AND THE TECHNIQUE WORTH STEALING, FOUND IN THIS TREE: `footbridge_sites_probe.py`'s `run_arm()`
CHECKS THE EXECUTION DISASSEMBLY AGAINST THE PLANTED WORDS. *** That is a *direct* defence against
the hand-assembled-encoding trap — it verifies the word decoded as intended — where my planned
small-nonzero row is only an indirect one. **Use both:** the disassembly check proves the right
instruction ran, and the `0xde` row proves it computed something only a correct execution produces.

*Denominator: eight ARM probe files opened, plus `debugger_cmds.c`, `debugger.c`, `core/memory.c`,
`memory_rw.c`, `cpu_dyntrans.c`, `cpu_arm.c`, `cpu_arm_instr.c`, `cpu_arm_coproc.c`,
`memory_arm.c`, `machine_test.c`, `core/emul.c`, `dev_ram.c`. No probe executed. It also flagged
honestly that `_scratchpad/gxprobe.py` was OUTSIDE the reading scope I set, so it could not
classify it — the scoping rule cutting against me, correctly reported rather than guessed around.*


### `mtesrcdup` (low) -- filed 2026-09-07: one source-TLB expression computed twice under two names

*Filed in the ledger during `#509` and NOT here, which section P caught: an open row that exists
only in the ledger is invisible to anyone reading the queue.*

`do_mte_transfer()` computes the same expression twice:

    :1312  int src     = (mode & MTE_MODE_SRC_BUF_MASK) >> MTE_SRC_TLB_SHIFT;
    :1333  int src_tlb = (mode & MTE_MODE_SRC_BUF_MASK) >> MTE_SRC_TLB_SHIFT;

**Byte-identical.** `src` guards `:1336 if (src > MTE_TLB_C)`; `src_tlb` builds `src_mode` at
`:1365`. They cannot disagree today, so **this is not a defect** -- it is recorded because the
two-names-for-one-value shape is exactly what `#508` found in `memory_alpha.c` (`ALPHA_PAGESHIFT`
and a local `pageSizeShift` both meaning 13), where the hazard is a later edit changing one and
not the other.

*The read that found it was checking something else: `:1336` tests `src`, not the `src_tlb`
computed one line above, which LOOKS like a variable mix-up until you find the earlier
declaration. That momentary alarm is the actual cost of the duplication.*

Documented-only unless a round is already editing that function.


### `armbfxwidth32` — THE FIX CHECKED, 2026-09-07: A AND B RATIFIED, AND THE BFI HALF IS A DESIGN
### QUESTION THE FORK DOES NOT SETTLE

A codex pass was given the proposed repair and asked to CHECK it (never to write one — the §C5
discriminator). It examined **6/6 supplied shift sites, both m88k mask examples, and 13
comparable decisions across the tree.**

**RATIFIED:**

* **A** — `uint32_t mask = (width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1);` — is correct for
  every width in `{1..32}`, checked at the boundaries: `1` → `0x1`; `31` → `0x80000000U - 1` =
  `0x7fffffff`, both operations unsigned; `32` selects the constant and **the shift arm is never
  evaluated**. It follows `cpu_m88k_instr.c:529`'s own unsigned-mask/full-width-special-case shape.
* **B** — hoisting `width < 32` above the `topBitMask` shift — preserves the branch condition
  across `{1..32}`; `x` and `width` are ordinary locals with no side effects, so reordering the
  `&&` operands cannot change the truth value. What changes is only that width 32 goes from
  *undefined* to *defined*.
* **A leaves `bfi`'s NEGATIVE width undefined** — confirming the prediction rather than
  contradicting it. `A` fixes the count-too-large case at all three mask sites and does nothing
  for `msb < lsb`.

*** THE OPTION SET WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, WHICH IS WHY THE GREP-THE-FORK STEP KEEPS
EARNING ITS PLACE: ***

**TWO MEMBERS I HAD NOT NAMED, each with an in-tree precedent:**

* **DIAGNOSE AND STOP EMULATION.** Decode rejection alone specifies no guest outcome — during
  execution the translation tail diagnoses and sets `cpu->running = 0`. That is a distinct
  disposition from "decline at decode", which I had listed as one thing.
* **CHOOSE ANOTHER DEFINED RESULT**, and this one has the closest precedent of any candidate:
  `cpu_arm_instr_loadstore.c:204` (`A__NAME__general`) **explicitly accepts aligned-down,
  unrotated data for an UNPREDICTABLE halfword load**, and `memory_arm.c:84` (`arm_check_access`)
  diagnoses an UNPREDICTABLE control-bit combination and returns "no access". *The fork already
  answers "the guest did something unpredictable" by picking a defined answer and saying so.*

*** AND A TRAP IN THE OPTION I FAVOURED, WHICH I WOULD HAVE WALKED INTO: ***

> **`X(und)` at `cpu_arm_instr.c:1020` expects `arg[0]` to contain a PC OFFSET before it calls
> `arm_exception()`. `bfi`'s `arg[0]` is a REGISTER POINTER.** Routing bfi's unchanged call record
> to `arm_instr_und()` would be incorrect — it would hand a pointer to code that reads an offset.

**NOTHING EXAMINED SETTLES BFI's CHOICE UNIQUELY**, and the seat said so rather than picking:
no-op has direct bitfield precedent, conditional UND has explicit ARM decoder precedent, and
**`#312`'s own comment argues AGAINST halting for its case** — so the existing halt paths must not
be read as a consistent policy. *That is a genuine design question and it goes to the flagship
adjudication rather than being settled by whoever writes the diff.*

**AND THE CLASS GREW AGAIN — two new sites, both READING findings, neither measured:**

    cpu_m88k_instr.c:513   m88k_rot     uint32_t mask = (1 << n) - 1;
    cpu_mips_instr.c:1757  MIPS X(ext)  uint32_t x = (rs << (32-lsb-size)) >> (32-lsb-size);

*The seat cited the FUNCTION starts (`:508`, `:1752`); the expressions are at `:513` and `:1757`
and are quoted above from the file. Both re-derived here before filing:*

* **`m88k_rot`** takes `n = reg(ic->arg[2]) & 0x1f` and is guarded by `if (n != 0)`, so
  **`n ∈ {1..31}`** — and at `n == 31`, `1 << 31` overflows a signed `int`. The same UB the
  `#509`-adjacent `sgirebufshiftub` row describes, in the same file as this round's own SAFE
  exemplar.
* **MIPS `X(ext)`** packs `arg[2] = (msbd << 5) + lsb`, so `lsb ∈ {0..31}` and
  `size = msbd + 1 ∈ {1..32}`. **`32 - lsb - size` therefore spans `{-31..31}` and is NEGATIVE
  for a large part of the encoding space.** MIPS requires `lsb + size <= 32` for EXT, so those
  encodings are architecturally invalid — **and the model does not check, which is the same
  unpredictable-guest-encoding-produces-host-UB shape as `bfi`'s negative width.** `rs` is
  `uint32_t`, so there is no signed overflow here; the defect is purely the shift count.

**The m88k one is the sharpest thing in the answer.** `cpu_m88k_instr.c` is the file this round
cites as carrying the fork's SAFE idiom — at `:532` and `:539`. **`:508`, twenty lines above, is
the unsafe form.** One file, one author, two neighbouring functions, opposite outcomes. *A
"the fork already knows how to do this" warrant is weaker than it sounds when the same file
contains both answers.*

**Site count is now EIGHT across three CPUs**, in three UB regions (count ≥ width, `1 << 31`
signed overflow, negative count). `A`+`B` address four; `1U` alone fixes `:2685`/`:2823`; the two
new ones are unexamined by any proposed repair.


### `alphapteprot` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: the Alpha walk ignores every protection bit

**Filed on the retrospective pass-2 seat's own recommendation:** *"No `alphapteprot` queue row
exists today. The disclosure is only the `#508` comment."* A disclosure in a comment is not a
queue row, and a reader working the queue would never find it.

`alpha_translate_v2p()` returns **2** for every successfully walked page. grok traced what that
means downstream: `memory_rw.c` puts `ok - 1` into the fast table and, at `ok == 2` with
`CACHE_DATA`, invalidates code translations — **so every walked page is cached WRITABLE.**

    flags                      never read
    ALPHA_PTE_KR / KW / UR / UW   never tested
    FAULT_ON_READ / WRITE / EXECUTE  never tested

`#508` disclosed all three in its comment and deliberately did not fix them, which was right: a
protection model needs a different oracle — *a write to a KW-clear page that must not store* --
and the reopening rule forbids bolting a second defect onto an offset repair.

*Distinct from [[alphafaultclaim]], which is the FAILED-walk path. This is the SUCCEEDED-walk
path returning a blanket "writable".*


### `gateworktree` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: the pre-commit gate validates the WORKING TREE, not
### what is being committed

**MEASURED, on my own commit.** `2956c7e` committed `regress/sgi_mte_fill_probe.py` and NOT the
`check_probe_wiring.py` MANIFEST entry that classifies it. A fresh clone at that SHA reds with
`UNCLASSIFIED sgi_mte_fill_probe.py`. **`precommit_check.sh` reported `PRECOMMIT_PASS 0 hard`
immediately before that commit**, because the working tree already carried the manifest edit --
it was simply never staged.

    git show HEAD:tools/pipeline/check_probe_wiring.py | grep -c sgi_mte_fill_probe.py   -> 0
    grep -c sgi_mte_fill_probe.py tools/pipeline/check_probe_wiring.py                   -> 1

> **A CHECK THAT VALIDATES A STATE OTHER THAN THE ONE THAT SHIPS CANNOT SEE A STAGING OMISSION.**
> It is not the check-that-cannot-fail shape -- this gate fails all the time and caught eleven
> real things tonight -- it is a check whose SUBJECT is one step to the left of the thing it is
> guarding.

*** AND IT INTERACTS WITH A POLICY THIS PROJECT ALREADY HOLDS, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH A ROW
RATHER THAN A NOTE. *** The carrier forbids `git add -A` and directory-level adds, so every commit
here stages by EXPLICIT PATH. That is strictly safer against INCLUDING the wrong file -- the
failure the rule was written for -- and strictly MORE EXPOSED to OMITTING the right one. **The two
rules pull in opposite directions and only one of them has a checker.**

**The same commit missed two more things, both caught by OTHER sections on the NEXT commit** --
its own pass-2 receipt (section F) and the ledger row naming it (section L). So the gate's
coverage is real; what it cannot do is bind that coverage to the staged set.

**THE CHEAP FIX, and it is not obviously right, which is why this is filed rather than built:**
run the gate against `git stash --keep-index`, or against a temporary checkout of the index. Both
are invasive -- the gate takes ~2 minutes and already stashes nothing, and a gate that manipulates
the working tree can lose uncommitted work if it dies mid-run. **That risk is worse than the
defect**, so the disposition is NOT "wrap it in a stash".

A narrower and safer candidate: **a single existence check comparing the STAGED set against a
short list of paired files** -- a new `regress/*.py` and its MANIFEST entry; a `src/` change and a
CHANGELOG round block. That is the `check_cited_artifacts.py` idiom (existence-only, forward-only
from a cutoff) rather than a re-run of everything.

*Not built here. It changes what every commit must satisfy, which is an owner decision and owes
two negative controls: prove it reds on a probe staged without its manifest entry, and prove it
stays green when both are staged.*

### warrant that has since decayed

`check_bugfile_sync.py` verifies that every OPEN LEDGER ROW is findable here. It does **not**
verify the reverse, and its docstring says why:

> *"The reverse direction is already clean (no OUTSTANDING_BUGS header lacks a ledger row), which

*** THAT SENTENCE IS NOW FALSE. *** Measured 2026-09-07: **190 headings, 398 ledger rows, and 33

> **This is the carrier's own ABSENCE-RECORD-IS-TIME-INDEXED class, applied to a checker rather
> than a mutant:** *an absence record must NAME ITS WARRANT, and any edit touching that warrant
> RE-RUNS THE DEATH MEASUREMENT.* The warrant is named -- honestly, and in exactly the right place
> -- and **nothing re-runs it**, so the check's scope quietly stopped matching its justification.

**WHY IT IS NOT SYMMETRY FOR ITS OWN SAKE.** The checker's own reasoning transfers unchanged:

*** AND THE INSTANCE THAT PROVES THE POINT IS THIS ROW ITSELF. *** I created `bugfilereverse` in

*Not built here: it changes what every commit must satisfy, and owes two negative controls -- red
on a heading with no row, green once the row exists.*


### `ubsanshiftlane` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: a UBSAN differential would pin the shift repairs a
### value probe provably cannot

`#510`'s pass 2 (grok) showed two one-line regressions that re-open real undefined behaviour and
score FULL MARKS on a 12-row guest-value probe:

    `1U' -> `1' in the mask ternary                     re-opens C99 6.5.7p4 at width 31
    restore `topBitMask = 1 << (width-1)' above the if  re-opens the second UB

**Neither is killable by any row, and the reason is structural rather than a gap in the row set:**
both are DEFINEDNESS repairs, and definedness has no guest-visible value on a non-trapping host.
`1 << 31` and `1U << 31` yield the same mask after the `- 1`; and with a correct 32-bit mask
`x |= ~mask` is `x |= 0`, so `s w32` pins the MASK and not `topBitMask`.

**BUT UBSAN IS ALREADY IN THIS TREE**, which I established after writing "unchecked" about it:

    build-asan/Makefile      -fsanitize=address,undefined
    build-asan/src/Makefile  -fsanitize=address,undefined
    regress/gate_asan_sweep.sh   exists

**THE SHAPE, and it is a differential rather than a row:**

    build-asan/gxemul + FIXED source     -> expect NO shift diagnostic
    build-asan/gxemul + `1U'->`1' mutant -> expect "shift exponent" / "left shift of" on stderr

That is the two-direction control this project demands, and it converts a DISCLOSED escape into a
COVERED one for a whole class -- `lcashiftub`, `sgirebufshiftub`, `m88k_rot:513`,
`cpu_mips_instr.c:1757` and the two `is_userpage` sites are all the same species, and all of them
are equally invisible to a value oracle.

**WHY IT IS NOT BOLTED ONTO `#510`:** it is a NEW MEASUREMENT LANE -- a second binary, and a
STDERR oracle instead of a value oracle -- and `#510`'s pass 2 has already run. A lane added after
a pass is a lane nobody reviewed. It owes its own round, its own pass, and two negative controls.

*Cost note, because it is the reason to want this: the shift-UB class now stands at EIGHT sites
across three CPUs, and a value probe can see NONE of them directly. It sees only the consequences
that happen to differ on this host's lowering -- which for width 32 was a wrong register value,
and for width 31 was nothing at all.*


### `ledgersevmissing` (WITHDRAWN 2026-09-07, same day) -- DUPLICATE of `queueunrated`
###
### *** Filed and withdrawn within the hour.  `queueunrated` was already open with the same
### finding, sharper numbers (73 rows UNRATED **and already witnessed**) and a better
### diagnosis -- that a keyword scan over titles is a CORRELATE, since what makes a row high
### is reachability and no keyword tests that.  The one thing this added -- that rows are
### STILL being created without a rating, so the writer-side check must land BEFORE the
### backfill -- is folded into `queueunrated`.  Kept as a heading rather than deleted so the
### record shows the duplicate was made, not that it never existed. ***

FILED 2026-09-07 by the main loop, from a survey run while picking the next round -- NOT from a
seat.  Found by trying to sort the open queue by severity and having the sort DIE on a KeyError.

**THE NUMBERS, DERIVED (re-run the deriver; do not quote these):**

    C:/.../python.exe -c "import json,io; L=json.load(io.open('tools/pipeline/ledger.json',encoding='utf-8'));
      rows=L['rows']; m=[r['id'] for r in rows if 'sev' not in r];
      print(len(rows), len(m), len([i for i in m if next(x for x in rows if x['id']==i)['state'] in ('open','in work')]))"

On the day of filing that printed **410 rows, 261 with no `sev` field at all, 78 of them open or in
work** -- against 62 low + 54 med + 11 high that DO carry one.  So the severity-bearing population
is a MINORITY of the live queue.

**WHY IT MATTERS, and it is not tidiness.**  Every triage this project runs -- "what is the next
round", "what are the critical bugs", the owner's own standing instruction to *prioritise critical
bugs and easy ones* -- is a severity sort.  A row with no `sev` is not sorted LAST; depending on
the tool it is **omitted entirely or crashes the sort**.  Both were observed on the day of filing.
That is the seat-failure-counted-as-agreement shape moved into triage: the row does not appear as
low-priority, it does not appear at all, so nothing ever says it was skipped.

**AND IT IS NOT A UNIFORM LEGACY BLOCK, which is what makes it worth a row rather than a sweep.**
The missing set spans the whole history -- `d1`/`a4`/`n1`..`n6` from the earliest rounds, but also
`wdcdataoutdrain`, `gdromlatchcross`, `divratchetband` and other rows opened in the last fortnight.
So it is not "old rows used an old schema"; **rows are STILL being created without it today**,
which means a one-off backfill fixes the past and not the cause.

The same survey found `witness` missing on a smaller set and `opened` missing on a large one; those
are recorded here but are NOT the same severity, because nothing sorts on them.

**DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED IN THE ROUND THAT FOUND IT.**  Assigning a severity to 78 rows is a
judgment call per row, not a mechanical default -- and defaulting them all to `med` would be worse
than the gap, because it would make 78 unassessed rows indistinguishable from assessed ones.  That
is this project's oldest rule about blanks: an unrun check and an inapplicable one must not render
the same.

**THE SHAPE OF A FIX, for whoever takes it:** (1) a writer-side check, the `check_cited_artifacts`
idiom -- forward-only from a cutoff, so a NEW row without `sev` fails and the 78 legacy ones warn;
(2) the backfill as its own pass, severity by severity, with the unassessable ones marked
explicitly rather than guessed.  (1) before (2), because (1) stops the bleeding and (2) without it
just refills.

*Not escalated to high: no measured decision has yet been lost to it -- the rows I have picked this
week came from OUTSTANDING_BUGS's dated tail and from panel residuals, not from a severity sort.
But that is luck about my habits, not a property of the ledger.*


### `refilingclass` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07: five already-recorded findings re-derived in one
### session, one of them filed as a duplicate row

FILED 2026-09-07 by the main loop, about the main loop.  **FIVE instances in ONE session**, every one
of them work that was already recorded, and I found none of them by checking -- I found them by
accidentally tripping over the record afterwards.

    1  "twelve of sixteen colour encodings reach the random arm"   already in a COMMITTED artifact,
                                                                   regress/artifacts/sgirandomcolour/
                                                                   codex_design_20260907.txt, with a full table
    2  "depth 8 transmits uninitialised stack bytes"               already in codex_pass1_20260907.txt AND
                                                                   already an open row, [[sgirebufuninit]]
    3  "`lin_b diag once' does not assert the (once) marker"       already an open row, [[randompixdiagonce]]
    4  "half the queue carries no severity"                        already an open row, [[queueunrated]] --
                                                                   and I FILED A DUPLICATE, [[ledgersevmissing]],
                                                                   into the ledger AND OUTSTANDING_BUGS before
                                                                   noticing.  Withdrawn same day.
    5  "the GET half consumes more bytes than it reads"            already in [[sgirebufuninit]]'s own note,
                                                                   almost verbatim

**THIS IS THE UNREAD-REVIEW CLASS, BUT NOT THE VERSION THE CARRIER DESCRIBES.**  That class is about
PANEL ANSWERS NOBODY OPENED -- a seat file sitting in a panel dir.  Every instance here is different and
worse: the knowledge was in **committed files** and **open queue rows**, i.e. in the two places this
project treats as its own memory.  Instance 4 is the sharpest, because the duplicate row PASSED THE
PRECOMMIT GATE and would have sat in the queue indefinitely as a second entry for one defect.

**THE COST IS NOT ONLY TIME.**  Instance 1 and 2 consumed a codex invocation on questions a committed
artifact had already answered -- against a standing directive to spend codex on the queue.  And a
duplicate row inflates the backlog the owner is trying to prioritise, which is the opposite of what
[[queueunrated]] is for.

*** WHAT MAKES IT A CLASS RATHER THAN CARELESSNESS: THE INVESTIGATION IS WHAT HIDES THE RECORD. ***
In every instance I reached the finding by READING SOURCE, and a source reading gives no signal that a
row exists.  The record lives under a row id I would only search for if I already suspected the answer.
Instance 3 is the clean demonstration: I derived the `(once)` gap from the probe, wrote it up as new,
and the row `randompixdiagonce` had been filed EARLIER THE SAME DAY under a name I would never have
guessed from the code.

**PROPOSED STRUCTURAL FIX, and it is deliberately two things because they catch different halves:**

* **(a) WRITER-SIDE, mechanical -- a duplicate check on ADDED ledger rows.**  When a commit adds a row,
  compare its title's content words against every open/in-work row's title and REPORT the nearest
  matches for a human to dismiss.  It cannot auto-reject (titles are prose and near-misses are real
  rows), so it warns; the value is that it fires at the moment of filing.  Forward-only from a cutoff,
  the `check_cited_artifacts` idiom.  **Owes two negative controls -- a genuine near-miss pair must NOT
  be reported as a duplicate, and an actual duplicate MUST be -- so it ships as its own harness round,
  not as a rider.**
* **(b) READER-SIDE, a habit with a command -- before investigating a device or a probe, list what is
  already open against that FILE.**  This is the half that would have caught instances 1, 2 and 5,
  which were never going to be caught at filing time because I never filed them.  The command is one
  line and the artifacts directory is the other half of it:

      grep -l "<file>" regress/artifacts/*/*.txt
      python -c "...print rows whose title or note names <file>..."

**HONEST LIMIT: (b) IS PROSE, AND THIS FILE'S OWN FINDING IS THAT PROSE DOES NOT FIRE.**  I am not
claiming it will.  It is recorded because (a) genuinely cannot catch instances 1, 2 and 5 -- there is no
filing event to hook -- and saying "no structure reaches this half" is more useful than pretending a
habit is a control.  If a later session finds a mechanical trigger for the reader side, that supersedes
this.

*Severity med, not high: nothing shipped wrong.  Every instance was caught, four of them within the
hour, and the one that reached the ledger was withdrawn the same day.  The cost is wasted effort and an
inflated backlog, not a defect in the emulator.*


### `lcaconfbus1kill` (high) -- filed 2026-09-07: an ACCEPTED write to LCA_IOC_CONF arms a
### host kill in a different function

FILED 2026-09-07.  Surfaced while verifying a claim in the grok seat's `lcabadval` pass-1 BODY (its
verdict line did not carry it) -- and **verified to be sharper than the seat stated it**, by opening
both functions.

**THE DEFECT: an ACCEPTED write to one register arms a host kill in a DIFFERENT function.**

`DEVICE_ACCESS(lca_ioc)`, `case LCA_IOC_CONF`:

    d->ioc_conf = idata;
    /*  Only bit 0 is implemented so far, the PCI bus 0 vs
        bus non-0 selection bit.  */
    if (idata & ~1) {
            fatal("TODO: Write to unimplemented bit of IOC_CONF: 0x%" PRIx64 "\n", ...);
            exit(1);
    }

**`0x1` PASSES that guard.**  `idata & ~1` is 0, so the write is accepted, stored, and the arm's own
comment describes bit 0 as the implemented selector.

`DEVICE_ACCESS(lca_pci_conf)` then consumes it:

    bus = d->ioc_conf & 1;
    if (bus == 0) {
            for (dev=0; dev<21; dev++)
                    if (tag & (0x800 << dev))
                            break;
            if (dev >= 21) {
                    /*  fatal("[ LCA: No bus 0 device? TODO ]\n");
                    exit(1);  */
                    dev = 0;
            }
    } else {
            fatal("TODO. Non-zero bus.\n");
            exit(1);
    }

So: **guest writes 1 to IOC_CONF (accepted), then performs any PCI configuration-space access, and
the host process exits.**  Two guest accesses, both to registers the model implements, neither of
them rejected.

*** WHY IT IS ITS OWN ROW AND NOT PART OF [[lcabadval]]. ***  Every kill `lcabadval` covers is a
guard REFUSING a value it does not recognise.  **This one fires on a value the guard ACCEPTS**, in a
different function, on a later access.  The acceptance and the kill are separated in both code and
time, which is why a per-arm audit of `lca_ioc` walks straight past it -- as mine did, twice.

*** AND THE SEAT'S FRAMING NEEDED CORRECTING, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING. ***  grok wrote
that this exit becomes *"newly reachable from a CONF extra-bit write that also sets bit 0; today
that write dies in the CONF guard first."*  That is true of an EXTRA-BIT write (e.g. `0x3`), and it
made the kill sound like a CONSEQUENCE of adopting option A.  **It is not: `0x1` alone reaches it
today, with no fix applied.**  A widens which CONF values arrive here; it does not open the door.
The door is open now.  *Checked by reading both arms rather than by accepting the seat's sentence --
which is this project's own rule, and the seat was right about the site while being wrong about the
timing.*

**THE IRONY, and it is a design signal rather than a joke:** the `bus == 0` branch is the file's own
graceful-degradation PRECEDENT -- a commented-out `fatal()`/`exit(1)` with `dev = 0;` substituted --
and [[lcabadval]] cites that very loop as a transferable in-tree warrant.  **The `else` five lines
below it is a bare kill.**  Same function, opposite dispositions, no comment explaining why.

**REACHABILITY, stated honestly rather than assumed.**  Bit 0 is a bus SELECTOR, so a guest reaches
this by selecting a bus the model does not implement and then doing config access -- plausible for
firmware or an OS that probes beyond bus 0, and trivially reachable by a probe.  **Whether any
shipped guest on `alphabook1` actually does it is NOT established here**, and the row does not claim
it.  What is established is that no guard stands between an accepted write and the kill.

**WITNESS: a rung-3 probe is available and most of it already exists.**  `device_add(machine, "lca")`
is `ST_ALPHABOOK1` ONLY (`machine_alpha.c`), and `regress/lca_confwidth_probe.py` ALREADY drives a
guest `stq`/`ldq` at `LCA_IOC_CONF` (`0xfffffc0180000020`, K0SEG | physical) on unmodified
`alphabook1`.  This row needs one more session: `stq 0x1` to CONF, then a PCI config-space access.
**Three traps that probe already paid for:** debugger `dump` skips `DM_DEFAULT` handlers; a debugger
`put d` of a killing value IS a host kill but is NOT a guest instruction, so it does not witness; and
HAE at window offset 0 silently succeeds, so a miss control must not use `LCA_IOC_BASE+0`.

**DISPOSITION, not yet adjudicated:** it is the same de-fatalisation family, but the option set
differs because the kill is not a value refusal -- the honest members here are DECLINE THE CONFIG
ACCESS (return without dispatching, with a latched announce) or IMPLEMENT bus != 0.  **Note the
architecturally correct error path is blocked for the same reason grok gave on the sibling row:
`LCA_IOC_STAT0`/`STAT1` have no case at all and hit the `default:` arm's `exit(1)`, so LCA cannot
report a device error through the register the header designates for it.**

sev HIGH: a guest-drivable host kill, reached by two ordinary accesses with no rejected value
anywhere on the path.


### `lcairqstubkill` (high) -- filed 2026-09-07: the LCA interrupt handlers are
### `fatal()+exit(1)` with no guard, and DEVINIT wires the ISA/IDE bus straight to them

FILED 2026-09-07.  **NOT a new discovery of the SITE** -- [[lcabadval]]'s eleven-kill census already
enumerated `:73` and `:85` and called them *"plausibly the most severe of the eleven"*.  What was
missing is a ROW: the census names them inside a row titled for VALUE GUARDS, which is the census's
own closing lesson (*a row named after one class hides the members of the others*), and
`OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md` mentioned them **zero** times.

**THE SITE, verbatim -- there is no predicate at all:**

    void lca_interrupt_assert(struct interrupt *interrupt)
    {
            fatal("lca_interrupt_assert: TODO\n");
            exit(1);
    }

    void lca_interrupt_deassert(struct interrupt *interrupt)
    {
            fatal("lca_interrupt_deassert: TODO\n");
            exit(1);
    }

*** THE WIRING, DERIVED BY READING `DEVINIT(lca)` -- AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS SEVERE. ***

    memset(&interrupt_template, 0, sizeof(interrupt_template));
    interrupt_template.line = 0;
    interrupt_template.name = interrupt_path;                        /*  "<machine>.lca"  */
    interrupt_template.extra = d;
    interrupt_template.interrupt_assert   = lca_interrupt_assert;
    interrupt_template.interrupt_deassert = lca_interrupt_deassert;
    interrupt_handler_register(&interrupt_template);

    bus_isa_init(devinit->machine, interrupt_path,
        BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1, LCA_ISA_BASE, LCA_ISA_MEMBASE);

**The stubs are registered as the handlers for `<machine>.lca`, and `bus_isa_init` is handed THAT
SAME PATH together with `BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1`.**  So the ISA bus -- both IDE controllers
included -- routes its interrupts into a function whose entire body is `fatal()` + `exit(1)`.  The
file's own comment above the stub says *"Line 0 = ISA interrupt."*

**WHY IT IS PLAUSIBLY THE WORST KILL IN THE FILE.**  Every other terminating call in `dev_lca.c`
needs a guest to write a value the model does not expect.  **This one needs only that an interrupt
is asserted** -- i.e. ordinary disk activity on a machine whose DEVINIT attaches two IDE channels.
No unusual value, no undocumented register, no firmware revision.

*** WHAT IS ESTABLISHED AND WHAT IS NOT -- read this before quoting the row. ***
* **ESTABLISHED, by reading:** the stubs terminate unconditionally; they are registered as the
  interrupt handlers; `bus_isa_init` receives the same interrupt path with both IDE channels.
* **NOT ESTABLISHED:** that any guest actually reaches them.  **No measurement has been made.**  A
  device could conceivably never assert on this path, and `interrupt_handler_register` semantics
  have not been read here.  The row does NOT claim "alphabook1 cannot boot"; it claims the wiring
  is present and the handler is a kill.

**NEXT STEP IS A RUNG-3 ATTEMPT, and the apparatus already exists.**
`regress/lca_confbus_probe.py` (shipped 2026-09-07 for [[lcaconfbus1kill]]) already boots
unmodified `alphabook1` under the debugger with a disk image attached and drives guest `ldq`/`stq`
through real decode.  The question is whether a guest access can make an IDE channel assert while
single-stepping -- **and the carrier's rule cuts against it: a step-based probe sees a SYNCHRONOUS
assert (a device handler reached inside the guest's own store) but NOT one that depends on a
host-timer callback.**  So the honest first question is *what produces the assert*, and if the
answer is `timer_add`, this needs a free-running probe rather than a stepped one.

**DISPOSITION: option-set MEMBER 7 (IMPLEMENT), and the set's other members do not apply.**  There
is no value being refused and nothing to decline, accept, mask or fault -- it is an entire path
stubbed out.  The carrier added member 7 on 2026-09-06 from this very file, using these very
functions as its example.  A cheaper interim is member 3 (decline + LATCHED announce): return
without asserting, announce once, and let the guest see a missing interrupt rather than a dead host
-- **but that trades a host kill for a silently lost interrupt**, which is the readback-lie shape
[[lcabadval]] is currently held on, so it is a design question and not an obvious win.

**TRANSFERABLE PRECEDENT, already closed in this tree:** [[lunaabsentcpu]] -- *"dev_luna88k.c
reassert_interrupts() calls the NULL interrupt callback of an UNCONFIGURED cpu slot"* -- same family
(a terminating/absent interrupt callback reached by ordinary operation), fixed, and closed with a
rung-3 probe witness (`regress/luna_absentcpu_probe.py`).  Read that round before designing this one.

sev HIGH on the wiring; it would be CRITICAL if a witness lands, and the row says so rather than
pre-judging it.


### `uninorthdevscan` (med, pending a reachability answer) -- filed 2026-09-07:
### a sign-extended mask can select the wrong PCI device on macppc

FILED 2026-09-07, split out of [[shiftubcensus]] item (A) because it is the only member of that
census with a **GUEST-VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE** rather than a language-level one, and it therefore owes a
witness the others do not.

**THE SITE**, `dev_uninorth.c`, in the PCI address-register write path:

    :56    uint64_t idata = memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len | MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN);
    ...
    :60    d->cur_addr = idata;
    :70    for (dev=11; dev<32; dev++)
    :71        if (idata & (1 << dev))
    :72            break;

**`idata` is `uint64_t` and `1 << dev` is an `int`.**  At `dev == 31` that is `0x80000000`, which as
a signed `int` is NEGATIVE, so converting it for the `&` against a `uint64_t` **SIGN-EXTENDS it to
`0xffffffff80000000`**.

> **CONSEQUENCE IF `idata` CARRIES ANY BIT IN 32..63: the loop matches at `dev == 31` when no
> device bit is set there, and the scan selects the WRONG DEVICE.**  The repair (`1U << dev`) is
> therefore NOT behaviour-preserving here -- unlike its sibling in `dev_v3.c`, where the operand's
> high bits are provably zero and the same edit changes nothing.

**REACHABLE AS A DEVICE:** `machine_macppc.c:68` calls
`dev_uninorth_init(machine, machine->memory, 0xe2000000, ...)`, and `dev_uninorth.c:141` registers
`"uninorth_pci_addr"` at `addr + 0x800000` = **0xe2800000**.  macppc is a supported machine here.

*** WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE QUESTION: CAN `idata` ACTUALLY CARRY BITS 32..63? ***
`memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len | MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN)` returns a value whose width follows the
ACCESS WIDTH.  On a 4-byte store -- the ordinary way a guest writes a PCI config address -- the
result cannot exceed 32 bits, the sign-extended ones meet only zeros, and **nothing observable
happens**.  The defect needs an **8-byte** access to that register.

**So the row is HELD at the reachability question, not at the arithmetic.**  A codex analysis is out
on exactly this (`regress/artifacts/shiftubcensus/UNINORTH_brief.md`), asking: what does
`memory_readmax64` return per width; what widths reach this handler on macppc; and -- the premise I
am least sure of -- whether `MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, which is OR'd into the `len` PARAMETER, can
perturb the length itself rather than only the byte order.

**SEVERITY DELIBERATELY LEFT AT `med` PENDING THAT ANSWER.**  If an 8-byte access reaches the
handler this is a guest-drivable mis-decode on a supported machine and should be HIGH; if it cannot,
this collapses into the same language-level hygiene as the other two census members and should be
LOW.  *Grading it before the answer would be picking the number I prefer.*

**THE REPAIR IS ONE TOKEN EITHER WAY** (`1U << dev`), and it is correct under both outcomes -- the
question is only what the round may CLAIM, and whether it owes a witness.


### `guestsrcunknown` (low) -- filed 2026-09-07: a contemporary guest OS source tree
### sits at the project root and nothing in the carrier mentions it

FILED 2026-09-07.  **NOT a defect -- a RESOURCE this project has and does not know it has**, filed
because I declared a hardware question unanswerable from this machine one paragraph before a seat
answered it from a file on disk.

*** `_guest-src-openbsd22/` SITS AT THE PROJECT ROOT AND CONTAINS THE ACTUAL GUEST OS SOURCE. ***
Derived rather than transcribed:

    8,138  .c files
    architectures: alpha  amiga  arc  arm32  atari  hp300  i386  kbus  m68k  mac68k  mvme68k
                   mvme88k  pc532  pmax  powerpc  sparc  sun3  vax  wgrisc

**Six of those are this fork's own emulation targets** -- `alpha` (alphabook1), `arc`, `arm32`,
`mvme88k` (the m88k/luna family), `pmax` (DECstation) and `powerpc` (macppc).  It is OpenBSD 2.2,
dated 1997, i.e. CONTEMPORARY with the hardware these device models emulate.

**IT IS NOT IN THE REPO.**  It lives at the project root, outside `GXEMUL-SEC/`, untracked -- which
is why nothing in the carrier or the harness mentions it and why a fresh session has no way to learn
it exists.

*** THE MEASURED PAYOFF, on the day it was noticed. ***  Working `lcaconfbus1kill`, I wrote into the
ledger that whether `ioc_conf & 1` is a bus selector or a cycle type is *"a statement about the
21066 ... not CHECKED here"*, because `_scratchpad/` holds no LCA datasheet.  The codex seat then
cited `_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/alpha/pci/lca_pci.c`, and reading it settled the question
outright:

    :103   *bp = (tag >> 16) & 0xff;      /*  bus      */
    :106   *dp = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f;      /*  device   */
    :127   if (secondary) { ... REGVAL(LCA_IOC_CONF) = 0x01; ... }

That is the fix's decode verbatim, plus proof that the register selects the configuration FORMAT.
**And it converted the row's own caution -- "NOT CLAIMED: that any shipped guest issues this
sequence" -- into the opposite finding: the sequence IS the driver's secondary-bus path.**

> **WHY THIS BEATS A DATASHEET FOR THIS PROJECT'S QUESTIONS.**  The recurring question here is not
> *what does the hardware do* but *what does a guest actually do* -- is a path travelled, is a
> register written, does a driver depend on this behaviour.  The witness ladder itself ranks a boot
> above a probe for exactly that reason ("a probe proves a path CAN be reached; a boot proves it IS
> travelled").  **A contemporary driver for the emulated chipset answers that class directly, and it
> is greppable in seconds.**

**PROPOSED, NOT DONE: a carrier line.**  `CLAUDE.md` tells a reader to `ls _scratchpad/*.pdf` before
reasoning from first principles about a device, and records that an absent-source note was
load-bearing and wrong for twelve days.  **This is the same shape one directory over**, and the
analogous line would be: *before calling a guest-behaviour or chipset question unanswerable, grep
`_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/<arch>/`.*  Editing the carrier is an owner-facing act and section J
checks its tracked copy, so it is **filed as a candidate for the 2026-09-09 adjudication** rather
than done unilaterally.

**A CAUTION THAT BELONGS WITH IT:** OpenBSD 2.2 is ONE guest at ONE version.  What it does is
evidence that a real driver does it; what it does NOT do is not evidence that no guest does.  And
the fork's models are not obliged to match this driver -- they are obliged to match the HARDWARE, of
which this is a well-informed second-hand reading.  *Cite it as "the OpenBSD 2.2 driver does X", never
as "the hardware does X".*


### `armbfiwidth` (med) -- filed 2026-09-07

cpu_arm_instr.c X(bfi): `(1 << width) - 1' where width = msb - lsb + 1 ranges [-30,32] -- 468 of 1024 encodable (msb,lsb) pairs reach an undefined shift on a 32-bit-int host (a DIFFERENT 496 have architecturally invalid field ordering).  #510 fixed the SAME expression at UBFX and SBFX and left this third site fifty lines below, and its `== 32' form covers none of the negative widths

FILED 2026-09-07.  **`#510` fixed TWO of THREE sites of one idiom and left the third, whose undefined
domain is WIDER than either it repaired.**  Found by reading an UNREAD codex answer
(`regress/artifacts/queueunrated/codex_bitsbytes_20260907.txt`) that had been sitting on disk,
cited nowhere.  Every element below was VERIFIED by opening the file, not taken from the seat.

*** THE DEFECT. ***  `src/cpus/cpu_arm_instr.c`, `X(bfi)` (Bit-Field Insert):

    int lsb = (uint8_t)ic->arg[2];
    int msb = ic->arg[2] >> 16;
    int width = msb - lsb + 1;
    x <<= lsb;
    uint32_t mask = (1 << width) - 1;        <-- UNDEFINED over most of its domain

**THE DECODE GIVES msb AND lsb INDEPENDENTLY, each 0..31** (verified at the `bfi` arm of the
decoder, `(iword & 0x0fe00070) == 0x07c00010`):

    int lsb = (iword >>  7) & 31;
    int msb = (iword >> 16) & 31;
    ic->arg[2] = (msb << 16) + lsb;

so **`width` ranges over [-30, 32]** and `1 << width` is undefined three separate ways:

    width <= 0    negative shift count                       C99 6.5.7p3
    width == 32   count >= width of the promoted type        C99 6.5.7p3
    width == 31   1 is `int'; 2^31 is not representable       C99 6.5.7p4 (signed overflow)

*** THE DENOMINATOR, and it is nearly half. ***  Of the **1024** encodable (msb, lsb) pairs:

    496   nonpositive width  (lsb >= msb + 1)   -- of which 465 are strictly negative
      1   width == 32        (msb=31, lsb=0)
      2   width == 31        (msb=lsb+30)
    ---
    499   of 1024 pairs reach an undefined shift

**That arithmetic was INDEPENDENTLY DERIVED TWICE and the first attempt was mine and wrong.**  A
codex answer on a different brief (`codex_shiftub_20260907.txt`) corrected it: *"`msb - lsb + 1 < 0`
requires `lsb >= msb + 2`, giving 465 negative widths.  Another 31 pairs produce zero; 496 is the
number of nonpositive widths."*  Recomputed here from the decode: pairs with `lsb >= msb+1` sum to
31+30+...+1 = **496**, and `lsb >= msb+2` sums to 30+29+...+1 = **465**.  *The seat was right.*

*** WHY THIS IS A SIBLING MISS AND NOT A NEW CLASS. ***  `#510` repaired the identical expression at
the UBFX and SBFX handlers, which now read:

    uint32_t mask = (width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1);

**`X(bfi)` sits about fifty lines below the second of those, in the same file, and was not touched.**
The carrier's mechanical rule 2 -- *when correcting a claim, grep for its siblings before calling it
fixed* -- is exactly the rule that was missed, and it is recorded there with a prior instance where
an "un-fakeable" claim was corrected in one place and survived in three.  **The BFX round's own
detector cannot see this**: `regress/arm_bfx_width_probe.py` plants UBFX/SBFX words only.

**AND THE BFX FIX DOES NOT TRANSFER UNCHANGED.**  BFX decodes `width = 1 + ((iword >> 16) & 31)`, so
its domain is {1..32} and a `width == 32` special case is sufficient.  **BFI's width can be zero or
negative, which no `== 32` test catches.**  A repair copied from the sibling would close one third of
this site's undefined domain and look right.

*** WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and it is the next step rather than a caveat. ***  **No witness has been
built and no host misbehaviour has been measured.**  UB is not by itself a defect this project ships
a fix for without a measurement -- `#510` shipped on a UBSAN differential (1 diagnostic pre-fix, 0
post-fix) plus a source pin, and this row owes the same.  The vehicle is cheap and already exists:
`arm_bfx_width_probe.py` plants instruction words and executes them on an unmodified machine, so the
witness is a planted `bfi` with `msb < lsb` under a UBSAN build.

**ARM architecturally leaves `msb < lsb` UNPREDICTABLE for BFI**, so a conforming guest does not emit
it.  *That is an argument about which guests reach it, not about whether the emulator may invoke host
UB when one does* -- which is the same argument `#510` made and shipped on.

**PROPOSED FIX (not adjudicated -- no panel has seen this):**

    uint32_t mask = (width <= 0) ? 0 :
        (width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1);

with `mask = 0` for the nonpositive case leaving `rd` unchanged, which is a defensible reading of
UNPREDICTABLE and the only one that inserts no bits.  **The `x <<= lsb` on the line above is SAFE**
(`lsb <= 31` by construction) and must not be "fixed" alongside it.

*** CORRECTED 2026-09-08 BY THE codex SEAT, AND THE ERROR WAS MINE.  Re-verified by brute force
before this edit. ***

**499 WAS WRONG.  THE TRUE FIGURE IS 468, AND I HAD CONFLATED TWO DIFFERENT QUANTITIES.**

    width < 0     465   UNDEFINED -- negative shift count
    width == 0     31   *** DEFINED.  `(1 << 0) - 1' is 0.  A shift count of ZERO is legal. ***
    width 1..30   525   defined
    width == 31     2   UNDEFINED -- signed left-shift result, 6.5.7p4
    width == 32     1   UNDEFINED -- count >= width, 6.5.7p3
    ----
                  468   pairs reaching UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR
                  496   pairs with ARCHITECTURALLY INVALID field ordering (msb < lsb)

**Those are different sets and I summed the wrong one.**  Every nonpositive width is an invalid
BFI encoding, but only the strictly NEGATIVE ones are undefined C.  *Three derivations agreed on 496
earlier -- and 496 was the right answer to a question I was not asking.*

**FOUR MORE CORRECTIONS FROM THE SAME ANSWER:**

* **P4 was partly wrong.**  `ddi0100i.txt` DOES contain zero `BFI`/`BFC` occurrences, but **its own
  architecture list includes ARMv6** (verified: *"ARMv4, ARMv4T, ARMv5T, (ARMv5TExP), ARMv5TE,
  ARMv5TEJ, and ARMv6"*), so calling it "the ARMv5 manual" is inaccurate.  BFI/BFC arrive with
  ARMv6**T2**, which is why they are absent.  And *"the broader claim that no other local reference
  exists remains unestablished."*
* **P5 CONFIRMED from the architecture, externally.**  ARM's BFI A1 description makes
  `msbit < lsbit` UNPREDICTABLE, and its constrained behaviour permits **an undefined instruction, a
  NOP, or an unknown destination value** -- so `mask = 0` is architecturally PERMITTED, not merely
  defensible.  **That settles Q1.**
* **P6 needs a host qualification, and it improves the FIX.**  `1U` is `unsigned int`, which C99
  permits to be 16 bits, so `(1U << width)` is not universally portable either.  codex recommends
  **`1UL` / `0xffffffffUL`**.  *** NOTE THIS MAKES `#510`'s SHIPPED REPAIR SUBOPTIMAL TOO -- it uses
  `1U` -- though harmless on every host this project builds on. ***
* **An early `return` IS sound here**, unlike the case the sketch rule was minted from: codex checked
  the macros -- `X` declares a void function and `Y` generates separate conditional wrappers -- so
  **there is no handler epilogue for a return to skip.**  *The sketch rule says to check the
  enclosing control flow, not that early returns are always wrong; here the check comes back clean.*

*** REACHABILITY IS ESTABLISHED: the BFI decoder branch has NO CPU-model or architecture-version
gate ***, and `machine_test.c` registers `testarm` defaulting to SA1110 -- so the site is reachable
in the simulator even though that CPU model predates the instruction.

**THE WITNESS DESIGN, from Q2, and it kills my one-word plan:**
* negative and excessive counts produce **DIFFERENT UBSan messages** (`shift exponent -1 is
  negative` vs `shift exponent 32 is too large for 32-bit type 'int'`), and width 31 is a *signed
  result* failure that plain shift-exponent checking MISSES;
* **one instruction encoding cannot exercise both count failures** -- the immediate fields fix
  `width`, and no register contents change it.  So the probe needs SEPARATE planted words per class.
* **Two apparatus traps, and the first is the error I made twice this session:** *"`session()`
  consumes child output through its PTY, while callers print parsed results.  Grepping the Python
  process's stderr can miss the sanitizer messages completely."*  And: UBSan suppresses repeat
  reports at an already-reported location, **so diagnostic totals are not execution counts** --
  require the intended site and diagnostic CLASS, not a total.

*Still outstanding before this can land, in codex's own words: "a fresh BFI sanitizer differential
and integration results from binaries tied to this exact tree.  I have not measured those or
established any host-visible wrong BFI result."*


### `armbfcdecode` (low) -- filed 2026-09-08

cpu_arm_instr.c: the bfi decoder accepts source field 15 and passes r[15] to X(bfi), but the architecture assigns that encoding to BFC (Bit Field Clear) -- so BFC is decoded as `BFI with Rn = PC'

FILED 2026-09-08 from the codex `armbfiwidth` design answer.  **BFC is BFI with Rn = 15**, and the architecture defines it as clearing the field rather than inserting from a register.  This fork's decoder does not distinguish them, so a BFC would insert bits taken from `r[15]` -- the PC -- instead of clearing.

**NOT VERIFIED HERE.**  It comes from one seat's source reading, and neither the decoder arm's exact guard nor the architectural claim has been re-derived by me. *The round-scope rule keeps it separate from `armbfiwidth`: same file and adjacent lines, but a different defect with a different fix and a different oracle, so it is a candidate ROUND rather than a rider.*
